teile.einleitung: When you **come of age**, you become an adult in the eyes of the law. In Switzerland you come of age at 18 and may then decide many things for yourself.
wichtigste: In Switzerland you come of age at 18.
Since 1 January 1996 the age has been 18; before that it was 20.
Anyone who is not yet 18 is a minor.
For minors, the parents usually decide important things.
Adults may make contracts themselves.
In Switzerland you may only marry from the age of 18.
“Mündig” is an older German word for having come of age.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss **Civil Code** states that anyone aged 18 is of age. From that birthday on, you may do many things without your parents' permission. But you are then also responsible for your own decisions. The right to vote and stand for election at federal level also begins at 18.

For a long time, people in Switzerland only came of age at 20. On 1 January 1996 the age was lowered to 18. Since then, young adults have been able to decide for themselves much earlier. In the past, instead of “volljährig” (of age), people often said **“mündig”**. The word is still known today, for example in “mündige Bürgerinnen und Bürger”, meaning responsible, grown-up citizens.

Anyone who is not yet 18 is a **minor**. For minors, the parents usually have **parental responsibility**. They decide important things, for example about school or health. In doing so, they should listen to the child's opinion and take it seriously. The older a child is, the more say they have.

Adults may sign **contracts** themselves, for example for a flat or a mobile phone contract. Before that, you often need your parents' consent. From 18 you may also marry. In Switzerland this is not possible any earlier, not even with your parents' permission. But anyone who has come of age is also personally liable if they get into debt.

gewusst: At 18, you may also vote in federal elections and referendums in Switzerland.
Children may already make small everyday purchases with their own pocket money themselves.

teile.einleitung: Intershops were shops in the GDR where you could buy Western goods. However, you did not pay with the GDR mark but with Western money such as the Deutschmark. In this way the state obtained badly needed foreign currency.
wichtigste: The Intershop trading company was founded on 14 December 1962.
The first sales stands were at Friedrichstrasse station in East Berlin.
Payment was made with freely convertible money such as the Deutschmark.
From 1974 GDR citizens were allowed to own Western money legally.
From 1979 GDR citizens had to pay in the Intershop with Forum cheques.
In 1988 there were 416 Intershop shops.

abschnitte.text: In an **Intershop** only **freely convertible money** was accepted, such as the **Deutschmark**, the currency of West Germany. The GDR mark was not accepted. The state needed such money, known as **foreign currency**, to buy goods and machines in the West. From 1985 the Intershops took more than a billion Deutschmarks a year.

The Intershop trading company was founded on **14 December 1962**. The first sales stands were at **Friedrichstrasse station** in East Berlin. This station was a border crossing between East and West. At first it was mainly cigarettes that were sold to travellers from the West.

Until 1974 GDR citizens were forbidden to own Western money. But many received money from relatives in the West. From **1974** owning it was allowed, and they could shop in most Intershops. From April **1979** they first had to exchange their Deutschmarks for **Forum cheques**. Only with these vouchers could they go on shopping in the Intershop.

The Intershop sold goods from the West that were otherwise hardly available in the GDR. These included **chocolate** and other sweets, **cosmetics**, clothes, coffee and electronics. The number of shops grew from 271 in the 1970s to **416** in 1988. They were found in towns, on motorways and at border crossings.

The Intershops caused resentment in the GDR. People with relatives in the West could buy nice things; others could not. This created a kind of two-class society. At the same time the full shelves showed how much there was in the West and how scarce many things were in the GDR.

gewusst: Many people from the GDR still remember the typical smell of soap, coffee and perfume in the Intershops.

teile.einleitung: Civil disobedience means deliberately and publicly breaking a rule in order to protest against an injustice. In doing so, you stay non-violent. Famous examples are Gandhi, Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King.
wichtigste: Civil disobedience is a deliberate, public and non-violent breach of the rules for reasons of conscience.
It often includes being willing to accept the legal consequences.
In 1849 Henry David Thoreau wrote the essay that became famous as “Civil Disobedience”.
In 1930 Gandhi protested against the British salt monopoly with the Salt March.
In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery.
In Switzerland, opponents of nuclear power occupied the site at Kaiseraugst in 1975.

abschnitte.text: In **civil disobedience**, someone deliberately breaks a law or rule to draw attention to an injustice. Three features are important: the action is **public**, **non-violent** and comes from **reasons of conscience**. Often those involved deliberately accept the punishment. In 1971, in “A Theory of Justice”, the philosopher **John Rawls** described this as an unlawful act aimed at changing a law or a policy.

The American writer **Henry David Thoreau** refused to pay taxes. In this way he protested against **slavery** and the war against Mexico, and he spent a night in prison for it. In 1849 his essay was published, originally called “Resistance to Civil Government”. Later it became famous as “Civil Disobedience”. The text influenced Gandhi and Martin Luther King.

In 1930 **Mahatma Gandhi** marched around 385 kilometres to the sea and made salt there. This broke the British salt law, and thousands followed him on the **Salt March**. In 1955 **Rosa Parks** in Montgomery refused to give up her seat on the bus to a white passenger and was arrested. This led to a large bus boycott. In 1963, while in prison, **Martin Luther King** wrote the “Letter from Birmingham Jail”, in which he distinguished just laws from unjust ones.

In 1975, opponents of nuclear power occupied the site at **Kaiseraugst**, where a nuclear power station was planned, for eleven weeks. The plant was never built, and the occupation is regarded as an important event in the anti-nuclear movement. In 2018, climate activists played tennis in a bank branch in **Lausanne**. A district court at first acquitted them, but in 2021 the **Federal Supreme Court** upheld their conviction, because it saw no state of necessity that justified the action.

Whether civil disobedience is right is judged differently. Supporters say it has helped to end great injustices. Critics stress that in a **democracy** everyone should obey the laws. In Switzerland, laws can be changed legally through the **initiative** and the **referendum**. Courts examine each individual case to decide whether an action is punishable.

gewusst: Gandhi's Salt March took him more than three weeks.
Martin Luther King wrote part of his famous letter from prison in the margins of a newspaper.

teile.einleitung: Eurocommunism is the name for a trend among communist parties in Western Europe in the 1970s. These parties wanted to achieve socialism by democratic means and broke away from the example of the Soviet Union.
wichtigste: The most important Eurocommunist parties were the Italian and the Spanish Communist Parties.
Enrico Berlinguer led the Italian Communist Party (PCI) from 1972 to 1984.
After the military coup in Chile in 1973, Berlinguer proposed the “historic compromise” with the Christian Democrats.
In 1976 the PCI achieved its best election result with 34.4 per cent.
The Eurocommunists gave up the dictatorship of the proletariat.
In 1977 Santiago Carrillo wrote the book “Eurocommunism and the State”.

abschnitte.text: For a long time the Soviet Union demanded that all communist parties follow its model. This included the **dictatorship of the proletariat**, meaning the rule of a single party in the name of the workers. The Eurocommunists gave up this idea. They wanted to keep elections, several parties and basic rights. They wanted to achieve socialism through majorities in parliament.

The **Italian Communist Party** was the largest communist party in Western Europe. From 1972 it was led by **Enrico Berlinguer** as general secretary. In 1976 it won 34.4 per cent of the vote and was only just over four percentage points behind the Christian Democrats. In the same year Berlinguer said in an interview that he felt safer under the protection of **NATO**. With this he clearly distanced himself from Moscow.

In 1973 the military in Chile overthrew the elected left-wing government of Salvador Allende. Berlinguer concluded from this that a left-wing government with a narrow majority can fail. He therefore proposed the **historic compromise**, a cooperation between communists and Christian Democrats. His most important partner was the Christian Democrat **Aldo Moro**. In 1978 Moro was kidnapped and killed by the terrorist group the Red Brigades. With that the compromise lost its most important supporter.

Eurocommunism also developed in Spain. **Santiago Carrillo**, general secretary of the Communist Party of Spain, published the book “Eurocommunism and the State” in 1977. In it he explained the break with the Soviet model. The French communists also moved closer to the movement for a time, but stayed closer to Moscow.

On 7 June 1984 Berlinguer suffered a stroke during an election speech in Padua and died a few days later. Hundreds of thousands came to his funeral. After his death Eurocommunism lost momentum. After the end of the communist states in Eastern Europe, the PCI changed its name in 1991 and became a social democratic party.

gewusst: Berlinguer came from Sassari on the island of Sardinia.
In Italian the historic compromise is called “compromesso storico”.

teile.einleitung: The Ampelmännchen, the “little traffic light man”, is the figure on the pedestrian lights of the former GDR (East Germany). With his hat and rounded shape, he is easy to recognise. After the fall of the Berlin Wall he became a popular symbol and souvenir.
wichtigste: The East German Ampelmännchen wears a hat.
The traffic psychologist Karl Peglau designed him in 1961.
In 1969 he lit up at a crossing in East Berlin for the first time.
The red figure stretches his arms out to the sides; the green one walks with big strides.
After 1990 he was to be replaced, but protests saved him.
In 1996 Hans-Jürgen Ellenberger designed a female traffic light figure.

abschnitte.text: In **1961**, the traffic psychologist **Karl Peglau** designed the GDR's Ampelmännchen. He wanted pedestrians to understand the lights **more quickly and safely**. That is why he drew easily recognisable, rounded figures. Children and older people should also recognise them immediately. That way **accidents** were to be avoided.

The East German Ampelmännchen can be recognised by his **hat**. The **red** figure stretches his arms out to the sides, clearly showing “stop”. The **green** figure walks with big strides. This makes him different from the slimmer West German traffic light man. In 1969 the figures were introduced at the crossing of **Unter den Linden** and Friedrichstrasse in East Berlin, and from 1970 they were standard in the GDR.

After German reunification in 1990, the East German Ampelmännchen were to be replaced by West German figures. Many people objected. There were **protests**, and the Ampelmännchen were kept. Today they light up in many East and also West German cities. They are among the few things from the GDR that almost everyone likes.

In **1996**, the graphic designer **Hans-Jürgen Ellenberger** designed a **female traffic light figure** as a counterpart. She has plaits and a skirt and today lights up in some German cities. The Ampelmännchen himself is a popular **souvenir** in Berlin. You find him on mugs, bags and postcards. He is regarded as a **symbol** that has survived from the GDR era.

gewusst: In Berlin there are shops that sell only souvenirs with the Ampelmännchen on them.
The West German traffic light man is slimmer and does not wear a hat.

teile.einleitung: In the USA, the parties choose their candidates for the presidency in **primaries**. These take place in all the states, spread over several months.
wichtigste: In the primaries, the parties choose their candidates for the presidential election.
There are two forms: the primary (a ballot vote) and the caucus (a party meeting).
Iowa traditionally opened the primary season with its caucuses.
By law, New Hampshire holds the first primary.
On Super Tuesday, many states vote at the same time.
The official nomination takes place at the national party convention.

abschnitte.text: In a **primary**, people vote by secret ballot, as in a normal election. In a **caucus**, party members meet at gatherings. There they discuss and often vote openly. In both cases, **delegates** are chosen. These later choose the candidate at the party convention.

In a **closed primary**, only people registered with the party may vote. In an **open primary**, independents or members of other parties can also take part. Each state decides for itself which form applies. That is why the rules differ from state to state.

From 1972, **Iowa** traditionally opened the primary season with its caucuses. The Democrats changed their calendar in 2024, while for the Republicans Iowa stayed first. **New Hampshire** requires by law that its primary takes place before all similar elections. In March comes **Super Tuesday**. On this Tuesday many states vote at the same time, and a large share of the delegates are awarded.

In the summer, the delegates meet at the **National Convention**, the national party conference. There the candidate is officially nominated. The person for the vice-presidency is also confirmed. The Democrats also have **superdelegates**: leading party figures such as members of Congress and governors who are delegates without a primary. Since 2018 they have not been allowed to vote in the first ballot.

gewusst: Small states such as Iowa and New Hampshire get a lot of attention because their contests come so early.
In Switzerland, the parties usually choose their candidates at party meetings, not in primaries open to the whole people.

teile.einleitung: Civil protection protects and looks after the population during disasters and emergencies. It helps, for example, during floods and supports the fire brigade and police. It also includes the sirens, the shelters and the Alertswiss app.
wichtigste: Civil protection protects and looks after the population during disasters.
Civil protection service is done mainly by men who are not fit for the army but are fit for civil protection.
The Confederation's Alertswiss app gives information about dangers and alarms.
Switzerland has more shelter places than inhabitants.
The siren test takes place every year on the first Wednesday in February.
The water alarm warns of a flood wave near reservoirs.

abschnitte.text: **Civil protection** helps when a disaster or emergency happens, for example during **floods**, landslides or major accidents. It looks after people who have had to leave their homes and supports the **fire brigade**, the **police** and the **health service**. Together they form **population protection**. Civil protection is organised mainly by the cantons and municipalities.

At **recruitment**, it is checked whether someone is fit for military service. Anyone who is not fit for the army but is fit for civil protection does **civil protection service**. Women and foreigners can volunteer. In courses, those serving learn, for example, how to look after people, operate equipment or repair damage.

Switzerland has a particularly large number of **shelters**. In principle, every inhabitant should have a place near their home. Many houses have a shelter in the basement, with thick walls and a heavy door. In total there are around 9 million shelter places, which is more than the number of inhabitants (as of 2025). In everyday life, the rooms are often used as cellars or storerooms.

Every year on the **first Wednesday in February**, the sirens all over Switzerland are tested, from 1.30 pm. With the **general alarm**, a steadily rising and falling wailing tone sounds for one minute. If you hear it outside the test, you should **listen to the radio**, check the **Alertswiss** app, follow the authorities' instructions and inform your neighbours. The **water alarm** consists of deep, continuous tones. Anyone who hears it must leave the danger zone below a reservoir immediately.

gewusst: During the siren test in February, thousands of sirens wail at the same time all over Switzerland.
Hardly any other country has as many shelter places in relation to its population as Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Hundred Flowers Campaign was a political campaign in China in 1956 and 1957. The Communist Party under Mao Zedong called on people to criticise openly. Shortly afterwards many critics were harshly punished.
wichtigste: The campaign took place from 1956 to 1957.
The slogan was “Let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend”.
Intellectuals were invited to criticise the party and the administration openly.
The criticism was harsher than expected, and in the summer of 1957 the campaign was stopped.
It was followed by the Anti-Rightist Campaign, in which officially around 550,000 people were labelled “rightists”.

abschnitte.text: In 1956 **Mao Zedong** called for an open discussion. The slogan was: “**Let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend.**” The second part refers to the “**Hundred Schools of Thought**” in ancient China. During the **Warring States** period many schools of thought arose, such as Confucianism, Daoism and Legalism. So what was meant was a contest of opinions.

The party leadership above all invited **intellectuals** to speak openly about problems in the party and administration. Intellectuals are people who work with their knowledge, for example teachers, professors and writers. In the spring of 1957 many expressed their opinions, in newspapers and on wall posters. The criticism was much harsher than the party had expected. In the summer of 1957 the campaign was stopped.

It was immediately followed by the **Anti-Rightist Campaign**. Many critics were now branded as “**rightists**”, that is, as enemies of socialism. According to official figures this affected around 550,000 people; some historians estimate the number to be higher. Many lost their jobs or were sent to labour camps. The campaign was largely organised by **Deng Xiaoping**, who later became a reformer.

After this experience, many people in China did not dare to criticise openly for a long time. It is still debated today whether Mao deliberately wanted to lure the critics out or whether he was surprised by how strong the criticism was. After 1978 most of those affected were **rehabilitated**. This means their condemnation was officially recognised as unjust.

gewusst: Of all people, it was Deng Xiaoping, who led the Anti-Rightist Campaign, who later made sure that many of those affected were rehabilitated.

teile.einleitung: From 1928 the Soviet Union under Stalin built up a large industry in a very short time. The state planned everything, from steelworks to power stations. The successes were great, but millions of people paid for them with hardship and forced labour.
wichtigste: From 1928 five-year plans steered the economy.
In a planned economy the state sets production and prices.
The state planning authority was called Gosplan.
Heavy industry, meaning steel, coal and machines, had priority.
From 1929 Magnitogorsk in the Urals was built around a huge steelworks.
Many major building sites were built by prisoners from the Gulag camps.

abschnitte.text: In a **planned economy** the state decides what is made, how much and at what price. Supply and demand hardly play a role. From 1928 the Soviet Union set its targets in **five-year plans**. The planning authority **Gosplan** calculated what each enterprise had to achieve. The first five-year plan was officially declared fulfilled after just over four years.

Stalin wanted to make the country strong quickly, militarily too. That is why **heavy industry** had priority: steel, coal, machines and weapons. Everyday goods such as clothes, shoes or furniture remained scarce. Many people lived in cramped flats and had to queue for a long time.

From 1929 the town of **Magnitogorsk** was built in the **Urals**. It grew up near Magnetic Mountain, which contained a lot of iron ore, around a huge steelworks. On the **Dnieper** river in Ukraine, the **Dneproges** hydroelectric power station went into operation in 1932; it was one of the largest of its time. Projects like these became symbols of Soviet industrialisation.

In 1935 the miner **Alexei Stakhanov** dug many times the prescribed amount of coal in a single shift. The party made him a role model for all workers. The **Stakhanovite movement**, which was meant to spur workers on to ever new records, was named after him. For many workers, however, this also meant higher quotas.

Many major building sites were built with **forced labour**. The **White Sea-Baltic Canal** was built from 1931 to 1933 almost entirely by prisoners from the **Gulag** camps. Many thousands died from cold, hunger and exhaustion. At the same time the peasants were forced to hand over their farms to collective farms. This led to severe famines in the early 1930s.

gewusst: Magnitogorsk was planned on the model of the steelworks in Gary in the USA, and American firms helped to build it.
In his record shift Stakhanov dug around 102 tonnes of coal, about fourteen times the quota.

teile.einleitung: The Baltic Way was a huge human chain through Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. On 23 August 1989, around two million people joined hands. In this way they peacefully demanded freedom for their countries.
wichtigste: The Baltic Way took place on 23 August 1989.
The chain stretched from Tallinn via Riga to Vilnius.
Around two million people took part.
The chain was about 650 kilometres long.
It commemorated the Hitler-Stalin Pact of 1939.
Since 2009 its documents have been part of UNESCO's Memory of the World.

abschnitte.text: The day was chosen on purpose. Exactly 50 years earlier, on 23 August 1939, Germany and the Soviet Union had signed the **Hitler-Stalin Pact**. In a **secret additional protocol**, the Baltic states were allocated to the Soviet Union. In 1940 Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were occupied. After that they were part of the Soviet Union for almost 50 years.

On the evening of **23 August 1989**, people lined up along the roads. The chain ran from **Tallinn** in Estonia via **Riga** in Latvia to **Vilnius** in Lithuania. It was around **650 kilometres** long. That is much further than from Geneva to Romanshorn. Over two million people took part, a large share of the population at the time.

The Baltic Way was part of the **Singing Revolution**. This is the name for the peaceful freedom movement in the Baltic states. In Estonia in 1988, hundreds of thousands gathered at song festivals and sang banned folk songs. The Baltic Way was organised by popular movements such as the Estonian **Rahvarinne** and the Lithuanian **Sąjūdis**. Sąjūdis was led by the music professor **Vytautas Landsbergis**.

The human chain showed the whole world the three countries' wish for freedom. On **11 March 1990**, Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare its independence. Landsbergis signed the declaration as chairman of parliament. Estonia and Latvia followed in 1991. Today all three countries are independent states.

gewusst: In 2009, UNESCO added the documents on the Baltic Way to its **“Memory of the World”** register.
The popular movements deliberately relied on songs and human chains instead of violence.

teile.einleitung: A ballot paper is a sheet of paper on which, in an election, you tick or write the names of the people you want to vote for. In a vote on an issue, the paper is called a voting slip. Switzerland has especially varied ballot papers, which let you decide very precisely whom you support.
wichtigste: On the ballot paper, you mark the people you want to vote for.
In votes on issues, the paper is called a voting slip.
In the National Council election, each party has its own list ballot paper.
You can cross out names, take names from other lists or write names twice.
The ballot paper goes into the voting envelope so that the vote stays secret.
A paper with identifying marks or insults is invalid.

abschnitte.text: A **ballot paper** is an official form on which you record your choice. In many countries you simply tick a name or a party. In Switzerland you often write names by hand or use pre-printed lists. For a vote on an issue there is the **voting slip**, on which you write yes or no. You receive both papers at home together with the voting documents.

abschnitte.titel: Lists in the National Council election
abschnitte.text: In the National Council election, you get a **list** for each party with its candidates. There is also a blank list with nothing printed on it, on which you can write names yourself. You take exactly one ballot paper and put it in. Each list has a number and a name, for example the name of a party. The number of lines matches the number of seats the canton has in the National Council.

You may cross out names on a pre-printed list. When **splitting your vote** (panaschieren), you add names from other lists. When **cumulating**, you write a name twice so that this person gets two votes. The empty lines on a list count as additional votes for the party whose list you used. That way every voter can have a very personal say.

First you fill in the paper and put it in the small **voting envelope**. Then you sign the **voting card**; without it, your vote does not count. Everything together goes into the big return envelope. You send this back by post or put it in the municipality's letterbox. You can also put the paper in the ballot box at the polling station in person.

A ballot paper must be filled in by hand; typewriters or copies are not allowed. A paper is invalid if it contains insulting remarks or if it could show who filled it in. A **blank ballot paper** is not counted for any person. If you hand in several papers for the same election, all of them are invalid. This is meant to keep the election fair and secret.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ballot paper with the pre-printed names of a party or group.
A small envelope into which you put the completed paper.
A document that shows you are entitled to vote.
An empty line on a list that counts as a vote for the party.

gewusst: In populous cantons such as Zurich, you receive a whole bundle with dozens of different lists for National Council elections.
In some countries, ballot papers are printed with pictures or symbols of the parties so that people who cannot read can also vote.

teile.einleitung: Fidel Castro was a Cuban revolutionary and politician who led the revolution in Cuba in 1959. After that he ruled the Caribbean island as its communist leader for almost 50 years. To some he was a hero who fought against the USA; to others he was a dictator who allowed no freedom.
wichtigste: Fidel Castro lived from 1926 to 2016.
In 1959 he led the revolution in Cuba and overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista.
He ruled Cuba as its communist leader for many decades.
Under him Cuba became an ally of the Soviet Union.
In 1962 Soviet missiles in Cuba led to the dangerous Cuban Missile Crisis.
Education and healthcare became free for everyone, but there were no free elections.
In 2008 he handed power to his brother Raúl Castro.

abschnitte.text: Fidel Castro was born in **1926** in Birán in the east of Cuba, the son of a rich landowner. He went to Jesuit schools and studied law in Havana. He was already very active in politics as a student. At that time Cuba was ruled by the dictator **Fulgencio Batista**, and many people in the countryside were very poor.

On 26 July 1953 Castro and a small group attacked the **Moncada Barracks**, but the attack failed and he went to prison. After his release he went to Mexico, where he met **Che Guevara**. At the end of 1956 they landed in Cuba on the small boat **Granma** and waged a guerrilla war from the mountains of the Sierra Maestra. On 1 January 1959 Batista fled, and the revolutionaries marched into Havana.

Castro nationalised companies and land, including American property. The USA then imposed a **trade embargo**, which still exists today. In 1961 an attack by Cuban exiles supported by the USA failed at the **Bay of Pigs**. In 1962 the Soviet Union stationed nuclear missiles in Cuba, and during the **Cuban Missile Crisis** the world came close to nuclear war.

Castro built up a free school and healthcare system, and almost all Cubans learned to read and write. At the same time only one party was allowed, the **Communist Party of Cuba**. Newspapers were controlled, and critics were sent to prison. Hundreds of thousands of people fled to the USA, especially to Florida.

Castro was prime minister from 1959 to 1976 and then president of Cuba until 2008. Because of a serious illness he handed power to his brother **Raúl Castro**, temporarily in 2006 and for good in **2008**. He died in Havana on 25 November **2016**. Opinions about him still differ greatly today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rapid, often violent overthrow of a government and the order of society.
Small armed groups that fight against an army from hiding places.
A ban on trading with a particular country.
A dangerous dispute between the USA and the Soviet Union in October 1962 over nuclear missiles in Cuba.

gewusst: Fidel Castro sometimes gave speeches that lasted several hours.
From 1961 to 2015 Switzerland represented the interests of the USA in Cuba, because the two countries had no embassies in each other's country.
In public Castro almost always wore an olive-green uniform and a beard.

teile.einleitung: Civil society is the area in which people join together voluntarily, outside the state, the market and the family. It includes clubs, associations, foundations and charities. In Switzerland it plays a large role.
wichtigste: Civil society includes clubs, associations, foundations, citizens' groups and non-governmental organisations.
They act voluntarily and are not mainly seeking profit or state power.
As early as 1835, Alexis de Tocqueville praised the importance of voluntary associations.
In Switzerland, Article 60 of the Civil Code regulates the founding of associations.
Through the consultation procedure, organisations can comment on draft laws.
In 2020 the Responsible Business Initiative was supported by over a hundred organisations.

abschnitte.text: **Civil society** lies between the **state**, the **market** and the **family**. It includes, for example, sports clubs, brass bands, environmental associations, charities and foundations. Many of these groups are also called **non-governmental organisations**, NGOs for short. They act voluntarily and pursue shared aims. Their goal is not mainly profit or power in the state.

The Frenchman **Alexis de Tocqueville** travelled to the USA and in 1835 wrote “Democracy in America”. He observed that people joined together in associations for almost every cause, and saw this as a **school of democracy**. The Italian **Antonio Gramsci** saw civil society as a place where groups compete for consent and **cultural hegemony**. In 2000, in “Bowling Alone”, the American **Robert Putnam** described how people were joining associations less often, and spoke of a decline in **social capital**.

Switzerland has a great many clubs and associations, from gymnastics clubs to yodelling clubs. Founding one is easy: according to **Article 60 of the Civil Code**, an association comes into being as soon as its **statutes** show that it intends to exist as a body. Registration in the commercial register is usually not necessary. Many people do **voluntary work** in clubs and take on roles such as president or treasurer.

Civil society can take part in Swiss politics in several ways. In the **consultation procedure**, cantons, parties, associations and anyone interested may submit their views on federal proposals. Organisations can also collect signatures for **popular initiatives** and **referendums**. One example is the **Responsible Business Initiative**: on 29 November 2020 it won around 50.7 per cent yes, but failed to win the **majority of the cantons**.

gewusst: Putnam chose bowling as his image because, although many people in the USA went bowling, fewer and fewer played in bowling leagues.
A popular initiative can fail despite a majority of the people if not enough cantons agree.

teile.einleitung: John Paul II was Pope from 1978 to 2005 and thus head of the Catholic Church. He came from Poland and his real name was Karol Wojtyła. He played an important part in the end of communism in Eastern Europe.
wichtigste: Karol Wojtyła was born in Wadowice in Poland in 1920.
On 16 October 1978 he was elected Pope.
He was the first Pope in more than 450 years who was not Italian.
In 1979 he visited his home country of Poland for the first time as Pope.
On 13 May 1981 he survived an assassination attempt in St Peter's Square.
He died on 2 April 2005, and in 2014 he was declared a saint.

abschnitte.text: **Karol Wojtyła** was born in **Wadowice** in Poland in 1920. He became a priest and later **Archbishop of Kraków**. On **16 October 1978** the cardinals elected him Pope, and he took the name **John Paul II**. Since 1523 all Popes had been Italian. The fact that a Pole from a communist country was now Pope caused a sensation around the world.

In June **1979** the Pope travelled to Poland for the first time in his new role. Millions of people came to his Masses. At that time Poland was governed by a communist party, which watched the Church with suspicion. The visit gave many Poles new courage. Shortly afterwards the free trade union **Solidarność** was formed, and the Pope supported it.

On **13 May 1981** the attacker Mehmet Ali Ağca shot the Pope in **St Peter's Square** in Rome and seriously injured him. John Paul II survived. Later he visited his attacker in prison and talked with him. Many people saw this as a sign of reconciliation.

In the Vatican he was protected by the **Pontifical Swiss Guard**, which has guarded the Pope since 1506. Its soldiers are young Catholic Swiss men. John Paul II visited Switzerland several times. In June **2004**, already seriously ill, he travelled to **Bern** and met thousands of young people there. It was his last trip to Switzerland.

John Paul II travelled to more than a hundred countries, more than any Pope before him. In 1989 communist rule ended in Poland and other countries of Eastern Europe. Many historians see him as one of those who paved the way for this change. He died in Rome on **2 April 2005**. In **2014** he was **declared a saint**.

gewusst: As a young man Karol Wojtyła acted in the theatre and wrote poems.
At more than 26 years, his time in office is one of the longest of all Popes.

teile.einleitung: In a two-party system, there are two large parties that take turns in government. The best-known examples are the USA and Great Britain. Switzerland, on the other hand, has a multi-party system.
wichtigste: In a two-party system, two large parties shape politics.
In the USA these are the Democrats and the Republicans.
The Republicans' symbol is the elephant, and the Democrats' is the donkey.
In Great Britain, the Conservatives or Labour have provided the prime ministers for around 100 years.
Duverger's law explains why majority voting in single-member constituencies often leads to two parties.
Switzerland has a multi-party system.

abschnitte.text: Since the middle of the 19th century, the **Democrats** or the **Republicans** have provided almost all the presidents and members of Congress in the USA. Their symbols are well known: the Republicans have the **elephant**, the Democrats the **donkey**. The elephant became famous in the 19th century through cartoons by **Thomas Nast**. On election maps, Democratic states are coloured **blue** and Republican ones **red**.

The two big parties choose their presidential candidates in **primaries** in the states. In **primaries** and **caucuses**, voters vote on the contenders. At the **party convention**, the candidate is then officially nominated. There are also smaller **third parties**, such as the Libertarian Party or the Green Party. But because of the electoral system, they hardly win any seats in Congress.

**Great Britain** is also seen as an example of a two-party system. Since the 1920s, the **Conservative Party** and the **Labour Party** have taken turns in government. There are other parties in parliament too, but they do not provide prime ministers. Whoever wins a majority of the seats in an election can usually govern alone.

In the USA and Great Britain, **majority voting** in **single-member constituencies** applies: in each constituency, only whoever has the most votes wins. The French political scientist **Maurice Duverger** described how this system often leads to two large parties. This is called **Duverger's law**. Small parties have hardly any chance of winning seats, so many people vote for a big party straight away.

Switzerland has a **multi-party system**. The National Council is elected by **proportional representation**, so smaller parties also get seats. Many parties are represented in the National Council, for example the SVP, SP, FDP, The Centre, the Greens and the Green Liberals. No party reaches a majority on its own. That is why the major parties work together in the Federal Council.

gewusst: The donkey as the symbol of the Democrats also became famous through cartoons by Thomas Nast.
The colours blue for Democrats and red for Republicans only became firmly established around the year 2000.

teile.einleitung: Kim Il-sung was the founder and first ruler of North Korea. He ruled the country as a dictator from 1948 until his death in 1994. He is still worshipped like a hero in North Korea today.
wichtigste: Kim Il-sung was born on 15 April 1912.
With the help of the Soviet Union he came to power after the Second World War.
In 1948 North Korea was founded, and Kim Il-sung became head of government.
In 1950 he started the Korean War with an attack on the south.
He ruled until his death in 1994.
His son Kim Jong-il succeeded him as ruler.
There is a huge cult of personality around him in North Korea.

abschnitte.text: Until 1945 Korea was occupied by Japan. After the **Second World War** the **Soviet Union** occupied the north and the USA the south. The Soviet Union supported Kim Il-sung as leader in the north. On **9 September 1948** the **Democratic People's Republic of Korea**, that is, North Korea, was founded. Kim Il-sung became its first head of government.

In **June 1950** North Korea attacked the south. This started the **Korean War**. UN troops led by the USA helped South Korea, and China supported the north. The war cost a great many lives. In 1953 it ended with a **ceasefire**, but without a peace treaty. That is why Korea is still divided today.

Kim Il-sung ruled North Korea as a **dictator** for almost **46 years**. There were no free elections and no freedom of opinion. After his death in July **1994**, his son **Kim Jong-il** took power. Today his grandson, **Kim Jong-un**, is already in charge. In 1998 Kim Il-sung was declared **“Eternal President”** in the constitution.

There is a huge **cult of personality** around Kim Il-sung. This is an exaggerated worship of a person. All over the country there are statues and pictures of him, and people must bow before his monuments. His birthday on **15 April** is celebrated as the **“Day of the Sun”**. His embalmed body lies in the **Kumsusan Palace** in **Pyongyang**.

gewusst: The Kumsusan Palace used to be Kim Il-sung's official residence and was turned into a mausoleum after his death.
His son and successor Kim Jong-il also lies in the Kumsusan Palace today.

teile.einleitung: Swiss men are obliged to do military service. Anyone who does neither military service nor civilian service has to pay money instead: the **military service exemption tax**. It is set out in the Federal Constitution.
wichtigste: The tax is paid by Swiss men who do neither military nor civilian service.
It amounts to 3 per cent of taxable income (as of 2025).
The minimum is 400 francs a year.
The obligation lasts at most until the age of 37.
Days of service completed reduce the tax.
People with a significant disability are exempt.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Constitution** says: Swiss men who do neither military nor alternative service owe a tax. This affects, for example, men who are considered unfit for service. It also affects men who do not complete their service in a particular year. The tax is a **substitute** for the service that others perform. The cantons collect it on behalf of the Confederation.

The tax amounts to **3 per cent** of taxable income (as of 2025). It is based on income for the direct federal tax. An example: with 50,000 francs, you calculate 50,000 times 0.03, which makes **1,500 francs**. Even people who earn little pay a **minimum amount** of 400 francs. An apprentice with an income of 10,000 francs would have to pay 300 francs, but because of the minimum amount pays 400 francs.

The obligation lasts from the age of 19 until at most the **age of 37**. In total, you pay no more than **11 annual payments**. Anyone who completes part of their days of service in a year gets a **reduction**. Depending on the number of days, the tax is reduced by one or more tenths.

Not everyone has to pay. People with a **significant disability** who receive a **disability insurance pension** are exempt. So is anyone whose health was damaged during service. Women are not obliged to do service and therefore do not pay the tax either. But they can do military service voluntarily.

gewusst: The military service exemption tax brings the Confederation millions of francs in income every year.
Anyone who does civilian service does not have to pay the military service exemption tax.

teile.einleitung: In Australia, voting is not only a right but a duty. Since 1924, all voters have had to take part in national elections. That is why **voter turnout** there is very high.
wichtigste: Australia has had compulsory voting in national elections since 1924.
In 1915, Queensland was the first state to introduce compulsory voting.
Anyone who does not vote without a good reason has to pay a fine.
Usually more than 90 per cent of those registered vote.
National elections always take place on a Saturday.
From the age of 18 you must register on the electoral roll.

abschnitte.text: In 1915, the state of **Queensland** was the first to make taking part in elections compulsory. In 1924, the Australian parliament decided on **compulsory voting** for national elections too. It applied for the first time in the 1925 election. Australia had been a pioneer in elections before: in 1856, Australian colonies introduced the secret ballot with official ballot papers, known as the **Australian ballot**.

From the age of 18 you must register on the **electoral roll**. At 16 or 17 you can register in advance voluntarily, but you may only vote from 18. Anyone who does not vote without a valid reason has to pay a **fine**. The result: usually **more than 90 per cent** of those registered cast their vote. In Switzerland, turnout in elections is often below 50 per cent.

In the election for the **House of Representatives**, voters number all the candidates in order of preference. Number 1 goes to their favourite. If that person drops out, the next preference counts. This is called **preferential voting**. That way a vote still counts even if your favourite has no chance.

National elections in Australia always take place on a **Saturday**. Many people have the day off, which makes voting easier. Outside many polling stations, volunteers sell barbecued sausages in bread. This **democracy sausage** is very popular. Schools and clubs use the money raised to support their projects.

gewusst: Belgium and Luxembourg also have compulsory voting.
In Switzerland, only the canton of Schaffhausen has compulsory voting.

teile.einleitung: The second homes initiative aimed to limit the building of holiday flats in Switzerland. The people narrowly accepted it on 11 March 2012. Since then, second homes may make up no more than 20 per cent of the homes in a municipality.
wichtigste: The second homes initiative was accepted on 11 March 2012.
Its title was “Put an end to the endless building of second homes!”.
It was launched by the environmentalist Franz Weber with the organisation Helvetia Nostra.
50.6 per cent voted yes, and the majority of the cantons was also narrowly reached.
No more than 20 per cent of the homes in a municipality may be second homes.
The rule is in Article 75b of the Federal Constitution; the Second Homes Act has applied since 2016.

abschnitte.text: A **second home** is a home where nobody lives permanently, for example a **holiday flat** in the mountains. In many holiday resorts, more and more such homes were built that stand empty for much of the year. The initiative, titled “Put an end to the endless building of second homes!”, wanted to stop this. It was meant to protect the **landscape** and prevent villages from sprawling.

Behind the initiative was the environmentalist **Franz Weber**. With his organisation **Helvetia Nostra**, he campaigned for the landscape and nature. Several environmental organisations supported the initiative. It is often called the **Lex Weber** after him. It should not be confused with the **Lex Koller**, which regulates the purchase of land by people abroad.

On **11 March 2012**, **50.6 per cent** voted yes. The **majority of the cantons** was also narrowly reached. Support came mainly from urban cantons such as **Basel-Stadt**, Geneva and Neuchâtel. The mountain cantons with many holiday resorts rejected it. Opposition was strongest in **Valais**, where only 26 per cent voted yes. Many mountain regions feared a building freeze and less work.

The initiative created **Article 75b** of the Federal Constitution. It is in the section on spatial planning and the environment. Since then, second homes may make up no more than **20 per cent** of a municipality's homes, which is one fifth. Many holiday resorts were already above this and can therefore hardly build any new second homes. The **Second Homes Act** came into force on 1 January **2016** and regulates exceptions and checks.

gewusst: The yes side won by a margin of only just over one percentage point.
Franz Weber was already fighting building projects in the 1960s, for example in the Engadine.

teile.einleitung: In an election, people decide who should take on an office or represent them. This could be the class representative at school or a member of the National Council. Elections are at the heart of every democracy.
wichtigste: In an election you choose people; in a vote you decide on issues.
Someone who stands in an election is called a candidate.
The National Council is elected every 4 years in October by proportional representation.
The members of the Council of States are elected by the voters of each canton.
The secret ballot protects you from anyone finding out whom you voted for.
In Switzerland, women have only been able to vote and stand for election at federal level since 1971.
The right to be elected yourself is called the passive right to vote.

abschnitte.text: In an **election**, many people together choose one or more people for a task. In a school class, for example, you elect a **class representative**. In politics, people are elected to parliament, the government or a court. Someone who stands for election is a **candidate**. Usually the person with the most votes is elected.

In Switzerland, elections take place at three levels: in the municipality, in the canton and in the Confederation. The **federal elections** take place every four years in October, most recently in 2023 and next in 2027. In them, the 200 members of the National Council and almost all 46 members of the Council of States are elected. The **Federal Council**, however, is not elected by the people but by the United Federal Assembly. Parliament also elects the judges of the Federal Supreme Court.

The National Council is elected by **proportional representation**. The parties get roughly as many seats as matches their share of the vote. With the **majority system**, on the other hand, whoever gets the most votes wins. Most cantons elect their members of the Council of States by majority vote; only Jura and Neuchâtel use proportional representation. Cantonal governments are also usually elected by majority vote.

In the National Council election, you can put in a party's list unchanged. But you can also **split your vote** (panaschieren), which means adding names from other lists to your list. When **cumulating**, you write the same name twice on the list to give that person extra support. That way you can show very precisely which people you want in parliament. This is possible in only a few countries.

Good elections are **universal**, equal, free and secret. Universal means that all voters may take part. Equal means that every vote counts the same. Free means that nobody may be forced or threatened in an election. The **secret ballot** means that nobody may find out whom you voted for.

There were already elections in ancient Athens and ancient Rome, but only for a small part of the population. In Switzerland, Swiss men have been able to vote at federal level since 1848. Women only gained this right in **1971**, much later than in most other countries in Europe. Since 1991, young people have been able to vote at federal level from the age of 18; before that, only from 20. In the canton of Glarus, people have been able to vote at cantonal and municipal level from the age of 16 since 2007.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who stands for election.
An electoral system in which seats are distributed according to the parties' share of the vote.
An electoral system in which whoever has the most votes wins.
Writing names from other electoral lists on your own list.
Writing the same name twice on a list.

gewusst: In National Council elections in large cantons such as Zurich, there are often hundreds of candidates on many different lists.
The word “candidate” comes from the Latin word for white, because in ancient Rome people seeking office wore a white toga.
In Switzerland, turnout in National Council elections is usually below 50 per cent.

teile.einleitung: Before an election, colourful **election posters** hang everywhere. They show faces, names and short slogans. An election poster is an advert for a person or a party.
wichtigste: An election poster advertises a person or a party.
It often shows a photo, the name and a short slogan.
A short advertising phrase is called a slogan.
The logo and colour show which party someone belongs to.
The municipality decides where posters may be put up.
Damaging other people's posters is forbidden.
After the election, the posters are taken down.

abschnitte.text: On many election posters you see a **photo** of the candidate. The **name** is written in large letters so that you can remember it easily. Then there is the party's **logo** and colour. That way you quickly see which party someone belongs to. Some posters only advertise a party or a list.

A **slogan** is a short phrase that is easy to remember. It should show the idea of the party or the person quickly. Because people often only glance at it, a poster has to be simple. A few words and a strong picture work best.

Rules are needed for posters on **public land**. The **municipality** decides where and for how long election posters may be put up. There are often special poster sites for this. After the election, the posters are no longer needed. The parties must **take them down** again.

Election posters belong to someone, for example a party. Anyone who damages them or scribbles on them is committing **criminal damage** and can be punished. Even if you have a different opinion, you leave other people's posters alone. In a democracy, every party may advertise its ideas.

gewusst: There are also lots of posters before popular votes; then they campaign for a yes or a no.
Some election posters became so famous that they are now shown in museums.

teile.einleitung: A **constituency** is an area in which an election takes place on its own. In the National Council elections, each canton forms its own constituency.
wichtigste: In the National Council elections there are 26 constituencies, one per canton.
The 200 seats are distributed among the cantons according to population.
Every canton has at least one seat.
In cantons with only one seat, the election is by majority vote.
You can only vote for candidates from your own canton.
In large cantons, a small share of the vote is enough for a seat.

abschnitte.text: The National Council has **200 seats**. Each of the 26 cantons forms its own **constituency**. Each canton has its own electoral lists. That is why you cannot vote in Bern for candidates from Lucerne. You only ever vote for people who are standing in your own canton.

The seats are distributed among the cantons according to **population**. What counts is the permanent resident population in the year after the last general election. So for the 2027 election, the year 2024 counts. Every canton gets at least one seat, even if it is very small. That is why in 2015 in **Appenzell Innerrhoden** there were only around 16,000 inhabitants per seat, while the average was around 40,000.

Some small cantons have only one seat, for example **Obwalden** and **Uri**. There the election is by **majority vote**: whoever has the most votes is elected. In these cantons, in principle any eligible person can be elected, even without registering as a candidate. For comparison: Zug has 3 seats, and Schaffhausen and Jura have 2 each.

In cantons with several seats, **proportional representation** applies. The seats are distributed according to the lists' share of the vote. Roughly, you calculate 100 divided by the number of seats plus one. With 4 seats that gives 100 ÷ 5 = 20 per cent. **Zurich** had 36 seats in 2023, so there about 100 ÷ 37, or roughly 2.7 per cent, was enough. That is why small parties have better chances in large cantons.

gewusst: Each canton is also its own constituency for the Council of States.
In some cantons, there are several constituencies within the canton for the cantonal parliament.

teile.einleitung: Josip Broz Tito was a Yugoslav partisan leader and politician who ruled Yugoslavia from 1945 to 1980. He ran the country as a communist state but stayed independent of the Soviet Union. This gave Yugoslavia a special position among the communist states.
wichtigste: Josip Broz Tito lived from 1892 to 1980.
In the Second World War he led the partisans in the fight against the German and Italian occupiers.
From 1945 he ruled Yugoslavia, and from 1953 as president.
In 1948 he broke with Stalin, and Yugoslavia stayed independent of the Soviet Union.
He was one of the founders of the Non-Aligned Movement.
Yugoslavs were allowed to travel abroad, and many worked in Switzerland or Germany.
After his death Yugoslavia broke up into several states in the 1990s.

abschnitte.text: Josip Broz was born in **1892** in **Kumrovec** in what is now Croatia, which at that time belonged to Austria-Hungary. He trained as a locksmith and worked in various countries, including in factories in Germany and Austria. In the First World War he was taken prisoner by the Russians and experienced the revolution there. Back in Yugoslavia he became a communist and later called himself **Tito**.

In 1941 Germany and Italy occupied Yugoslavia. Tito led the communist **partisans**, who fought against the occupiers in the mountains. The war was very cruel, and different ethnic groups in Yugoslavia also fought each other. In 1945 the partisans liberated the country largely by their own efforts.

After the war Tito became head of a communist **Yugoslavia** made up of six republics. But he did not want **Stalin** to tell him how to govern. In 1948 there was a break, and Yugoslavia was expelled from the alliance of communist parties. After that the country went **its own way** and later did not join the Warsaw Pact either.

Instead of a pure planned economy, Tito introduced **workers' self-management**, in which the workforce partly helped to run their enterprises. In 1961 he hosted the first conference of **Non-Aligned States** in Belgrade; these countries wanted to belong neither to the West nor to the East. Yugoslavs were free to travel, and many went to Germany, Austria and **Switzerland** as guest workers. Even so, Yugoslavia was a one-party dictatorship in which opponents were locked up, for example on the prison island of Goli Otok.

Tito died in Ljubljana on 4 May **1980**, and state guests from all over the world came to his funeral. He is buried in the **House of Flowers** in Belgrade. Without him the tensions between the ethnic groups grew stronger. In the 1990s Yugoslavia broke up in bloody wars into several states, such as Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fighters who do not belong to a regular army and fight against occupiers.
Countries that did not want to join either the West or the East during the Cold War.
People who went to another country to work, for example to Switzerland.
A state in south-eastern Europe that existed from 1918 until the 1990s.

gewusst: In 1974 Tito was named president for life.
Representatives from more than 120 states came to Tito's funeral in 1980.
In many towns of the former Yugoslavia, streets and squares still bear Tito's name today.

teile.einleitung: The Commonwealth of Independent States, CIS for short, is an association of former Soviet republics. It was formed in December 1991, when the Soviet Union broke up.
wichtigste: Russia, Ukraine and Belarus founded the CIS in December 1991.
On 21 December 1991 eight more republics joined in Alma-Ata.
At the end of 1991 the Soviet Union officially dissolved.
The CIS has its seat in Minsk, the capital of Belarus.
The Baltic states never joined the CIS.
Georgia left after its war with Russia; its withdrawal took effect in 2009.

abschnitte.text: In December 1991 the leaders of **Russia**, **Ukraine** and **Belarus** signed an agreement founding the CIS. It was drawn up in Belarus, not far from **Minsk**. With it they declared the Soviet Union to be over. On 21 December 1991 in **Alma-Ata**, today's Almaty in Kazakhstan, eleven former Soviet republics signed a joint declaration.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Soviet Union
abschnitte.text: On 25 December 1991 **Mikhail Gorbachev** resigned as president of the Soviet Union. The next day the Soviet Union officially dissolved. **Russia** was recognised as the **continuing state**. It took over the Soviet Union's permanent seat on the **UN Security Council**, its embassies and its nuclear weapons.

abschnitte.titel: Who is in and who is not
abschnitte.text: The Baltic states of **Estonia**, **Latvia** and **Lithuania** never joined. They saw themselves as occupied countries and sought to join the EU and NATO. **Georgia** announced its withdrawal after the war over South Ossetia in 2008, and this took effect in 2009. **Turkmenistan** downgraded its membership to associate status in 2005 because it sees itself as permanently neutral. **Ukraine** never ratified the CIS Charter and ended its participation in the bodies in 2018.

The CIS is meant to make cooperation in the economy, transport and security easier. Its **Executive Committee** has its seat in Minsk. In 1992 several states signed the Collective Security Treaty in **Tashkent**. In 2002 this gave rise to a military alliance around Russia, to which only some CIS states belong. Overall the CIS is more of a loose association than a firm union.

gewusst: In December 1991 the founders of the CIS met in a hunting lodge in a large forest area in Belarus.
Turkmenistan's permanent neutrality has been recognised by the UN since 1995.

teile.einleitung: With a popular initiative, the people themselves can propose a change to the Federal Constitution. It is an important part of direct democracy in Switzerland.
wichtigste: With a popular initiative, voters propose a new rule.
A federal popular initiative aims to change the Federal Constitution.
It needs 100,000 valid signatures in 18 months.
The popular initiative has existed at federal level since 1891.
If it succeeds, the people and the cantons vote on it.
In everyday speech, people often just say “initiative”.

abschnitte.text: A **popular initiative** comes from the people, not from the government or parliament. **Voters** join together in a committee and write down their idea. A federal initiative aims to change the **Federal Constitution**, the country's most important law. In everyday speech people often just say **“initiative”**. There are initiatives in the cantons and municipalities too.

For an initiative to **succeed**, it needs **100,000 valid signatures**. The committee has **18 months** to collect them. From 1891 to 1977, 50,000 signatures were enough. Then the number was doubled to 100,000. At the end, the Federal Chancellery checks whether there are enough valid signatures.

Once an initiative has succeeded, the **Federal Council and parliament** debate it. They make a recommendation and can put forward a **counter-proposal**. At the end there is a **popular vote**. Swiss citizens aged **18 and over** may vote. The initiative is accepted if **the people and the cantons** agree, that is a majority of voters and a majority of the cantons.

The popular initiative for the whole of Switzerland was introduced in **1891**. So it is already over 130 years old. Usually an initiative asks for a **partial revision**, that is a change to individual articles. But you can also ask for a **total revision**, a completely new Federal Constitution. The only initiative of this kind that succeeded failed in the popular vote in **1935**.

gewusst: Most popular initiatives are rejected by the people, yet they often bring new topics into political debate.
With the popular initiative, the people in Switzerland can put forward new ideas themselves; this is possible in only a few countries.

teile.einleitung: Charter 77 was a civil rights movement in communist Czechoslovakia. In January 1977, its signatories demanded that the state respect the human rights it had itself recognised. Many of them were persecuted for this.
wichtigste: Charter 77 was published in January 1977.
One of the reasons for it was the trial of the band The Plastic People of the Universe.
It referred to the CSCE Helsinki Final Act of 1975.
At first around 240 people signed, and by 1989 almost 2,000.
The philosopher Jan Patočka was one of the first spokespeople.
The regime organised a counter-declaration, the “Anti-Charter”.

abschnitte.text: In 1976, musicians from the underground band **The Plastic People of the Universe** were put on trial and convicted. The regime did not like their music. Many **intellectuals** were outraged. This gave rise to the idea of a joint declaration. The co-founders included the writer **Václav Havel**.

In 1975 Czechoslovakia had signed the **CSCE Helsinki Final Act** and recognised human rights covenants. Charter 77 demanded that the state actually keep these commitments. It did not want to be a party of its own, but to point out wrongs. At first the declaration had around **240 signatures**. By 1989, almost **2,000** people had signed in total.

The regime reacted harshly. Signatories lost their jobs, were interrogated or went to prison. The philosopher **Jan Patočka**, one of the first three spokespeople, died of a brain haemorrhage in March 1977 after hours of interrogation. He became a symbol of the movement. In January 1977, well-known artists had to sign a counter-declaration in the National Theatre, the so-called **Anti-Charter**.

Charter 77 kept the idea of human rights alive for many years. It was an important part of the **opposition** in the Eastern Bloc. In the **Velvet Revolution** of 1989, many of its members played a leading role. At the end of 1989, Václav Havel became president of Czechoslovakia.

gewusst: A rock band set off one of the best-known civil rights movements in Eastern Europe.
Anyone who did not sign the Anti-Charter risked no longer being allowed to perform.

teile.einleitung: After every election, people ask: who won? The **election winner** is whoever did best. Parties that gain a lot of seats are also often called winners.
wichtigste: The election winner is whoever has won the most votes or seats.
More seats than before is called a gain in seats; fewer seats is a loss of seats.
In 2023 the SVP gained nine seats in the National Council, reaching 62 seats.
In 2023 the Green Liberals lost six seats and the Greens five.
In the Council of States, The Centre was the strongest party after the 2023 election, with 15 seats.
In Switzerland, no party governs alone.

abschnitte.text: In an election for a single person, the winner is whoever gets the most votes. In parliamentary elections it is more complicated. Often the party with the most seats is called the election winner. But people also often speak of winners when a party **gains** strongly. If a party gets more seats than before, it has a **gain in seats**. If it loses seats, it is a **loss of seats**.

In the 2023 National Council elections, the **SVP** gained nine seats. That was the biggest increase of any party. It reached 62 of the 200 seats, making it the largest parliamentary group. The **Green Liberals** lost the most seats, six. The **Greens** lost five seats.

In the **Council of States** things look different. After the 2023 election, **The Centre** was the strongest party there, with 15 seats. It was followed by the FDP and the SP. This shows: a party can be very strong in one chamber and less so in the other. In Council of States elections, individual personalities often play a big role.

In many countries, the election winner forms the government. In Switzerland it is different. Several large parties sit together in the **Federal Council**. This is called **concordance**. So even the election winner has to work with other parties. On election night, those elected usually thank everyone who voted for them and supported them.

gewusst: The SVP has been the party with the most votes in Switzerland since the 1999 National Council elections.
Members of the Federal Council are not elected by the people but by the United Federal Assembly.

teile.einleitung: Antonio Gramsci was an Italian philosopher, journalist and communist politician. Under Mussolini's fascist regime he was sentenced to a long prison term. In prison he wrote down thoughts about power and culture that are still much discussed today.
wichtigste: Gramsci was born in 1891 on the island of Sardinia.
In 1921 he took part in founding the Communist Party of Italy in Livorno.
In 1928 he was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison.
In prison he wrote around 30 notebooks, the Prison Notebooks.
His most important concept is cultural hegemony.
He died in Rome in 1937 as a result of his imprisonment.

abschnitte.text: Antonio Gramsci was born in **1891** in Ales on the island of **Sardinia**. He grew up in **poor circumstances** and was in poor health. Thanks to a **scholarship**, he was able to study in **Turin**. There he got to know the workers' movement. He became a journalist and wrote for socialist newspapers.

In **1921**, at the Socialist party congress in **Livorno**, the left wing split off. This created the **Communist Party of Italy**, which Gramsci helped to found. Later he became its general secretary. Under **Mussolini** he was arrested in 1926. At his trial in 1928, the prosecutor is said to have demanded that this **brain** be stopped from working for twenty years. Gramsci was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison.

Despite illness, Gramsci wrote down his most important thoughts in prison. The result was around **30 notebooks**, in Italian **“Quaderni del carcere”**, the **Prison Notebooks**. They deal with politics, culture, history and philosophy. Gramsci died in Rome in April **1937** as a result of his long imprisonment. His sentence had ended shortly before.

Gramsci's most important concept is **cultural hegemony**. Hegemony means dominance. According to Gramsci, a ruling group secures its power not only through **force** but above all through **consent**. Its values then come to seem obvious. School, church and the press, for example, contribute to this.

abschnitte.titel: Intellectuals and the war of position
abschnitte.text: Gramsci believed that every social class produces its own thinkers. He called them **organic intellectuals**. For Western societies he used the image of a **war of position**: there, he said, civil society had to be won over step by step. In Russia, on the other hand, a rapid **war of movement** had been possible. Today Gramsci's ideas are taken up in politics and scholarship by people with very different views.

gewusst: In prison, Gramsci also wrote many letters, which later became famous as the “Prison Letters”.
His Prison Notebooks were secretly smuggled out of Italy and only published after the Second World War.

teile.einleitung: Historical materialism is the view of history held by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. According to this theory, it is mainly economic conditions that determine how a society develops. History is understood as a series of class struggles.
wichtigste: The term “historical materialism” was made popular by Friedrich Engels; Marx himself did not use it.
According to the “Communist Manifesto”, the history of all society so far is a history of class struggles.
Marx took over dialectics from Hegel but put material conditions first.
According to Marx, when the productive forces come into conflict with the relations of production, an era of social revolution begins.
In the classic scheme, feudalism is followed by capitalism.
A short summary can be found in the preface to “A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy” (1859).

abschnitte.text: In everyday life, “materialistic” means that someone cares a lot about possessions. In philosophy, **materialism** means something different: people's real, material living conditions come first, and ideas follow from them. Marx believed that the way people work and make goods shapes their thinking, their laws and their politics. The term **historical materialism** was used mainly by **Friedrich Engels** from around 1890, and after that it became established.

The philosopher **Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel** described history as a **dialectical** development of the mind or spirit. Dialectics means that something new develops through opposites and the overcoming of them. Marx and Engels took over this method but wanted to “turn it upside down” in a materialist way. For them it is not ideas that develop, but economic and social conditions.

abschnitte.titel: Productive forces and relations of production
abschnitte.text: The **productive forces** include tools, machines and people's skills. The **relations of production** describe who owns the factories and the land and who works for whom. According to Marx, when the productive forces grow, at some point they burst the old relations apart. Then an **era of social revolution** begins. Marx briefly summed up these ideas in 1859 in the preface to “A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy”.

The “Communist Manifesto” of 1848 says: the history of all society so far is the history of **class struggles**. In the classic scheme the forms of society follow one another: **primitive society**, **slave society**, **feudalism**, **capitalism** and finally socialism or communism. Whether history really follows such a plan is very much disputed among historians.

As early as 1845 Marx wrote the short “**Theses on Feuerbach**”. The eleventh thesis says that philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways; the point is to change it. In 1845 and 1846 Marx and Engels wrote “**The German Ideology**” together. In it they set out their view of history in detail for the first time. The complete work was not published until 1932.

gewusst: Marx and Engels could not find a publisher for “The German Ideology” and, in their own words, left the manuscript “to the gnawing criticism of the mice”.
Today the eleventh thesis on Feuerbach is written in large letters in the entrance hall of the Humboldt University in Berlin.

teile.einleitung: The secret files scandal shook Switzerland in 1989. It came out that for decades the Federal Police had secretly kept index cards on hundreds of thousands of people and organisations.
wichtigste: “Fichen” are index cards on which the Federal Police collected notes about people.
Around 900,000 such cards were found.
During the Cold War, it was mainly people thought to be left-wing or communist who were watched.
The cards were discovered by a parliamentary commission of inquiry (PUK) led by Moritz Leuenberger.
On 3 March 1990 around 30,000 people demonstrated in Bern against the “snooping state”.
More than 300,000 people asked to see their own file card.

abschnitte.text: The word **“Fiche”** comes from French and means index card. The **Federal Police** had made such cards about many people and organisations. They contained notes, for example about meetings people had attended, journeys or contacts. The people concerned knew nothing about it. More than 700,000 people and organisations were recorded.

In January 1989 **Elisabeth Kopp**, the first woman Federal Councillor in Switzerland, resigned. Parliament then set up a **parliamentary commission of inquiry**, PUK for short. It examined how the Federal Department of Justice and Police was being run, in particular the work against money laundering and drug trafficking. In doing so it came across a large room full of file cards. The chairman of the PUK was National Councillor **Moritz Leuenberger**, who was elected to the Federal Council in 1995.

During the **Cold War**, many people feared the influence of the Soviet Union. **State security** therefore mainly kept watch on left-wingers, trade unionists, peace activists and people from abroad. Harmless activities were often enough for an entry, such as taking part in a demonstration. Much of the information was unimportant or even wrong.

The discovery caused great outrage. On 3 March 1990 around 30,000 people in **Bern** protested against the so-called **snooping state**. It was one of the largest demonstrations of that time in Switzerland. More than 300,000 people made a request to **see** their file card. They received copies in which the names of other people had often been blacked out.

The scandal changed Swiss politics. Parliament demanded better **oversight** of state security. Later new laws were passed that set out more precisely whom and what the state may watch. How much surveillance is needed to protect the country is still being debated in Switzerland today.

gewusst: The writer Max Frisch also had a file card.
When they read them, many of the people concerned found that their file card contained only very ordinary or wrong information.

teile.einleitung: Unofficial collaborators, IM for short, were the secret informers of the GDR's State Security. They reported on people around them without those people knowing. In this way the Stasi kept watch on large parts of the population.
wichtigste: IM stands for “Inoffizieller Mitarbeiter”, unofficial collaborator of the Ministry for State Security.
In 1989 there were around 189,000 active IMs.
On top of these there were more than 90,000 full-time Stasi employees.
The Stasi saw itself as the “shield and sword of the party”.
Erich Mielke was Minister for State Security from 1957 to 1989.
The first head of the authority for the Stasi records was Joachim Gauck.

abschnitte.text: The **Ministry for State Security**, **Stasi** for short, was the secret police of the GDR. Besides its permanent staff, it used **unofficial collaborators**. These were quite ordinary people who secretly reported on colleagues, neighbours, friends and even family members. Some took part out of conviction, others for advantages or because they were put under pressure. In 1989 there were around **189,000** active IMs.

abschnitte.titel: Shield and sword of the party
abschnitte.text: The Stasi saw itself as the “**shield and sword of the party**”. So it served above all to **keep the SED in power**. From 1957 to 1989 **Erich Mielke** led the ministry and expanded it greatly. Foreign espionage was led for a long time by **Markus Wolf**. By the end the Stasi had more than 90,000 full-time employees.

In the autumn of 1989 the SED's power collapsed. On 13 November 1989 Mielke spoke in front of the **People's Chamber**, the GDR's parliament. When members booed him, he called out: “Ich liebe doch alle, alle Menschen.” This means “But I love all, all people.” After decades of surveillance this sentence seemed grotesque and was laughed at.

The Stasi headquarters were on **Normannenstrasse** in Berlin-Lichtenberg. On **15 January 1990** demonstrators stormed the site. They wanted to stop the files from being destroyed. Today it houses the **Stasi Museum**, where you can visit Mielke's office, for example.

After reunification an authority was created for the **Stasi records**. Its first head, from 1990 to 2000, was **Joachim Gauck**, so it was popularly called the “**Gauck authority**”. Gauck later became Federal President of Germany. Since 1992 the people affected have been able to read their own files. In this way many found out who had spied on them.

gewusst: If all the Stasi files were placed side by side on shelves, they would stretch more than 100 kilometres.
At the end of 1989 Stasi staff tried to tear up files. Today the scraps are painstakingly being put back together.

teile.einleitung: A five-year plan is a state economic plan that sets out what is to be produced over the next five years. The Soviet Union introduced the first such plan in 1928 in order to become an industrial country quickly. Later many other countries, such as China or the GDR, took over this idea.
wichtigste: A five-year plan is a state economic plan with production targets for five years.
The Soviet Union's first five-year plan began in 1928 under Joseph Stalin.
An authority called Gosplan worked out how much each factory should make.
Above all, the amount of steel, coal, machines and electricity was meant to grow quickly.
At the same time farms were forcibly merged into large collectives.
Industry grew strongly, but many people suffered from hunger and forced labour.
China still works with five-year plans today.

abschnitte.text: In a **planned economy** it is not the market but the state that decides what is made.
