In the USA itself, however, Labour Day is celebrated in September as “Labor Day”.

In Switzerland 1 May is **not a national public holiday**. The cantons decide for themselves. In Zurich it is treated like a Sunday, and it is also a day off in Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft. In many other cantons people work as normal. Even so, trade unions and parties hold marches and speeches in the larger cities every year.

Many participants wear a **red carnation** on their lapel on 1 May. Red is the traditional colour of the workers' movement. Flags, banners and speeches in public squares are typical. In Germany and Austria 1 May is a public holiday by law. In many areas there are also older spring customs, such as the maypole.

gewusst: Of all places, in the USA, where May Day began, it is not a holiday. “Labor Day” falls on the first Monday in September.
The demand “eight hours of work, eight hours of free time, eight hours of sleep” was a well-known slogan of the workers' movement.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Republic of Germany, FRG for short, was founded in 1949. Until 1990 it was the western of the two German states. Since reunification, the whole of Germany has had this name, and it is one of Switzerland's neighbours to the north.
wichtigste: FRG is the abbreviation for Federal Republic of Germany (in German BRD).
It was founded on 23 May 1949 with the Basic Law.
Bonn was the capital until reunification.
The flag has black, red and gold stripes.
Before the euro, people paid with the Deutschmark.
The government is led by the federal chancellor.
In the south, Germany borders Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Germany was divided into occupation zones. The **Federal Republic of Germany** was formed from the zones of the USA, Great Britain and France. It was founded on **23 May 1949**, when its **Basic Law** came into force. In the east, the **GDR** was created in the same year. Because the FRG lay to the west of the GDR, people also spoke of **West Germany**.

The small city of **Bonn** on the Rhine became the capital of the FRG. But it was only regarded as a temporary capital, because people hoped for reunification. The first federal chancellor was **Konrad Adenauer**. In the 1950s the FRG experienced a great boom, the so-called **economic miracle**. The **Deutschmark**, the German mark, became a strong currency.

Germany is a **federal state** with federal states (Länder), similar to Switzerland with its cantons. The government is led by the **federal chancellor**. In Switzerland, the **Federal Council**, with seven members of equal rank, has this role. The German parliament is called the **Bundestag**. The flag has **black, red and gold** stripes and no coat of arms in the middle.

After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the two German states moved closer together. On **3 October 1990**, the GDR joined the Federal Republic. Since then there has been a united Germany again, which is still called the **Federal Republic of Germany**. **Berlin** became the capital. Since 2002, people in Germany have paid with the **euro**.

Germany lies to the north of Switzerland. The border runs, for example, along the **Rhine** near Basel and Schaffhausen and along Lake Constance. There is a lot of trade and travel between the two countries. Many people commute across the border to work every day.

gewusst: 3 October is a public holiday in Germany, the **Day of German Unity**.
The canton of Schaffhausen lies mostly north of the Rhine and is almost completely surrounded by Germany.

teile.einleitung: With the Belovezha Accords, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus sealed the end of the Soviet Union in December 1991. At the same time they founded the Commonwealth of Independent States, CIS for short.
wichtigste: The agreement was signed on 8 December 1991.
The place was the government dacha Viskuli in the Belovezha Forest in Belarus.
It was signed by Boris Yeltsin, Leonid Kravchuk and Stanislav Shushkevich.
The three founded the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).
Gorbachev resigned as president of the Soviet Union on 25 December 1991.

abschnitte.text: The signing took place at the government dacha **Viskuli**. It lies in the **Belovezha Forest**, an area of ancient forest on the border between Belarus and Poland. **Boris Yeltsin** signed for Russia, **Leonid Kravchuk** for Ukraine and **Stanislav Shushkevich** for Belarus. Kravchuk had only been the first elected president of Ukraine since December 1991.

The three heads of state declared that the **Soviet Union** no longer existed. In its place they founded the **Commonwealth of Independent States**, **CIS** for short. A few days later, on 21 December 1991, other former Soviet republics joined in Alma-Ata. After the agreement, Yeltsin first phoned US President **George Bush**. Gorbachev only found out through a phone call from Shushkevich and felt humiliated.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Soviet Union
abschnitte.text: Mikhail **Gorbachev** no longer had the power to stop the end. On **25 December 1991** he announced on television that he was resigning as president of the Soviet Union. That same evening the Soviet flag was lowered over the **Kremlin**. After that, the flag of Russia flew there.

gewusst: The end of the Soviet Union was decided not in Moscow but in a remote hunting lodge in the forest.

teile.einleitung: Economic freedom is a fundamental right in the Swiss Federal Constitution. It allows everyone to choose a job freely and run their own business. The state may only restrict it for good reasons.
wichtigste: Economic freedom is set out in Article 27 of the Federal Constitution.
Above all, it includes the free choice of profession.
You may freely start and carry out a private business activity, for example opening a shop.
This right used to be called freedom of trade and industry, guaranteed since the constitution of 1874.
According to Article 94, the Confederation and the cantons must abide by the principle of economic freedom.
The Competition Commission and the Price Supervisor make sure competition is fair.

abschnitte.text: Article 27 of the Federal Constitution guarantees **economic freedom**. In particular it includes the **free choice of profession**, free access to private economic activity and the freedom to carry it out. This means: you may decide for yourself whether you want to become a baker, a computer scientist or a gardener. You may also set up your own company. **Article 94** adds the principles of the economic order.

The Federal Constitution of 1874 already guaranteed **freedom of trade and industry**. Before that, in many places there were guilds and cantonal barriers that made trade difficult. With the new Federal Constitution of 1999, the right was renamed **economic freedom**. Its core content stayed the same: the economy should in principle be free and not directed by the state.

Like other fundamental rights, economic freedom may be restricted. This requires a **legal basis** and a **public interest**, and the restriction must be proportionate. An example: anyone who wants to treat patients as a doctor needs training and a **licence**. That way the population's health is protected. Special rules also apply to taxis, restaurants and pharmacies.

The constitution allows some exceptions to the free market. An old example is the **salt monopoly**: trading in salt is traditionally a monopoly of the cantons. Article 94 requires that departures from the principle of economic freedom are only allowed if the constitution provides for them. **Shop opening hours** are not the same everywhere either, because the cantons generally set them themselves.

Freedom alone is not enough if big companies make secret agreements. That is why there is the **Competition Commission**, **COMCO** (WEKO) for short. It takes action against cartels and against companies that unfairly exploit their market power. The **Price Supervisor** makes sure that prices are not abusive where there is no effective competition, for example for fees or electricity. In everyday speech he is called “Monsieur Prix”.

gewusst: The Price Supervisor is called “Monsieur Prix” all over Switzerland, including in German-speaking Switzerland.
Because of cantonal rules, a shop in one canton may stay open later in the evening than in the neighbouring canton.
The salt monopoly is one of the oldest rights of the cantons and still exists today.

teile.einleitung: An **electoral list** contains the names of the people you can vote for. In Switzerland you may change a list: cross out names, write names twice or add names from other lists.
wichtigste: An electoral list contains the names of the candidates.
Each list has a name and a list number.
Cumulating means writing a name twice.
Splitting your vote means adding names from other lists.
You may cross out names you do not want.
Changes must be made by hand.
On the blank list, you write the names yourself.

abschnitte.text: For the **National Council election**, the parties submit one or more **electoral lists**. Each list gets a **list number** and a name. A list must contain at least one name. At most it may have as many names as the canton has seats. If you put in a pre-printed list unchanged, you give a vote to everyone on it.

**Cumulating** means piling up. You write a name a second time on the list. That person then gets two votes from one voter. A name may not appear on a list more than twice. To do this you often have to cross out another name, because the number of lines is limited.

abschnitte.titel: Splitting your vote and crossing out
abschnitte.text: **Panaschieren**, splitting your vote, comes from the French word for mixing. You write names from other lists on your list. That way you can vote for people from different parties. You may **cross out** names you do not want to vote for. All changes must be made **by hand**. That way it is clear that the voter made them themselves.

There is also a **blank list** with no pre-printed names. On it you write the people you want to vote for yourself. You can also enter a list number at the top. In the National Council election, however, only names of people standing on an official list count. Other names are not counted.

gewusst: Cumulating and splitting votes give voters in Switzerland a particularly large influence on which people are chosen.
Parties can link their lists together in a list alliance to have better chances when the seats are distributed.

teile.einleitung: Friedrich Engels was a German businessman, philosopher and writer of the 19th century. He was the closest friend and co-author of Karl Marx. Together they wrote the famous Communist Manifesto, which shaped the workers' movement all over the world.
wichtigste: Friedrich Engels lived from 1820 to 1895.
He was born in Barmen, which is now part of the city of Wuppertal.
He was the close friend and co-author of Karl Marx.
In 1848 the two of them published the Communist Manifesto.
Engels worked in his family's textile factory in Manchester in England.
With his money he supported Marx and his family for many years.
After Marx's death he published the last volumes of Marx's main work, Capital.

abschnitte.text: Friedrich Engels was born on 28 November **1820** in **Barmen**, today part of **Wuppertal**. His father owned a textile factory and was a devout, wealthy businessman. Friedrich was also meant to become a merchant and did an apprenticeship in the family business. On the side he was very interested in philosophy, politics and languages.

In 1842 Engels went to **Manchester**, at that time one of the most important industrial cities in the world. There he saw how hard the factory workers' lives were: long working days, dirty homes, child labour and disease. In 1845 he wrote about this in the book **The Condition of the Working Class in England**. It made him well known and also influenced Karl Marx.

In 1844 Engels and **Karl Marx** met in Paris and became close friends. In 1848 they wrote the **Communist Manifesto** together, which called on the workers of all countries to unite. During the revolution of 1848 and 1849 Engels fought in Baden and then fled via **Switzerland** to England. There he worked in the family business again and regularly sent Marx money.

When Marx died in 1883, Engels sorted out his notes. He published the second and third volumes of **Capital**, which Marx had not been able to finish. He also wrote books of his own, for example about the origin of the family and the state. He advised many socialist parties in Europe and was an important adviser to the workers' movement until his death.

Engels died in London on 5 August **1895**. As he had wished, his ashes were scattered in the sea off the English coast. His ideas influenced social democratic and communist parties. Later communist dictatorships also referred to him, even though he never lived to see these states himself.

begriffe.erklaerung: A public declaration in which a group sets out its aims.
The joining together of working men and women to fight for better wages and rights.
The period when machines and factories replaced work done by hand.
Someone who owns and runs a company.

gewusst: Engels was himself the son of a rich factory owner, yet he fought for workers' rights.
He spoke and read a great many languages, reportedly more than a dozen.
In Wuppertal a museum in the Engels House now recalls his life.

teile.einleitung: Apollo 11 was the first mission in which people landed on the Moon. In July 1969, two American astronauts set foot on the surface of the Moon. The landing was a high point in the space race between the USA and the communist Soviet Union.
wichtigste: Apollo 11 launched in July 1969 on the huge Saturn V rocket.
Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon, and Buzz Aldrin the second.
Michael Collins stayed in the command module “Columbia” and orbited the Moon.
Armstrong spoke of one small step for a man and one giant leap for mankind.
The University of Bern set up a solar wind sail on the Moon.
The mission was part of the space race with the Soviet Union.

abschnitte.text: During the **Cold War**, the USA and the communist **Soviet Union** also competed in space. In 1957 the Soviet Union sent the first satellite, **Sputnik**, into space. In 1961 **Yuri Gagarin** became the first person to orbit the Earth. After that, US President **John F. Kennedy** set the goal of landing people on the Moon before the end of the 1960s. With Apollo 11, the USA reached this goal.

On **16 July 1969**, Apollo 11 launched in Florida. The **Saturn V** rocket was over 100 metres tall. It is one of the most powerful rockets ever built. On board were three astronauts: **Neil Armstrong**, **Buzz Aldrin** and **Michael Collins**. After about four days they reached the Moon.

Armstrong and Aldrin landed on the Moon in the lunar module **“Eagle”**. Collins stayed in the command module **“Columbia”** and orbited the Moon. He never set foot on it. Armstrong got out first and said: **“That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.”** Aldrin followed shortly afterwards. The two stayed outside for about two and a half hours.

**Switzerland** took part too. Researchers from the **University of Bern** had built a sail made of **aluminium foil**. It caught particles coming from the Sun, known as the **solar wind**. The astronauts set it up on the Moon even before the US flag. Afterwards they brought the foil back to Earth to be examined.

On **24 July 1969**, the capsule with the three astronauts landed in the **Pacific**. They brought back rock and dust from the Moon. Hundreds of millions of people had followed the landing on television. In Europe it was the middle of the night. By 1972, five more Apollo missions had landed on the Moon.

gewusst: After their return, the astronauts had to spend three weeks in quarantine, because people feared they might bring germs back from the Moon.
The astronauts' footprints can probably still be seen on the Moon today, because there is no wind there.

teile.einleitung: Erich Honecker was a German politician and for many years the most powerful man in the GDR. From 1971 to 1989 he led the ruling party, the SED, and with it the whole country. Under his rule the Berlin Wall was strictly guarded until it fell in the autumn of 1989.
wichtigste: Erich Honecker lived from 1912 to 1994.
For many years he was head of state of the GDR, that is, communist East Germany.
As a young communist he spent around ten years in prison during the Nazi period.
In 1961 he organised the building of the Berlin Wall.
In 1971 he replaced Walter Ulbricht as leader of the SED party.
In October 1989 he had to resign after huge protests.
He died in Chile in 1994.

abschnitte.text: Erich Honecker was born in 1912 in **Neunkirchen** in the Saarland. He trained as a roofer and joined the communist youth movement while still a teenager. After the Nazis came to power in 1933, he fought against them underground. In 1935 he was arrested and stayed in Brandenburg prison until the end of the war in **1945**.

After the war, in 1946, Honecker founded the **Free German Youth (FDJ)**, the youth organisation of the GDR. He rose higher and higher in the **SED** party. In August 1961 he directed the building of the **Berlin Wall**, which divided East and West Berlin. In 1971 he took over the leadership of the party from Walter Ulbricht, and from 1976 he also held the office of Chairman of the Council of State.

Honecker promised people more homes and better supplies, and indeed many prefabricated blocks of flats were built. At the same time there was often a shortage of goods such as tropical fruit or cars; people waited many years for a Trabant. The secret police, the **Stasi**, watched millions of people. Anyone who tried to leave the GDR without permission risked prison or death at the border.

In 1989 many GDR citizens fled to the West via Hungary, and in cities such as Leipzig hundreds of thousands demonstrated peacefully. Honecker did not want reforms like those in the Soviet Union under Mikhail Gorbachev. On **18 October 1989** he had to resign, and Egon Krenz became his successor. A few weeks later, on 9 November 1989, the Wall fell.

After the end of the GDR, Honecker fled to the Soviet Union, but in 1992 he was brought back to Germany. There he stood trial for the deaths at the Wall. Because he was seriously ill with cancer, the trial was stopped in 1993. He travelled to his wife Margot in **Chile**, where he died in May 1994.

begriffe.erklaerung: The German Democratic Republic, a communist state in East Germany from 1949 to 1990.
The Socialist Unity Party of Germany, which governed the GDR on its own.
The Ministry for State Security, the secret police of the GDR.

begriffe.wort: Chairman of the Council of State
begriffe.erklaerung: The office of head of state in the GDR.

gewusst: In 1987 Honecker became the first GDR head of state to make an official visit to West Germany, and he was received in Bonn.
His wife Margot Honecker was the GDR's education minister for more than 25 years.
As late as January 1989 Honecker said the Wall would still be standing in 50 and even 100 years.

teile.einleitung: The “hotline” was a direct communication link between the governments of the USA and the Soviet Union. It was set up in 1963 after the Cuban Missile Crisis so that the two superpowers could quickly reach an understanding in an emergency.
wichtigste: The hotline connected Washington and Moscow.
It was set up after the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.
The agreement was signed in Geneva in June 1963.
The link went into operation on 30 August 1963.
At first it was not a telephone but a teleprinter.
It is often popularly called the “red telephone”.

abschnitte.text: In October 1962 the Soviet Union stationed **nuclear missiles** in Cuba, close to the USA. There was a threat of nuclear war. During the **Cuban Missile Crisis** it often took hours for messages to arrive between Washington and Moscow. Some first had to be translated and passed on through embassies. Both sides realised how dangerous such delays were.

Representatives of the USA and the Soviet Union signed the hotline agreement in **Geneva** in June 1963. During the **Cold War** the city was often a place for negotiations, because Switzerland is neutral. On **30 August 1963** the link went into operation. It ran through several countries in Europe.

At first the hotline was not a telephone at all. Written texts were sent with a **teleprinter**. This is a kind of typewriter that sends texts along a line. Written messages had one advantage: they could be translated carefully and precisely. This made misunderstandings easier to avoid.

To test it, an English sentence was sent: “The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog's back”. It is about a quick brown **fox** jumping over the back of a lazy **dog**. This sentence contains every letter of the English alphabet. That is why it was well suited for checking all the keys.

In films and in everyday speech people often talk about the “**red telephone**”. Red stands for danger and importance. The line was used to clear up **misunderstandings**, so that a nuclear war would not break out by mistake. Later the technology was renewed several times, for example with satellites.

gewusst: The test sentence with the fox and the dog is still often used today to check fonts and keyboards.
The link was tested regularly so that it would be sure to work in an emergency.

teile.einleitung: The civil registry office officially records the most important events in a person's life: birth, marriage and death. They are called civil status events. Every municipality in Switzerland belongs to a civil registry office.
wichtigste: The civil registry office records births, marriages, registered partnerships and deaths.
All events are recorded in the electronic register Infostar.
To marry, both people must be at least 18 years old.
Since 1 July 2022, same-sex couples have also been able to marry.
There are just over 170 civil registry offices in Switzerland.
The civil registry offices are supervised directly by the canton.

abschnitte.text: The **civil registry office** keeps records of people's **civil status**. It records births, marriages, registered partnerships and deaths. These are called **civil status events**. Changes of name are also recorded here. From the entries, the office issues documents, for example a **birth certificate**.

In the past, each **place of origin** kept its own family register on paper. Since the mid-2000s, all civil status events in Switzerland have been recorded in the central electronic register **Infostar**. That way every civil registry office can call up the data quickly. If a family has a **family booklet**, a new child is added to it.

Anyone who wants to marry registers with the civil registry office. Both people must be at least **18 years** old and may not be closely related. The wedding takes place in the civil registry office's wedding room; a church ceremony can follow later. From 1 January **2007**, same-sex couples could enter into a **registered partnership**. Since **1 July 2022**, **marriage for all** has applied.

There are just over **170 civil registry offices** in Switzerland. Each office is responsible for a **civil registry district**, made up of one or more municipalities. The offices report directly to the **supervisory authority** of their canton. The rules for everyone are in the Civil Code and in the Confederation's Civil Status Ordinance.

gewusst: Marriage for all was accepted in a popular vote in September 2021.
In Switzerland, every person with Swiss citizenship has a place of origin, even if they have never lived there.

teile.einleitung: In the Bay of Pigs invasion in April 1961, Cuban exiles with help from the USA tried to overthrow Fidel Castro's government in Cuba. The attack failed after about three days and became a serious defeat for the USA.
wichtigste: The landing began on 17 April 1961.
The CIA intelligence service planned the invasion and trained the Cuban exiles.
The unit was called Brigade 2506 and had about 1,400 men.
President John F. Kennedy gave the order.
The main fighting took place near Playa Girón.
At the end of 1962 the prisoners were released in exchange for food and medicine.

abschnitte.text: In 1959 **Fidel Castro** took power in Cuba after a revolution. He nationalised many companies, including American ones, and moved closer to the Soviet Union. Many Cubans fled to the USA. The US government wanted to overthrow Castro. The plan was drawn up by the **CIA** intelligence service while Eisenhower was still president.

The CIA trained around 1,400 Cuban exiles, **Brigade 2506**. Its name came from the service number of a member who had died in an accident during training. President **John F. Kennedy** gave the order in April 1961. On **17 April 1961** the invaders landed in the **Bay of Pigs** on the south coast of Cuba, at **Playa Girón** and Playa Larga. Officially, the involvement of the USA was supposed to stay hidden.

The Cuban army reacted quickly and was much stronger than expected. The hoped-for support from the population did not come. After about three days the invasion had failed. More than 1,100 invaders were taken prisoner. Kennedy publicly took responsibility for the failure. CIA director **Allen Dulles** had to leave his post at the end of 1961.

In December 1962 Cuba released the prisoners. In return it received **food and medicine** worth around 53 million dollars. In Cuba the event is still named after the beach of **Playa Girón** today and is celebrated as a victory.

On the eve of the fighting, Castro declared the Cuban revolution to be **socialist**. After that Cuba sought even more protection from the **Soviet Union**. In 1962 the Soviet Union stationed nuclear missiles on the island, which led to the **Cuban Missile Crisis**. Because the USA and Cuba no longer had relations, from 1961 **Switzerland** represented the interests of the USA in Cuba as the protecting power.

gewusst: Switzerland represented the interests of the USA in Cuba for more than 50 years, until an American embassy was opened again in 2015.
In Spanish the Bay of Pigs is called “Bahía de Cochinos”.

teile.einleitung: Every year, the Federal Assembly elects a president and a vice-president from among the members of the Federal Council. The vice-president is the deputy and also continues to head their own department.
wichtigste: The vice-president of the Federal Council is elected by the United Federal Assembly.
The office lasts one calendar year.
In 2023, Viola Amherd was vice-president, and Alain Berset was President of the Confederation.
In 2024, Karin Keller-Sutter was vice-president, and Viola Amherd was President of the Confederation.
In 2025, Guy Parmelin was vice-president, and Karin Keller-Sutter was President of the Confederation.
A President of the Confederation cannot become vice-president the following year.

abschnitte.text: The president and vice-president of the Federal Council are elected afresh **every year**. The election is carried out by the **United Federal Assembly**, that is the National Council and the Council of States together. Only people from among the **federal councillors** are elected. Like the presidency, the vice-presidency lasts one **calendar year**. After that there is a new election.

Whoever becomes vice-president remains **head of their department**. The task of **deputy** is simply added on. If the President of the Confederation is unable to act, the vice-president takes over their duties, such as chairing the meetings. The office brings no staff of its own and no special power. All the members of the Federal Council continue to decide together.

Usually the vice-president becomes **President of the Confederation** the following year. Recent years show this too. In **2023**, Alain Berset was President of the Confederation and **Viola Amherd** was his deputy. In **2024**, Viola Amherd was then President of the Confederation and **Karin Keller-Sutter** vice-president. In **2025**, Karin Keller-Sutter became President of the Confederation, and **Guy Parmelin** was her vice-president.

The **Federal Constitution** rules out the President of the Confederation becoming vice-president the year after. Nor can they be re-elected for the following year. That way the **offices change** regularly. Nobody should be at the top for too long. This fits the Federal Council as a **collegial body**, in which all members have equal rights.

gewusst: From the list of vice-presidents, you can usually tell who will be President of the Confederation the following year.
The election of the presidency always takes place in December during the winter session.

teile.einleitung: Every day, clean water flows out of our taps. The **water supply** makes sure of this. In Switzerland, the municipality is usually responsible for it.
wichtigste: About 80 per cent of drinking water comes from springs and groundwater.
Most of the rest comes from lakes.
In Switzerland, tap water is drinking water and is checked regularly.
Drinking water is stored in a reservoir.
Waste water flows through the sewers to the sewage treatment plant.
The fire brigade gets water for firefighting from a hydrant.

abschnitte.text: About **80 per cent** of drinking water in Switzerland comes from **spring water** and **groundwater**. Groundwater is water that seeps into the ground and collects there. Most of the rest comes from **lakes**. Lake water is treated especially thoroughly before it is drunk. Switzerland has a lot of water and is therefore sometimes called the water tower of Europe.

A **reservoir** is a large water store, often on a hill. From there the water flows through **pipes** under the ground into the houses. Because the reservoir is higher up, the water has enough pressure. The **water meter** measures how much water a house uses. From this, the municipality calculates how much you have to pay.

In Switzerland, tap water is often called **“Hahnenwasser”**. It is drinking water and is **checked** regularly. So you can drink it without worrying. Tap water is much cheaper than bottled water. Many fountains in villages and towns also provide drinking water.

Dirty water from the washbasin, shower and toilet is called **waste water**. It flows through the **sewers**, a network of pipes under the street. The sewers carry it to the **sewage treatment plant**. There the water is cleaned before it goes back into a river or lake. That way rivers and lakes stay clean.

Along many streets there are **hydrants**. They are connected to the water main. When there is a fire, the **fire brigade** connects its hoses there. That is why the water supply must always keep enough water ready, including for emergencies.

gewusst: Many Swiss towns and cities have public fountains you can drink from.
Swiss sewage treatment plants now clean almost all the waste water from households.

teile.einleitung: Boris Yeltsin was the first freely elected president of Russia. He became famous in 1991 when he stood on a tank in Moscow and called for resistance against a coup. He governed Russia at a time of great upheaval.
wichtigste: Yeltsin began his party career in the Sverdlovsk region in the Urals.
From 1985 he was party leader in Moscow; in 1987 he was removed.
In 1990 he publicly left the Communist Party.
In June 1991 he won Russia's first free presidential election.
In August 1991 he called for resistance against the coup from a tank.
On 31 December 1999 he resigned, and Vladimir Putin became his successor.
Yeltsin died in Moscow in 2007.

abschnitte.text: Boris Yeltsin was born in 1931 and first worked as a **civil engineer**. From 1976 to 1985 he led the party in the **Sverdlovsk** region in the Urals, today's Yekaterinburg. In 1985 **Mikhail Gorbachev** brought him in as a reformer to head the Moscow party organisation. Because he sharply criticised the pace of reform, he lost this post in 1987. In July 1990 he publicly left the **Communist Party of the Soviet Union** at the party congress.

On **12 June 1991**, Yeltsin won the first free presidential election in Russia. He took office in July 1991. At that time Russia was still part of the Soviet Union. Yeltsin campaigned for more independence for Russia. This made him the most important opponent of the old party leadership.

On **19 August 1991**, communist hardliners tried to seize power. In front of the **White House** in Moscow, Yeltsin climbed onto a tank and called for resistance. The picture went around the world. After three days the coup failed. At the end of 1991 the Soviet Union was dissolved, and Yeltsin now led an independent Russia.

From 1992 Russia carried out **shock therapy**: prices were freed quickly, and many state-owned companies were privatised. This led to high **inflation**, and a few so-called **oligarchs** became very rich. In October 1993, in a dispute with parliament, Yeltsin had the White House shelled. After that he pushed through a new **constitution** with a strong president.

In his final years, Yeltsin was in poor health. On **31 December 1999** he resigned unexpectedly. He handed over the presidential duties to his prime minister, **Vladimir Putin**, who was elected president in March 2000. Boris Yeltsin died in Moscow on 23 April **2007**, aged 76.

gewusst: The same White House that Yeltsin defended in 1991, he had shelled two years later.
Yeltsin's resignation came on New Year's Eve 1999, just before the turn of the millennium.

teile.einleitung: The **Westminster system** is a model of government from Great Britain. It is named after the parliament building in London. Many Commonwealth countries have adopted it.
wichtigste: The Westminster system is named after the Palace of Westminster in London.
The House of Commons is elected by relative majority voting in single-member constituencies.
Whoever leads the majority in the House of Commons becomes prime minister.
The largest opposition party forms a shadow cabinet.
Canada, Australia, New Zealand and India are governed according to this model.
Switzerland, on the other hand, has a directorial system.

abschnitte.text: In the **Palace of Westminster** in London, the two chambers of the British parliament meet: the **House of Commons** (lower house) and the House of Lords (upper house). The model of government that developed there is called the Westminster system. Later, many states of the **Commonwealth** adopted it, for example Canada, Australia, New Zealand and India.

In elections to the House of Commons in Great Britain, the **“first past the post”** system applies. In each constituency, whoever gets the most votes wins. This is called **relative majority voting** in single-member constituencies. This system favours large parties. It often produces a clear majority for one party.

Formally, the monarch appoints whoever has the confidence of the House of Commons. That is normally the leader of the majority party. This person becomes **prime minister**. The largest opposition party chooses a spokesperson for each ministry. This is called the **shadow cabinet**. That way an alternative government is ready.

abschnitte.titel: Debates in the House of Commons
abschnitte.text: Since 1997, the prime minister has answered questions from Members of Parliament for half an hour every **Wednesday** while parliament is sitting. These **Prime Minister's Questions** are often heated. The debates are led by the **Speaker**. After being elected, the Speaker leaves their party and chairs the sittings impartially. With the call “Order!”, the Speaker brings the chamber to quiet.

Switzerland has a **directorial system**. The Federal Council is elected by parliament for four years and cannot be brought down by a vote of no confidence. Several parties sit together on the Federal Council. That is why there is no official opposition with a shadow cabinet.

gewusst: In the House of Commons, government and opposition sit on benches directly facing each other.
In Canada and Australia, the British monarch is still formally head of state today.

teile.einleitung: **Voter turnout** shows how many voters actually cast their vote in an election. In Switzerland, fewer than half of voters take part in National Council elections.
wichtigste: Voter turnout is the share of all those entitled to vote who actually vote.
In the 2019 National Council elections it was 45.1 per cent, and in 2023 46.6 per cent.
It was lowest in 1995, at around 42 per cent.
The canton of Schaffhausen is the only one with compulsory voting.
Anyone in Schaffhausen who does not vote without a good reason pays 6 francs.
Young adults vote less often than older people.

abschnitte.text: To work out **voter turnout**, you divide the number of people who voted by the number of **people entitled to vote**. An example: a municipality has 4,000 voters, and 1,840 of them vote. You calculate 1,840 ÷ 4,000 = 0.46. So voter turnout is 46 per cent.

In the 2019 **National Council elections**, 45.1 per cent of voters went to vote. In 2023 the figure rose slightly to 46.6 per cent. Turnout was lowest in 1995, at around 42 per cent. Older figures cannot be compared directly: **women's right to vote** at federal level only came in 1971. Before that only men were allowed to vote, so the group of voters was much smaller.

The canton of **Schaffhausen** is the only canton that still has **compulsory voting**. Anyone who does not take part without an excuse pays a small fine of 6 francs. Even so, it works: turnout there is usually much higher than in the rest of Switzerland. In 2023, Schaffhausen reached 61.6 per cent, the highest of all the cantons.

abschnitte.titel: Why some people do not vote
abschnitte.text: Election studies show that **young adults** vote less often than older people. Turnout usually rises with age. The choice of candidates also plays a role. In 2023, in **Appenzell Innerrhoden**, only one candidate stood for the single National Council seat. Turnout there fell from 48.7 to 24.5 per cent.

gewusst: In some popular votes in Switzerland, more people go to the polls than in the National Council elections.
Many voters today vote by post from home.

teile.einleitung: The Era of Stagnation is the name for the years in which Leonid Brezhnev led the Soviet Union, roughly from 1964 to 1982. The economy hardly grew any more, and the leadership became older and older. The term stagnation, meaning standstill, was later coined by Mikhail Gorbachev.
wichtigste: The Era of Stagnation refers mainly to the Brezhnev years.
From 1986, Mikhail Gorbachev used the term standstill for this period.
The economy depended heavily on exports of oil and natural gas.
The Soviet Union had to import a lot of grain from the West.
Alongside the planned economy, a shadow economy grew.
Around 1980 the country was ruled by very old men; this is called gerontocracy.

abschnitte.text: **Stagnation** means standstill. In 1964 **Leonid Brezhnev** became party leader of the Soviet Union. He led the country until his death in 1982. During this time, life was calmer and more secure for many people than before. But the economy grew more and more slowly, and there were no reforms. From 1986, **Mikhail Gorbachev** called these years “zastoi”, meaning standstill. He used this to explain why he needed reforms.

In 1965, Prime Minister **Alexei Kosygin** tried with the **Kosygin reform** to give businesses more responsibility and incentives to make a profit. But the reform was soon watered down. The economy kept afloat mainly through **exports of oil and natural gas**. After the **1973 oil crisis**, prices rose sharply, and new deposits were opened up in **Siberia**. When the oil price fell in the mid-1980s, the crisis became much worse.

**Collective farming** was not very productive. From the 1970s the Soviet Union therefore regularly bought **grain** from the USA and Canada. Many things were missing from the shops, and people often had to queue for a long time. People got hold of goods through connections, in Russian “**blat**”, and on black markets. This **shadow economy** grew strongly and undermined the **planned economy**.

Towards the end of the Brezhnev years, the leading politicians were very old. A regime led by old men is called a **gerontocracy**. Brezhnev died in office in 1982, aged 75. His successor, **Yuri Andropov**, had previously been head of the **KGB** secret service for 15 years. He died as early as February 1984. His successor, **Konstantin Chernenko**, also died after a short time. Between 1982 and 1985, three party leaders died one after another.

During the Brezhnev years there were phases of **détente** with the West. In 1975 the Soviet Union signed the **Helsinki Final Act**. At the same time, it kept the countries of the Eastern Bloc firmly under control. In 1979 the Soviet army invaded **Afghanistan**. That is why many Western countries boycotted the **1980 Olympic Games in Moscow**. Switzerland took part anyway, with a small team.

gewusst: Andropov and Chernenko were 68 and 72 years old when they took office.
Gorbachev was only 54 when he was chosen in 1985, much younger than his predecessors.

teile.einleitung: Base and superstructure are two terms from the teachings of Karl Marx. They describe how a society's economy is connected with law, politics, religion and art. According to Marx, economic conditions shape the way people think.
wichtigste: The base is the sum of the relations of production, that is the economic structure.
The superstructure includes law, the state, politics, religion, philosophy and art.
According to Marx, social being determines consciousness.
Engels stressed that the economy is only determining “in the last instance”.
According to Marx, the ruling ideas are the ideas of the ruling class.
In 1970 Louis Althusser coined the term “ideological state apparatuses”.

abschnitte.text: By **base**, Marx means the economic foundation of a society. This includes how goods are produced and distributed. It also matters who owns the **means of production**, that is factories, machines and land. For Marx, these **relations of production** form the foundation. Everything else rises up on top of it.

The **superstructure** includes **law**, the **state**, **politics**, **religion**, **philosophy** and **art**. In his preface of 1859, Marx wrote: it is not consciousness that determines being, but **social being** that determines consciousness. Put simply: the way people live and work shapes their thinking. As early as 1844, Marx called religion the **“opium of the people”**. It comforted people in their misery, he said, without removing its causes.

Marx and Engels believed that the ruling ideas of an era are the ideas of the **ruling class**. Whoever owns the material means of production also controls the means of intellectual production. That way this class shapes what is regarded as right and normal in a society. Critics argue, however, that ideas also arise independently of the economy.

In 1890, in a letter to Joseph Bloch, Friedrich **Engels** wrote that the economy is only determining **“in the last instance”**. The superstructure, he said, also has an effect on history. In 1970 the French Marxist **Louis Althusser** coined the term **ideological state apparatuses**. By this he meant school, church, family and media, which secure rule through ideas rather than through force.

gewusst: The famous preface of 1859 belongs to the work **“A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy”**.
Engels warned that anyone who makes the economy the only determining factor distorts the theory.

teile.einleitung: The February Revolution of 1917 ended the rule of the tsars in Russia. Within a few days, protests against hunger and war turned into an overthrow, after which a Provisional Government took charge.
wichtigste: The revolution began in Petrograd, today's St Petersburg.
It is called the February Revolution because Russia still used the Julian calendar. By our calendar it was March.
On International Women's Day, women textile workers took to the streets.
The soldiers in the capital refused to shoot at the demonstrators.
Tsar Nicholas II abdicated, and Prince Georgy Lvov then led the Provisional Government.
From July 1917 Alexander Kerensky was head of government.

abschnitte.text: Russia had been fighting in the **First World War** since 1914 and had suffered heavy losses. In the winter of 1917 there was a shortage of food and fuel. Long queues formed outside the bakeries in **Petrograd**. The city had had this name since 1914 because the old name “Petersburg” sounded too German. Many people were exhausted and angry with the tsar's government.

Until 1918 Russia used the **Julian calendar**. At that time it was 13 days behind the **Gregorian calendar**, which we use today. So 23 February in the old style corresponds to 8 March. On that day, **International Women's Day**, women textile workers went on strike. Within a few days their protests turned into a **general strike**.

The tsar ordered the unrest to be crushed. But many regiments in Petrograd refused to shoot at the people and went over to the rebels. With that the government lost its power in the capital. Tsar **Nicholas II** abdicated in March 1917. The rule of the Romanov family, which had lasted more than 300 years, was over.

Politicians from the **Duma**, the parliament, formed a **Provisional Government**, that is, a temporary government. At first it was led by **Prince Georgy Lvov**, and from July 1917 by **Alexander Kerensky**. At the same time the **Petrograd Soviet** was formed, a council of workers and soldiers. With **Order No. 1** it placed the soldiers under elected committees. Because both sides held power, this is called dual power.

abschnitte.titel: The road to the October Revolution
abschnitte.text: The Provisional Government carried on the war against Germany. This made it unpopular with many soldiers and workers who were tired of war. In April 1917 **Lenin** returned from exile in Switzerland; he had most recently lived in Zurich. He demanded peace and “all power to the soviets”. In the **October Revolution** his Bolsheviks overthrew Kerensky's government.

gewusst: In 1917 Lenin travelled from Zurich by train right across Germany to Russia. The German government allowed the journey because it hoped the fighting in the east would end.
By our calendar, the October Revolution actually took place in November too.

teile.einleitung: When it snows or there is black ice, the **winter road service** goes into action. It clears snow and spreads salt so that roads and pavements stay safe. The work often starts in the middle of the night.
wichtigste: The snowplough pushes the snow off the road.
Salt makes ice melt; grit stops you slipping.
The winter road service often starts very early in the morning.
Snow poles show where the road ends.
Small clearing vehicles clear pavements and cycle paths.
Municipal roads are usually cleared by the municipality's public works service.

abschnitte.text: The **snowplough** has a wide blade at the front. With it, it pushes the snow to the side. For **pavements** and cycle paths, small narrow clearing vehicles are needed, because large ploughs are too wide. The winter road service often starts during the night or **very early in the morning**. That way the roads are clear when people go to work and school.

On icy roads, the winter road service spreads **salt** or **grit**. Salt makes ice and snow melt. Grit consists of small stones that stop you slipping. Salt works well but can damage plants and soil. That is why it is used as sparingly as possible.

In autumn, **snow poles** are put up along the side of the road. When there is a lot of snow, you can no longer see the edge of the road. The poles show the snowplough where the road ends. That way it does not drive into a ditch or across a meadow.

In many municipalities, the municipality's **public works service** clears the municipal roads. Larger roads are often cleared by the **canton**. The **Confederation** is responsible for the motorways. In some municipalities, homeowners must make sure themselves that the path in front of their house is safe.

It is easy to slip on **black ice**. That is why you walk carefully and wear shoes with a good tread. A snowplough drives slowly and throws snow to the side. That is why cars keep **enough distance** and do not overtake dangerously.

gewusst: On many mountain pass roads, the winter road service would be so demanding that the passes are closed completely in winter.
Some municipalities store hundreds of tonnes of road salt before winter.

teile.einleitung: Andrei Sakharov was a Soviet nuclear physicist who became one of the best-known campaigners for human rights. He worked for peace and freedom of expression. For this he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1975 and was later sent into internal exile.
wichtigste: As a nuclear physicist, Sakharov worked on developing Soviet nuclear weapons.
From the late 1950s he campaigned for an end to nuclear tests above ground.
In 1968 his essay on progress, coexistence and intellectual freedom circulated underground.
In 1970 he co-founded the Moscow Human Rights Committee.
He was married to the civil rights activist Yelena Bonner.
In December 1986, after a phone call from Gorbachev, he was allowed to return from exile.
He died in December 1989; in 1988 the European Parliament named a prize after him.

abschnitte.text: Andrei Sakharov was born **in Moscow in 1921**. As a young **physicist** he worked in secret weapons research. He played a leading part in developing the Soviet **hydrogen bomb**. From the late 1950s he warned that radioactive fallout from **nuclear tests** harms people. In 1963, in the **Moscow Treaty**, the great powers banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere.

In **1968** Sakharov wrote the essay **“Reflections on Progress, Peaceful Coexistence and Intellectual Freedom”**. In it he called for East and West to move closer together. The essay spread through **samizdat**, meaning it was secretly copied by hand, and was published in the West. After that Sakharov lost his job in weapons research. In 1970 he and other scientists founded the **Moscow Human Rights Committee**.

In **1975** Sakharov received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. The government would not let him travel to Oslo, so his wife **Yelena Bonner** accepted the prize. She was a doctor and herself a well-known dissident. In 1980 Sakharov criticised the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. As a result, he was exiled to the city of **Gorky**, where he was closely watched.

In **December 1986**, a **telephone** was specially installed in Sakharov's flat in Gorky. Through it **Mikhail Gorbachev** called him and told him he could return to Moscow. His release was seen as a sign of the new openness, **glasnost**. In 1989 Sakharov was elected as a member of parliament. On **14 December 1989** he died, shortly after giving a speech. Tens of thousands came to his funeral.

Since **1988**, the **European Parliament** has awarded the **Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought**. It honours people and groups who work for human rights and freedom of expression. The prize is awarded every year in **Strasbourg**. Those honoured have included Nelson Mandela and Malala Yousafzai. That way Sakharov's work lives on.

gewusst: Sakharov took part in developing the hydrogen bomb and later became one of the best-known peace activists.
The city of Gorky, to which he was exiled, is now called Nizhny Novgorod again.

teile.einleitung: Basel used to be a single canton. Since 1833 there have been two half-cantons: **Basel-Stadt** and **Basel-Landschaft**. Again and again there have been votes on whether they should join together again.
wichtigste: In 1833 the canton of Basel was divided.
The battle at the Hülftenschanz sealed the separation.
In 1969 the city voted yes to reunification, but Basel-Landschaft voted no.
In 2014 Basel-Stadt voted yes by around 55 per cent, but Basel-Landschaft rejected it.
A merger needs the approval of both cantons.
Today the two Basels work together as partners.

abschnitte.text: In the early 1830s, the countryside demanded more political rights from the city. There was unrest. On 3 August 1833, the city's troops were defeated at the **Hülftenschanz** near Frenkendorf. After that, the **Diet** (Tagsatzung) divided the canton. Since then there have been Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft.

In the 20th century, the wish for **reunification** grew. A constitutional council drew up a common constitution. On 7 December 1969 the city said yes, but **Basel-Landschaft** clearly said no. Since then, the guiding idea in Basel-Landschaft has tended to be **partnership instead of merger**.

On 28 September 2014, both cantons voted at the same time on a **merger initiative**. If both had said yes, a joint **constitutional council** would have drawn up a constitution for a new canton. There would have been another vote on this later. Basel-Stadt said yes by around 55 per cent. Because Basel-Landschaft rejected it, the yes had no effect.

A merger changes the existence of two cantons. That is why the voters in **both cantons** must agree. According to Article 53 of the Federal Constitution, the approval of **the people and the cantons** of the whole of Switzerland would also be needed. Joint projects can fail too: in 2019 Basel-Stadt rejected a joint **hospital group**, even though Basel-Landschaft approved it.

Instead of merging, the two cantons work closely together in many areas. For example, they jointly fund the **University of Basel**. They regulate many tasks through **intercantonal agreements**. That way they can work together and still remain independent.

gewusst: The University of Basel was founded in 1460 and is the oldest university in Switzerland.
In terms of area, Basel-Stadt is one of the smallest cantons in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Joseph Stalin was the dictator of the Soviet Union from the 1920s until his death in 1953. Under his rule the country became an industrial power and defeated Hitler's Germany in the Second World War. At the same time millions of people were persecuted, locked up in camps or killed.
wichtigste: Joseph Stalin lived from 1878 to 1953 and came from Georgia.
He was the dictator of the Soviet Union, under whom millions of people were persecuted.
His real name was Ioseb Jughashvili; Stalin means “the man of steel”.
After Lenin's death in 1924 he won the power struggle against his rivals.
With five-year plans and forced collectivisation he built up industry.
In the Great Terror from 1936 to 1938 he had hundreds of thousands executed.
In the Second World War he led the Soviet Union to victory over Germany.

abschnitte.text: Stalin was born in December **1878** in **Gori** in Georgia; his name was Ioseb Jughashvili. His mother wanted him to become a priest and sent him to a seminary in Tiflis. But there he became a revolutionary and joined Lenin's **Bolsheviks**. Because he took part in robberies and uprisings, he was arrested several times and exiled to Siberia.

After the Russian Revolution of 1917, Stalin rose in the party and in 1922 became its **general secretary**. After **Lenin's** death in 1924, several politicians fought for the leadership. Stalin got rid of his rivals, such as Leon Trotsky, one after another. By the end of the 1920s he was the undisputed sole ruler of the Soviet Union.

With the **five-year plans**, Stalin had huge factories, power stations and towns built in a short time. The peasants were forced to hand over their farms to **kolkhozes**. This led to severe famines, such as the Holodomor in Ukraine. Many building projects were carried out by prisoners from the **Gulag**.

Stalin distrusted everyone and had supposed enemies persecuted. In the **Great Terror** from 1936 to 1938 about 700,000 people were shot, including many officers and party members. In **show trials** the accused had to confess to crimes they had never committed. Whole ethnic groups, such as the Chechens or the Crimean Tatars, were deported to distant regions.

In 1939 Stalin signed a **non-aggression pact** with Hitler, but in 1941 Germany attacked the Soviet Union. After heavy losses the Red Army won victories, for example in the Battle of **Stalingrad**, and captured Berlin in 1945. Around 27 million people from the Soviet Union died in the war. After the war Stalin brought Eastern Europe under Soviet influence, and the Cold War began.

Stalin died on 5 March **1953** at his dacha near Moscow. During his lifetime he was worshipped like a hero and his pictures hung everywhere; this is called a **cult of personality**. In 1956 his successor Nikita Khrushchev criticised Stalin's crimes in a secret speech. Today historians see him as one of the cruellest dictators of the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ruler who governs alone and without control by a parliament or the courts.
When a ruler has to be worshipped excessively like a hero or demigod.
A trial in which the verdict has been decided in advance and which serves only as propaganda.
Forcibly moving people to another area.
The head of the Communist Party in the Soviet Union.

gewusst: From 1925 to 1961 the city of Volgograd was called Stalingrad.
In photos from Stalin's time, people who had fallen out of favour were often retouched out afterwards.
In Gori, Stalin's birthplace, there is still a large Stalin Museum today.

teile.einleitung: Diversity means that people are different, for example in appearance, language, origin or belief. In Switzerland, a great many different people live together.
wichtigste: Diversity means that there are many different kinds.
Switzerland has four national languages.
About one person in four in Switzerland does not have a Swiss passport.
People celebrate different festivals, such as Christmas, Hanukkah, Eid al-Fitr or Diwali.
In a diverse class, you can learn from each other.
Despite all their differences, all people have the same dignity.

abschnitte.text: **Diversity** means that people are different. They look different, speak other languages or believe in different things. Some like playing football, others prefer reading or making music. That is exactly what makes life colourful. In a class, children with different experiences bring different ideas, so **everyone learns from each other**.

Switzerland has four **national languages**: German, French, Italian and Romansh. On top of that there are many other languages that people here speak. According to the **Federal Statistical Office**, at the end of 2025 about **one person in four** did not have a Swiss passport. Many of them have lived here for a long time or were born here. The preamble of the Federal Constitution speaks of living out **diversity in unity**.

At **Christmas**, Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus; in Switzerland, 25 December is a public holiday. At the end of the month of fasting, **Ramadan**, Muslims celebrate the festival of breaking the fast, also known as the **“Sugar Festival”** (Eid al-Fitr). The Jewish festival of lights, **Hanukkah**, lasts eight days, and every evening one more candle is lit on a candlestick. Many Hindus celebrate **Diwali**, the great festival of lights with lots of small lights.

People are different, yet every person has the **same dignity**. This is also written in the **Federal Constitution**. Nobody may be disadvantaged, for example because of their origin, language, religion or a disability. This is called the **ban on discrimination**. If you respect others, you help everyone live together well.

gewusst: Many festivals of different religions have something in common: lights and candles play an important role.
Romansh is spoken only in the canton of the Grisons, and yet it is a national language of the whole of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: According to Karl Marx, the classless society is the final goal of the communist movement. It means a society without rich and poor, in which factories, land and machines belong to everyone together. This goal has never been reached in any country in the world.
wichtigste: According to Karl Marx, the classless society was the long-term final goal of the communist movement.
In it there was to be no more private ownership of the means of production.
According to Marx, without owners and people who own nothing there would also be no classes and no class struggle.
The way there was to lead through a revolution and a transition period.
In the end even the state was to become unnecessary and wither away.
No communist country has ever reached this goal.
Instead a new, privileged ruling class often formed in these states.

abschnitte.text: A **classless society** is a society in which there are no longer classes such as workers and factory owners. Factories, machines and land, the so-called **means of production**, are to belong to everyone together. But you may still own personal things such as clothes, furniture or books. Nobody should have to work for someone else any more so that the other person becomes rich.

Marx imagined the path in several stages. First the workers were to take power in a **revolution**. In a transition period, which he called the **dictatorship of the proletariat**, the working class was to run the state. This was to be followed by **socialism** and finally by communism as a classless society.

abschnitte.titel: What it was meant to look like
abschnitte.text: In communism the rule was to be: from each according to their abilities, to each according to their needs. This means everyone works as well as they can and gets what they need. Because there would be no more classes fighting each other, the **state** with its police and army would also no longer be needed. Engels said that the state would then **wither away**.

In states such as the Soviet Union, China or the GDR, private ownership of factories and land was abolished. But instead of disappearing, the state became more and more powerful and controlled the whole of life. A new upper class of party officials emerged, known as the **nomenklatura**. In 1957 the Yugoslav politician Milovan Djilas described this group in his book The New Class.

abschnitte.titel: Similar ideas on a small scale
abschnitte.text: The idea of a community without rich and poor is much older than Marx; as early as 1516 the Englishman Thomas More described the imaginary island of **Utopia**. In Israel there are the **kibbutzim**, villages in which for a long time the inhabitants owned everything together and lived together voluntarily. **Cooperatives**, such as the housing cooperatives in Switzerland, also belong jointly to many members. But they are part of a market economy and not a classless society.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of people in a similar economic situation, for example the working class.
Something that belongs to a single person or company.
The idea of an ideal society that does not yet exist in reality.
The privileged ruling class in communist states.
An association of people who jointly own a business.

gewusst: The word Utopia was invented by Thomas More and means something like “no place”.
Switzerland's two largest retailers, Migros and Coop, are organised as cooperatives.
Marx himself never described exactly what everyday life in a classless society would be like.

teile.einleitung: The magic formula is a rule for how the seven seats on the Federal Council are shared among the major parties. It was created in 1959 and lasted for over four decades. It is an example of Swiss concordance, in which the most important parties govern together.
wichtigste: The magic formula was first applied in December 1959.
It shared the seats like this: 2 FDP, 2 Catholic Conservatives, 2 SP and 1 BGB.
Martin Rosenberg, general secretary of the Catholic Conservatives, is regarded as its architect.
The official SP candidate, Walther Bringolf, was not elected in 1959.
In 2003 the SVP gained a second seat at the expense of the CVP.
In 2007 Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf was elected instead of Christoph Blocher.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Council** has seven members. The **magic formula** sets out how many seats each major party gets. From 1959, the Free Democrats (**FDP**), the Catholic Conservatives (later the **CVP**) and the Social Democrats (**SP**) each got two seats. The Farmers', Traders' and Citizens' Party (**BGB**, later the **SVP**) got one seat. That way the four strongest parties were represented in the government.

Between 1954 and 1959, the SP was not on the Federal Council. Its federal councillor, **Max Weber**, had resigned at the end of 1953 after his finance proposal was rejected. **Martin Rosenberg**, general secretary of the Catholic Conservatives, planned the SP's return with two seats. This was also meant to push back the influence of the Free Democrats. On **17 December 1959**, the Federal Assembly elected the new line-up.

The SP proposed **Walther Bringolf**, the mayor of Schaffhausen. He was controversial because of his communist past. The Federal Assembly therefore elected a different Social Democrat in his place. This shows a special feature of Switzerland: parliament is not bound by the parties' official candidates.

In the 1990s the SVP grew stronger and stronger. In December **2003**, **Christoph Blocher** was elected instead of the sitting federal councillor **Ruth Metzler**. This gave the SVP two seats and left the CVP with only one. In December **2007**, the Federal Assembly elected the SVP politician **Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf** from the Grisons instead of Blocher. The SVP parliamentary group then declared itself to be in opposition for a time.

The magic formula is based on **concordance**. This means that the major parties govern together and look for compromises. In Switzerland this is important because the people have a great deal of say through the **referendum** and the **initiative**. A government with broad support has a better chance of getting its proposals accepted at the ballot box. How the seats should be fairly shared is still discussed again and again today.

gewusst: The magic formula of 1959 remained unchanged for 44 years, until 2003.
The magic formula is not written in any law: it is an agreement between the parties.

teile.einleitung: Kim Jong-un is the ruler of North Korea, one of the most isolated countries in the world. He has ruled the communist country since the end of 2011 as the successor to his father and grandfather. He is known around the world mainly because of his country's nuclear weapons and missile tests.
wichtigste: Kim Jong-un rules communist North Korea today.
He came to power at the end of 2011 after the death of his father Kim Jong-il.
His grandfather Kim Il-sung founded North Korea in 1948.
As a teenager he went to school near Bern under a different name.
Under him North Korea has tested several atomic bombs and many missiles.
In 2018 and 2019 he met US President Donald Trump several times.
In North Korea there are no free elections, no free press and prison camps for opponents.

abschnitte.text: Kim Jong-un was born in the 1980s; the exact year is not known for certain, and **1984** is usually given. He is a son of **Kim Jong-il**, who ruled North Korea from 1994 to 2011. As a teenager he lived for some years in **Switzerland** and went to a school in Liebefeld near Bern under a false name. After that he studied at a military university in Pyongyang.

North Korea has been ruled by the same family since it was founded in **1948**. First **Kim Il-sung** ruled, then his son Kim Jong-il, and since December **2011** his son Kim Jong-un. The Kim family is worshipped like heroes in North Korea, and their pictures hang everywhere. Kim Jong-un is head of the ruling **Workers' Party of Korea** and head of state.

Under Kim Jong-un North Korea has greatly expanded its **nuclear weapons** and carried out several underground nuclear tests, the last in 2017. The country also repeatedly tests missiles that can fly very long distances. The United Nations has therefore imposed strict **sanctions** on North Korea. Neighbouring countries such as South Korea and Japan feel threatened by this.

In 2018 Kim Jong-un became the first North Korean ruler to meet a sitting US president, **Donald Trump**, in Singapore. This was followed in 2019 by a meeting in Hanoi and a short meeting at the border in **Panmunjom**. He also met the South Korean president several times. But no lasting agreement on nuclear weapons was reached.

North Korea is a strict **dictatorship** and almost completely cut off from the world. People may not travel freely, and the internet is blocked for almost everyone. Critics of the government are sent to **prison camps**, and even high-ranking people have been executed, such as Kim's uncle in 2013. Many people are poor, and there have been repeated famines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who holds power in a state, often without having been elected.
Penalties against a country, for example a ban on trade.
A form of rule in which one person or group has all the power and the people cannot vote freely.
The capital of North Korea.

gewusst: Kim Jong-un is said to have been a big basketball fan during his school days in Switzerland.
North Korea has its own calendar, which begins with the year Kim Il-sung was born.
When he came to power, Kim Jong-un was only about 27 years old.

teile.einleitung: Civilian service is service for the community without weapons. It is done by men who cannot reconcile military service with their conscience. It has existed in Switzerland since 1996.
wichtigste: Civilian service has existed in Switzerland since 1996.
It is for people who cannot reconcile military service with their conscience.
Civilian service lasts one and a half times as long as military service.
People doing civilian service carry no weapons.
They work in recognised placement organisations, for example in hospitals, care homes for the elderly, schools or nature conservation.
Before 1996, people who refused military service were punished, often with prison.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, men are **obliged to do military service**. Anyone who cannot reconcile service with weapons with their **conscience** may do **civilian service** instead. Personal convenience is not a good enough reason. Civilian service is service **without weapons**. Someone doing it is called a **“Zivi”** in everyday speech.

People doing civilian service work in a recognised **placement organisation**. This can be a hospital, a care home for the elderly, a home for people with disabilities or a school. In **nature conservation**, they look after meadows, hedges and footpaths and so help plants and animals. Others support mountain farmers or help after storms. A placement can be worthwhile anywhere people or nature need help.

Civilian service lasts **one and a half times as long** as military service. So anyone who would have to serve 100 days in the army serves 150 days in civilian service. The longer duration is regarded as proof that you are serious about your conscience. This is called the **proof by action**. Since 2009 there has no longer been an oral examination of conscience in front of a commission.

For a long time there was no civilian alternative service in Switzerland. **People who refused military service** were sentenced by military courts, often to **prison sentences**. After long political debates, the people approved a constitutional article for civilian service in 1992. The **Civilian Service Act** came into force in **1996**. Today many thousands of men do civilian service every year.

gewusst: A person doing civilian service can split their service into several placements, for example in different organisations.
In Switzerland, women are not obliged to do military service and so cannot do civilian service.

teile.einleitung: The vice-president of the Federal Council stands in for the President of the Confederation when the president is unable to act. By tradition, the vice-president becomes President of the Confederation the following year.
wichtigste: The vice-president stands in for the President of the Confederation when needed.
The vice-president is elected each December by the United Federal Assembly.
By tradition, the vice-president becomes President of the Confederation the following year.
Who becomes vice-president depends on length of service, the principle of seniority.
Article 176 of the Federal Constitution rules out the President of the Confederation becoming vice-president the following year.
In 2026, Ignazio Cassis is vice-president; he heads the FDFA.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Council has seven members. One is **President of the Confederation**, another is **vice-president**. If the President of the Confederation is absent, the **vice-president chairs the meetings** and takes on representative duties. Otherwise the vice-president runs their own **department** as normal. The office lasts one year.

The President of the Confederation and the vice-president are elected each year during the **winter session in December**. The election always applies to the **following year**. They are elected by the **United Federal Assembly**, that is the National Council and the Council of States together. By tradition, it elects the previous vice-president as the new **President of the Confederation**. Legally, however, it is not obliged to do so.

The two offices rotate according to the **principle of seniority**. Seniority means length of service. Whoever has gone longest without being president, or has never been president, moves forward in the queue. **Article 176** of the Federal Constitution rules out the President of the Confederation being re-elected or elected vice-president for the following year. This ensures that the offices change regularly.

In **2026**, **Ignazio Cassis** is vice-president of the Federal Council. Since 2017 he has headed the **Federal Department of Foreign Affairs**, **FDFA** for short. So the vice-president in 2026 is also the foreign minister. The President of the Confederation this year is Guy Parmelin. By tradition, Cassis would become President of the Confederation in 2027.

gewusst: The President of the Confederation is not a head of state with special powers but “first among equals” in the Federal Council.
Because the offices change every year, almost every member of the Federal Council becomes vice-president once during their time in office.

teile.einleitung: Customs duty is a charge on goods that come across the border. In Switzerland, the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security deals with this. It checks goods and protects the border.
wichtigste: Customs duty is a charge on certain goods that come across the border.
Switzerland borders five countries: Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.
Switzerland and Liechtenstein have formed a common customs area since 1924.
Since 2022 the customs authority has been called the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security, FOCBS for short.
Customs dogs help find hidden drugs.
Since 2025, the duty-free limit for shopping abroad has been 150 francs per person per day.

abschnitte.text: **Customs duty** is a charge that you pay for certain goods when they are brought into a country. Customs also checks whether forbidden things are being brought across the border, such as drugs or dangerous weapons. There are special rules for animals, plants and food. That way people, nature and the domestic economy are protected.

Switzerland borders **five countries**: Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein. There are customs offices on roads, at railway stations and at airports. Switzerland and **Liechtenstein** have formed a common **customs area** since **1924**. That is why there are no customs checks on this border. By the way, people in Liechtenstein also pay with Swiss francs.

Since 2022 the Confederation's customs authority has been called the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security**, **FOCBS** (BAZG) for short. It used to be called the Federal Customs Administration. The staff check lorries, parcels and travellers. **Customs dogs** help them. They have a very sensitive nose and can sniff out drugs or money in suitcases.

Many people in Switzerland go shopping just across the border. Up to a certain value, you may bring goods back without paying **VAT**. Since 2025 this **duty-free limit** has been **150 francs** per person per day; before that it was 300 francs. For some goods, such as meat, alcohol or tobacco, there are also limits on quantities. Anyone who brings back more must declare the goods at customs.

gewusst: There is a federal app for declaring purchases, with which you can pay the charges even before reaching the border.
Customs dogs are specially trained and work as a team with their handler.

teile.einleitung: The Soviet Union was founded on 30 December 1922. It was a union of Soviet republics led by the Communist Party and lasted until 1991.
wichtigste: The founding treaty was signed in Moscow on 30 December 1922.
The full name was the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, USSR for short.
Four republics founded the state: Russia, Ukraine, Belorussia and Transcaucasia.
In 1924 the Soviet Union received its first constitution.
The flag was red and showed a hammer, a sickle and a star.
Until 1944 the Internationale was the anthem of the Soviet Union.

abschnitte.text: In 1917 the Bolsheviks under **Lenin** had taken power in Russia. This was followed by a long civil war, which they won. Soviet republics were also set up in other areas of the former Russian Empire. On **30 December 1922** their representatives signed the founding treaty in **Moscow**. This created the **Union of Soviet Socialist Republics**, **USSR** for short. In Russian the abbreviation was SSSR.

The Soviet Union was founded by four republics: **Russia**, **Ukraine**, **Belorussia** and the **Transcaucasian Republic**. The last of these united Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan and lasted until 1936. After that the three countries became separate Union republics. Already in 1922 there was a dispute over Georgia, the so-called **Georgian Affair**. Stalin acted harshly against Georgian communists, which Lenin sharply criticised.

At the beginning of **1924** the USSR received its first **constitution**. Later constitutions followed in 1936 and 1977. The **flag** was red and showed a **hammer and sickle** in the top left corner with a star above. The hammer and sickle stood for the workers and the peasants. Until 1944 the anthem was the **Internationale**, the battle song of the workers' movement from France.

For a long time Switzerland had **no diplomatic relations** with the Soviet Union. In 1923 the Soviet diplomat **Vatslav Vorovsky** was shot dead in Lausanne. A Swiss court acquitted the killer, which greatly angered the Soviet Union. Only in 1946 did the two countries establish diplomatic relations.

Over time more republics were added, for example in Central Asia. The **Baltic states** were occupied and annexed in 1940. In the end the Soviet Union consisted of 15 Union republics. It was the largest state on Earth by area. In 1991 it broke up into independent states.

gewusst: Lenin barely lived to see the first constitution; he died in January 1924.
The Soviet Union stretched across eleven time zones, from Europe to the Pacific.

teile.einleitung: The Brezhnev Doctrine was a principle of Soviet policy from 1968. It stated that the sovereignty of socialist states was limited. The Soviet Union used it to justify crushing the Prague Spring.
