wichtigste: The doctrine was formulated in 1968 after the invasion of Czechoslovakia.
Its core statement: the sovereignty of socialist states is limited.
It is named after the Soviet party leader Leonid Brezhnev.
Romania did not take part in the 1968 invasion.
In 1989 it was replaced by the so-called Sinatra Doctrine.
In 1968 Switzerland took in around 12,000 refugees from Czechoslovakia.

abschnitte.text: In January 1968, **Alexander Dubček** became party leader of Czechoslovakia. He introduced reforms and spoke of **“socialism with a human face”**. People gained more freedom of expression, and censorship was relaxed. The Soviet Union saw this as a danger to its rule in Eastern Europe.

During the night of **20 to 21 August 1968**, troops of the **Warsaw Pact** invaded Czechoslovakia. The Prague Spring was ended. **Romania** did not take part; its leader Nicolae Ceaușescu publicly condemned the invasion. The GDR did provide troops, but they did not cross the border. Dubček was removed and replaced by **Gustáv Husák**.

The doctrine provided the justification for the invasion afterwards. If socialism was threatened in a **brother country**, the other socialist states were entitled to intervene. That is why it is also called the doctrine of **limited sovereignty**. In Czechoslovakia, the so-called **normalisation** followed: reformers were removed from the party and from their jobs. Around half a million party members were expelled or struck off.

After the invasion, many people left Czechoslovakia. **Switzerland** took in around **12,000** refugees. They were taken in without much red tape, and the welcome was regarded as especially warm. Many of these people stayed and built a new life for themselves in Switzerland.

Under **Mikhail Gorbachev**, the Soviet Union abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine. In 1989 the government spokesman **Gennadi Gerasimov** jokingly spoke of the **Sinatra Doctrine**. He was referring to Frank Sinatra's song “My Way”: every country in the Eastern Bloc should be allowed to go its own way. Shortly afterwards, communist rule ended in many countries of Eastern Europe.

gewusst: The name “Sinatra Doctrine” comes from a song that ends with the words “I did it my way”.
Many of the 1968 refugees are still regarded today as an example of successful integration in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A veto is the right to stop a decision. Especially well known is the veto of the President of the USA against laws passed by Congress.
wichtigste: “Veto” is Latin and means “I forbid”.
The US president has ten days, not counting Sundays, to sign or reject a bill.
With a veto, the bill goes back to the chamber where it was introduced.
Congress can overrule a veto; this is called an override.
With a pocket veto, the president simply leaves a bill unsigned.
Franklin D. Roosevelt used the most vetoes, 635.

abschnitte.text: **Veto** is Latin and means **“I forbid”**. It comes from the verb “vetare”, to forbid. In ancient **Rome**, the **tribunes of the people** could already stop decisions with this word. Today there are rights of veto in many states and organisations. In the **UN Security Council**, for example, the five permanent members have a right of veto.

When **Congress** passes a bill, the president has **ten days**, not counting Sundays. They can sign it or use a **veto**. With a veto, they send the bill back with their reasons to the **chamber** where it was introduced. If they do nothing and Congress is still sitting, the bill becomes law even without a signature. Franklin D. Roosevelt used **635 vetoes** in his more than twelve years in office, more than anyone else.

Congress can **overrule** a veto. For this, both chambers must pass the bill again with a **two-thirds majority**. This is called an **override**, and afterwards the law comes into force without the president's signature. It is different with the **pocket veto**: if Congress adjourns within the ten-day period, the president can simply leave the bill unsigned. This veto cannot be overruled.

A **partial veto** would allow individual items to be struck out of a budget. The **Line Item Veto Act** of 1996 gave the US president this right. But in 1998 the **Supreme Court** declared the law **unconstitutional** in the case of Clinton v. City of New York. Since then, the president has had to accept or reject a bill as a whole. In Switzerland, the Federal Council has no right of veto against laws passed by parliament.

gewusst: In second place among the presidents with the most vetoes is Grover Cleveland.
In the UN Security Council, the USA, Russia, China, France and Great Britain have a right of veto.

teile.einleitung: A ballot box is a container into which you put your ballot paper in an election or vote. It makes sure that nobody can see how someone voted. Only when the polling station closes is the ballot box opened and the votes counted.
wichtigste: A ballot box is a container into which you put your ballot paper.
The ballot box is locked so that nobody can take papers out or smuggle them in.
It is only opened after the election has ended; then the polling staff count the votes.
In Switzerland, people say “going to the urn” (an die Urne gehen) when they go to vote.
Today most people in Switzerland vote by post.
The German word Urne comes from Latin and means jug.

abschnitte.text: A **ballot box** is a box or case with a narrow slot at the top. Through this slot you put your folded **ballot paper**. The ballot box is locked before the election and often sealed. That way nobody can take papers out or add any afterwards. Some countries use see-through ballot boxes so that everyone can see they are empty at the start.

The ballot box stands in the **polling station**, which is often set up in a school or the municipal hall. Members of the **polling committee** sit there and make sure that everything runs correctly. Anyone who wants to vote shows their voting card and then puts their paper in. In many Swiss municipalities, the polling station is only open briefly on Sunday morning or on the days before. Once voting closes, the counting begins.

In Switzerland today, only a minority still go to the ballot box in person. The vast majority vote **by post**: they send their ballot papers by post or put them in the municipality's letterbox. Since the 1990s, postal voting has been allowed in all cantons. Even so, people still speak of **going to the polls** (Urnengang). Some cantons are also testing electronic voting over the internet, known as **e-voting**.

When voting has closed, the ballot box is opened in the presence of the polling committee. The papers are sorted, counted and checked. Invalid papers, for example with insults or identifying marks, are set aside. The results of each municipality go to the canton and then to the Confederation. In federal votes, there is often a result by Sunday evening.

The German word for a ballot box, **Urne**, comes from the Latin word “urna”, meaning a jug or vessel. In ancient Rome and ancient Athens, people already voted by putting pebbles, pieces of pottery or small tablets into vessels. In Switzerland, many cantons used to decide by a show of hands at the **Landsgemeinde**. Today Landsgemeinden exist only in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden. Everywhere else, people vote at the ballot box or by post.

begriffe.erklaerung: The paper on which you write yes or no in a vote.
A group of people who supervise an election and count the votes.
Another way of saying taking part in an election or vote.
Voting in elections or referendums over the internet.

gewusst: An urn for the ashes of someone who has died is also called an urn, because both words go back to the Latin word for jug.
In Switzerland, several million ballot papers are often counted on a single voting Sunday.

teile.einleitung: Glasnost is a Russian word meaning “openness”. That was the name Mikhail Gorbachev gave to his policy of relaxing censorship in the Soviet Union from 1985. Together with perestroika, it changed the country greatly.
wichtigste: Mikhail Gorbachev became General Secretary of the CPSU in March 1985.
Glasnost means openness, perestroika means restructuring.
Newspapers were increasingly allowed to criticise problems openly.
The Chernobyl disaster in 1986 gave glasnost new momentum.
Banned books such as “Doctor Zhivago” were allowed to be published.
In 1990 Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize.

abschnitte.text: In the Soviet Union the Communist Party decided what appeared in newspapers, books and on television. Criticising the government was dangerous. The economy was hardly making progress. In March 1985 **Mikhail Gorbachev** became General Secretary of the **CPSU**, that is, head of the party. He wanted to renew the rigid system and relied on **glasnost**, on openness, to do so.

Alongside glasnost there was **perestroika**. The word means “restructuring” or “reshaping”. Perestroika was meant to modernise the **planned economy**, that is, the economy run by the state. Glasnost was meant to make sure that problems were discussed openly. Gorbachev believed that mistakes can only be fixed if people talk about them.

In April 1986 the **Chernobyl reactor accident** happened in Ukraine. At first the authorities kept quiet about the disaster for days, even though radioactive clouds drifted as far as Western Europe. Increased radiation was measured in Switzerland too. Gorbachev concluded that more openness was needed. After that, glasnost gained momentum.

With glasnost, **censorship** was relaxed. The media reported on corruption, environmental problems and government mistakes. People were allowed to speak openly about the **crimes under Stalin**, when millions of people were persecuted. At the end of 1986 the civil rights campaigner **Andrei Sakharov** was allowed to return to Moscow from exile in Gorky. In 1988 Boris Pasternak's long-banned novel “**Doctor Zhivago**” was published in the Soviet Union too.

In March 1990 **Article 6** of the constitution, which had laid down the leading role of the party, was changed. This made other parties possible. In the same year Gorbachev received the **Nobel Peace Prize** for his part in the peaceful end of the Cold War. But the new openness also strengthened independence movements in many republics. At the end of 1991 the Soviet Union broke up.

gewusst: In the 1980s the words “glasnost” and “perestroika” became widely known in Switzerland and the rest of the West too.
Pasternak was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1958, but he had to turn it down under pressure from the government.

teile.einleitung: The First International was an alliance of workers' organisations from many countries. It was founded in London in 1864 and its official name was the International Workingmen's Association. Switzerland played an important part in its history.
wichtigste: The First International was founded in London in 1864.
In 1869 its congress met in Basel.
In 1868 Bakunin founded the Alliance of Socialist Democracy in Geneva.
In 1872 Bakunin and James Guillaume were expelled.
In the same year the anti-authoritarian International was founded in Saint-Imier.
In 1876 the First International was dissolved in Philadelphia.

abschnitte.text: In 1864 representatives of workers' organisations from several countries met in **London**. They founded the **International Workingmen's Association**, later called the **First International**. The aim was for working people to support each other across national borders. **Karl Marx** belonged to the leading **General Council** and shaped the organisation strongly. Several congresses took place in Switzerland, for example in Geneva, Lausanne and Basel.

In **Geneva** the German revolutionary **Johann Philipp Becker** organised the German-speaking sections. He had taken part in uprisings in 1848 and 1849 and published the magazine “Der Vorbote” (The Herald). In 1869 the congress met in **Basel**. There people argued about abolishing the right of inheritance, and the conflict between Marx and Bakunin came clearly into the open.

In 1868 the Russian anarchist **Mikhail Bakunin** founded the **Alliance of Socialist Democracy** in Geneva. He rejected every kind of state, even a workers' state. The General Council around Marx saw the Alliance as an attempt to take over the International from within. Bakunin found support in the **Jura Federation**, an association of watchmakers in the Swiss Jura. Its leading figure was the Neuchâtel teacher **James Guillaume**.

At the **Hague Congress** in 1872, Bakunin and Guillaume were expelled. The General Council was moved to **New York** to keep it away from the influence of Bakunin's followers. In September 1872 these followers founded the **anti-authoritarian International** in **Saint-Imier** in the Bernese Jura. The First International quickly lost importance. In 1876 a conference in **Philadelphia** decided to dissolve it.

gewusst: The Congress of Saint-Imier is seen as the birth of the anarchist movement.
The watchmakers in the Jura often worked in small workshops and valued running their own affairs.

teile.einleitung: The Bolsheviks were a party in Russia led by Vladimir Ilyich Lenin. In 1917 they took power in the October Revolution and later founded the Soviet Union. The Communist Party, which ruled for over 70 years, grew out of them.
wichtigste: The Bolsheviks were the party led by Lenin that took power in Russia in 1917.
In Russian, the name means roughly “members of the majority”.
They emerged in 1903 from a split in the Russian Social Democrats.
Their rivals within the movement were the Mensheviks.
In the October Revolution of 1917 they overthrew the government in Petrograd.
In 1918 they renamed themselves the Communist Party.
Before the revolution, Lenin lived in exile in Switzerland for several years.

abschnitte.text: The **Bolsheviks** were the radical wing of the Russian workers' movement. They wanted to overthrow the Tsar and create a society based on the ideas of **Karl Marx**. Their leader was **Lenin**, who wanted a tightly organised party of professional revolutionaries. Important members also included Leon Trotsky and Joseph Stalin. Their aim was rule by the workers and peasants.

In **1903**, the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party held a congress in Brussels and London. The members argued about how the party should be organised. Lenin's group won an important vote and therefore called itself the Bolsheviks, the **“members of the majority”**. Their opponents around Julius Martov were called **Mensheviks**, meaning members of the minority. Later the Mensheviks were at times even larger, but kept this name.

From 1914 to 1917, Lenin lived in **exile** in Switzerland, first in Bern and then in Zurich, on the Spiegelgasse. From there he wrote texts and kept in touch with his followers. After the Tsar was overthrown in February 1917, he wanted to get to Russia as quickly as possible. In April 1917 the German government let him travel through Germany in a train. It hoped he would weaken Russia and take it out of the First World War.

In October 1917 according to the Russian calendar of the time, which was November by our calendar, the Bolsheviks struck. Armed workers and soldiers occupied important buildings and the **Winter Palace** in Petrograd, today's St Petersburg. The Provisional Government was overthrown. This seizure of power is called the **October Revolution**. After that, Russia made peace with Germany and took land and factories away from large landowners and factory owners.

Various opponents, known as the Whites, fought against Bolshevik rule. In the **Russian Civil War** from 1918 to about 1922, the **Red Army** finally won. The Bolsheviks banned other parties and persecuted their opponents with a secret police. As early as 1918 they renamed themselves the Communist Party. In 1922 they founded the Soviet Union, which lasted until 1991.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rapid, fundamental overthrow of the rulers of a country.
The more moderate part of the Russian Social Democrats, opponents of the Bolsheviks.
Living abroad because you are persecuted in your own country.
The army of the Bolsheviks and later of the Soviet Union.

gewusst: Because Russia still used the old Julian calendar at the time, the anniversary of the October Revolution was later celebrated in November.
In Zurich, a plaque on the Spiegelgasse marks the place where Lenin lived.

thx0pov.t: Founding of the People's Republic of China

teile.einleitung: On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing. Before that, the communists had won the civil war against the Kuomintang. Today the day is China's national holiday.
wichtigste: Mao proclaimed the People's Republic on 1 October 1949 from the Gate of Heavenly Peace.
The Kuomintang government under Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan.
Beijing became the capital again; before that, the Kuomintang had governed from Nanjing.
Zhou Enlai became the first premier.
The Common Programme served as a provisional constitution.
In 1950 China signed a treaty of friendship with the Soviet Union.

abschnitte.text: For decades two parties fought for power in China: the **Communist Party** under **Mao Zedong** and the nationalist **Kuomintang** under **Chiang Kai-shek**. After the Second World War the **civil war** flared up again. In 1949 the communists won. Chiang Kai-shek withdrew with his government and army to the island of **Taiwan**, where the Republic of China still exists today.

In September 1949 the **Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference** met. It brought together communists, smaller parties and organisations. It elected the government and decided on the flag, the anthem and the capital. Around this time Mao spoke the famous sentence: “The Chinese people have stood up.” On **1 October 1949** he proclaimed the People's Republic from the **Gate of Heavenly Peace** on Tiananmen Square.

**Beijing** became the capital again; the Kuomintang had previously governed from Nanjing. The first **premier** was **Zhou Enlai**, who led the government until his death in 1976. The **Common Programme**, adopted in September 1949, served as a provisional constitution. A proper constitution followed in 1954.

The flag of the People's Republic is red and shows five yellow stars. The **large star** stands for leadership by the Communist Party. The four small stars stand for the social classes of the people. They all point towards the large star.

In February 1950 Mao and **Stalin** signed a treaty of friendship and alliance in Moscow. The Soviet Union then helped China with loans and experts. At first many Western countries recognised only the government in Taiwan. But **Switzerland** was one of the first Western states to recognise the People's Republic, in January 1950.

gewusst: On 1 October the “Golden Week” begins in China, a holiday week in which millions of people travel.
A large portrait of Mao still hangs on the Gate of Heavenly Peace today.

teile.einleitung: From 1961 to 1989, the Berlin Wall separated East Berlin from West Berlin. It was built by the GDR to stop its citizens from fleeing to the West. Its fall on 9 November 1989 is one of the most famous events in recent history.
wichtigste: The Berlin Wall was built from 13 August 1961.
It separated East and West Berlin and completely enclosed West Berlin.
The GDR wanted to use it to stop its citizens from fleeing to the West.
At least 140 people died at the wall.
On 9 November 1989 the wall was opened.
Today, memorials and remains of the wall commemorate the division.
The wall was a symbol of the Cold War.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, Germany was divided into the **FRG** (West Germany) in the west and the **GDR** (East Germany) in the east. Up to 1961, about three million people fled from the GDR to the West, many of them via Berlin. Among them were many young and well-educated people. The GDR leadership under **Walter Ulbricht** wanted to stop this. Officially, the GDR called the wall the “anti-fascist protective rampart”, although it mainly locked in its own citizens.

During the night before **13 August 1961**, soldiers and police sealed off the border to West Berlin with barbed wire. In the following days and weeks, a wall of stone and concrete was built. Families and friends were separated overnight. In the first few days, some people still jumped into the West from the windows of border houses on **Bernauer Strasse**. The West protested but did not intervene militarily.

The border installations around West Berlin were about 155 kilometres long. The outer wall was around 3.6 metres high. Behind it lay the so-called **death strip**, with watchtowers, dog runs and alarm fences. Border guards had orders to shoot at people trying to escape; this is called the **order to shoot**. At least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall, among them 18-year-old Peter Fechter in 1962.

abschnitte.titel: The fall of the wall in 1989
abschnitte.text: In autumn 1989, hundreds of thousands of people in the GDR protested peacefully for freedom. On the evening of **9 November 1989**, the SED politician **Günter Schabowski** announced new travel rules at a press conference, which he said applied immediately. That same night, thousands of East Berliners streamed to the border crossings until they were opened. People hugged each other in tears and danced on the wall at the **Brandenburg Gate**. Less than a year later, Germany was reunited.

From 1990 the wall was almost completely torn down. Today a double row of cobblestones in the ground shows in many places where it ran. At the **East Side Gallery** there is a colourfully painted section of wall more than a kilometre long. The **Berlin Wall Memorial** on Bernauer Strasse shows a preserved border strip with a watchtower. Pieces of the wall now stand in many countries of the world, including Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The heavily guarded area behind the wall, in which people trying to escape were shot at.
The order to border guards to stop people escaping with weapons.
The opening of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989.
The GDR's name for the forbidden escape to the West.

gewusst: The wall stood for 28 years, and in 2018 it had been gone for exactly as long as it had stood.
People also escaped through tunnels they had dug themselves, in hot-air balloons or hidden in converted cars.
Shortly before the wall was built, Walter Ulbricht said publicly that nobody intended to build a wall.

teile.einleitung: Democracy means rule by the people: it is not a king or a small group who decide, but the citizens. Switzerland is a particularly lively democracy, because here the people may not only elect but also vote on issues several times a year. This is called direct democracy.
wichtigste: Democracy means rule by the people; all voters have a say.
In an election you choose people; in a vote you decide on an issue.
In Switzerland you may take part in federal votes from the age of 18.
The government of Switzerland, the Federal Council, has seven members.
A federal popular initiative needs 100,000 signatures in 18 months.
Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Power is divided between parliament, government and the courts.

abschnitte.text: The word **democracy** comes from Greek: “demos” means people and “kratos” means rule. About 2,500 years ago, ancient **Athens** already had a people's assembly, although only free men were allowed to take part. In a democracy, fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and equality before the law apply. There are free elections, and the majority decides without violating the rights of the minority. The opposite is a **dictatorship**, in which a single person or party decides alone.

In most countries, the people elect a parliament, which then makes all the decisions. In Switzerland, the people can also vote directly on issues; this is called **direct democracy**. There are federal voting Sundays about four times a year. With a **popular initiative**, you can demand a constitutional amendment with 100,000 signatures in 18 months. With a **referendum**, you can force a vote on a new law with 50,000 signatures in 100 days.

So that nobody has too much power, it is divided into three areas; this is called the **separation of powers**. Parliament, the **Federal Assembly** with 200 members of the National Council and 46 members of the Council of States, makes the laws. The **Federal Council**, with seven members, governs and puts the laws into practice. The courts, headed by the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne, administer justice. Each branch keeps a check on the others.

Switzerland is a **federal state** with three levels: around 2,100 municipalities (as of about 2025), 26 cantons and the Confederation. Each level has its own tasks, its own parliaments and governments. In many small municipalities, the municipal assembly decides, and all voters may take part. In the cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden there is still the **Landsgemeinde**, where people vote in the open air by a show of hands. This system is called **federalism**.

Modern Switzerland was created in 1848 with the first **Federal Constitution**. The referendum has existed at federal level since 1874 and the popular initiative since 1891. Women only gained the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971. Since 1991 the voting age has been 18. The Federal Constitution in force today dates from 1999.

You can practise democracy at school. In the **class council** or the school parliament, children discuss and vote on proposals. Many municipalities and cantons have youth parliaments, in which young people contribute their ideas. It is important to listen to other opinions and stay fair, even if you lose. That way you learn how democracy works in everyday life.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of government in which the people decide.
A decision by the people on an issue, with yes or no.
The division of power between parliament, government and the courts.
A system in which municipalities and cantons decide many things for themselves.
An open-air assembly at which the voters vote.

gewusst: No country in the world holds as many national popular votes as Switzerland.
The Federal Council has no boss: the presidency passes to a different member every year.
At the Landsgemeinde in Glarus, 16-year-olds can already vote.

teile.einleitung: The Communist International, Comintern for short, was a worldwide alliance of communist parties. It was founded in Moscow in 1919 and dissolved again in 1943. Its leadership was firmly in the hands of the Soviet Union.
wichtigste: The Comintern was founded in Moscow in 1919.
It is also called the Third International.
From 1920 parties had to meet 21 conditions to be admitted.
The Executive Committee in Moscow gave the parties binding instructions.
In 1935 it decided on the Popular Front against fascism.
Georgi Dimitrov was general secretary from 1935 to 1943.
Stalin dissolved the Comintern in 1943.

abschnitte.text: The Comintern was founded in **Moscow** in **March 1919** on **Lenin's** initiative. Its aim was **world revolution**. It is also called the **Third International**. It saw itself as the successor to Marx's First International and as the counterpart to the social democrats' **Second International**. The Communist Party of Switzerland also became a member.

In **1920** the second world congress adopted the **21 conditions of admission**. Anyone who wanted to become a member had to accept strict discipline and break with moderate socialists. Between the world congresses the organisation was led by the **Executive Committee**, **ECCI** for short. It sat in Moscow and gave binding instructions to the parties in the individual countries.

Around **1929** the Comintern fought the social democrats with the slogan **“social fascism”**. In this way it put them on the same level as the fascists. This attitude made joint resistance against Nazism harder in Germany. After Hitler seized power the course changed: in **1935** the seventh world congress decided on the **Popular Front** against fascism. Popular Front governments were formed in France and Spain.

From 1935 to 1943 the Bulgarian **Georgi Dimitrov** was general secretary. He had become well known in 1933 at the **Reichstag fire trial** in Leipzig, because he defended himself skilfully and was acquitted. In **May 1943** **Stalin** dissolved the Comintern. During the Second World War he wanted to reassure his Western allies in this way.

gewusst: The word “Comintern” is an abbreviation from Russian for Communist International.
After the Reichstag fire trial, Georgi Dimitrov lived in Moscow and led the Comintern from there.

teile.einleitung: A newcomer (Zuzüger) is a person who moves to a municipality. In Switzerland, people often say “zügeln” for moving house. After the move there are quite a few things to do, and lots of new things to discover.
wichtigste: Newcomers are people who move to a municipality.
Someone who moves away is called a Wegzüger.
In Switzerland, people often say “zügeln” for moving house.
After moving, you register with the new municipality and tell the post office your new address.
Children usually go to school where they now live.
In a club you quickly get to know new people.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who moves house **“zügelt”**, as they say in Switzerland. On **moving day**, furniture and boxes are carried into the new flat. Friends and family often help. Someone who comes to a municipality for the first time is a **newcomer** (Zuzüger or Zuzügerin). Someone who leaves a municipality is a **Wegzüger** or **Wegzügerin**.

After moving, you register with the **residents' registration office** of the new municipality. In the old municipality you deregister. You also tell the **post office** your new address. Then it brings your letters to the right place and can forward them for a while. Children usually go to **school where they now live**.

abschnitte.titel: Having a say in the new municipality
abschnitte.text: Adult Swiss citizens may vote in elections and referendums where they live. For this they must be **registered** in the municipality. Then they receive their **voting papers** at home. Many small municipalities have a **municipal assembly**. There newcomers can also have their say and decide on things in the village.

Many municipalities invite newcomers to a **welcome event**. There you get to know the authorities and other new arrivals. You find contacts especially quickly in a **club**, for example the gymnastics club, the brass band or the fire brigade. Newcomers often bring experience from other places. That way **new ideas** come into village life.

gewusst: The word “zügeln” for moving house is used mainly in Switzerland.
In many cities, spring and autumn are popular times to move, because tenancy agreements often end then.

teile.einleitung: The Virginia Declaration of Rights is a declaration of fundamental rights from 1776. It is regarded as the first modern catalogue of fundamental rights and became a model for many later declarations of human rights.
wichtigste: The Virginia Convention adopted the declaration in June 1776.
Its main author was George Mason.
It is regarded as the first modern catalogue of fundamental rights.
It says that all power comes from the people.
It calls freedom of the press one of the great bulwarks of liberty.
It was a model for the American Bill of Rights of 1791.
At that time, the rights did not apply to enslaved people.

abschnitte.text: **Virginia** was one of the 13 British colonies in North America. In **June 1776** the Virginia Convention adopted the declaration. That was even **before** the Declaration of Independence of the United States of 4 July 1776. Most of the text was drafted by **George Mason**, a planter and politician from Virginia. The declaration stood at the beginning of Virginia's new constitution.

The declaration says that all people are **by nature free** and independent. They have **inherent rights**, such as the rights to life, liberty and property. It also states that **all power lies with the people**. Office holders are accountable to the people; this is called **popular sovereignty**. Freedom of religion and fair trials are also mentioned.

The sentence on **freedom of the press** is especially well known. Freedom of the press, it says, is one of the **“great bulwarks of liberty”**. A bulwark is a strong protective wall. Only despotic governments, that is tyrants, would restrict it. So as early as 1776, a free press was seen as a protection for everyone.

The declaration is regarded as the **first modern catalogue of fundamental rights** in a binding state document. The **Bill of Rights**, the first ten amendments to the US Constitution of 1791, took over many of its phrases. The French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 was also influenced by it. From today's point of view, however, there is a big **contradiction**: **slavery** continued in Virginia. George Mason himself also kept slaves.

gewusst: The Virginia Declaration of Rights is older than the famous US Declaration of Independence, if only by a few weeks.
Thomas Jefferson, the author of the Declaration of Independence, also came from Virginia.

teile.einleitung: Checkpoint Charlie was the best-known border crossing between East and West Berlin. It was on Friedrichstrasse and, at the time of the Berlin Wall, was a flashpoint of the Cold War. Today it is a popular destination for tourists.
wichtigste: Checkpoint Charlie was a border crossing between East and West Berlin.
It was on Friedrichstrasse in the centre of Berlin.
It was used mainly by members of the Allied forces, diplomats and foreigners.
The name comes from the letter C in the NATO phonetic alphabet.
In October 1961, American and Soviet tanks faced each other here.
In June 1990 the checkpoint hut was taken down.
Today a replica of the checkpoint hut stands there.

abschnitte.text: **Checkpoint Charlie** was a checkpoint on the border between the American sector and the Soviet sector of Berlin. It was on **Friedrichstrasse**, between the districts of Kreuzberg and Mitte. On their side, the Americans carried out checks from just a small wooden hut. On the eastern side, by contrast, there were large GDR border installations. It was set up after the wall was built in 1961.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the name come from?
abschnitte.text: The word checkpoint is English and means a control point. In the **phonetic alphabet**, “Charlie” stands for the letter C. There were several Allied checkpoints named after the alphabet. Checkpoint Alpha was at Helmstedt on the inner German border, and Checkpoint Bravo at Dreilinden on the edge of Berlin. Checkpoint Charlie was the third checkpoint on the route through the GDR to West Berlin.

West Berliners and West Germans were not allowed to use this crossing; there were other crossings for them. Checkpoint Charlie was used mainly by soldiers and members of the **Allies**, that is the USA, Great Britain and France. Diplomats and other foreigners also crossed the border here. For GDR citizens, the way to the West was blocked. Even so, some tried to escape here hidden in cars.

In October 1961 there was a dispute because the GDR wanted to check an American diplomat. The USA insisted on free passage for its people. On 27 and 28 October 1961, American and Soviet **tanks** faced each other directly at Checkpoint Charlie. The world feared a new war. After about 16 hours, both sides pulled back.

On 22 June 1990 the checkpoint hut was ceremonially taken down; it is now in the **Allied Museum** in Berlin. Since 2000, a replica with sandbags and a sign reading “You are leaving the American sector” has stood on the original site. Right next to it, the **Wall Museum** at Checkpoint Charlie shows escape stories and escape vehicles. The site is one of the most visited sights in Berlin. Large photos of an American and a Soviet soldier commemorate the division.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where you may cross a border under supervision.
The victorious powers of the Second World War: the USA, Great Britain, France and the Soviet Union.
A list of words for letters, so that they can be understood clearly over the radio.
A part of Berlin that was run by one of the victorious powers.

gewusst: The famous warning sign at Checkpoint Charlie was written in English, Russian, French and German.
Checkpoint Charlie appears in many spy films and novels about the Cold War.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who holds a political office must stand for election again after a certain time. If the person is elected again, this is called **re-election**. If they are not elected, they have been **voted out**.
wichtigste: With re-election, someone may stay in office.
Anyone who is not re-elected has been voted out.
There is no legal limit on re-election to the National Council.
In the USA, you may be elected president no more than twice.
Those already in office are often better known than new candidates.
Re-election shows that voters trust someone.

abschnitte.text: In a **re-election**, someone who is already in office gets enough votes again. That way they can carry on. People who are already in office are called **incumbents**. The National Council is elected afresh every four years. Anyone who wants to stay must stand again and get enough votes.

When someone is **voted out**, they lose their office because they get too few votes. This happens to incumbents too. Even members of the **Federal Council** have failed to be re-elected, for example Ruth Metzler in 2003 and Christoph Blocher in 2007. So re-election is never completely certain.

Federal law sets no limit for the **National Council**. You may be re-elected as often as you like. Some parties, however, have their own rules on terms of office. In the **USA** it is different. Since 1951 the constitution has stated that a president may be elected no more than twice.

The **United Federal Assembly** elects the Federal Council afresh every four years. In this **general election**, all seven seats are filled again. Federal councillors who want to continue stand for re-election. They are usually confirmed. Incumbents often have an advantage, because many people already know them.

gewusst: Re-election shows that many voters are happy with a person's work.
Some cantons and municipalities have term limits for certain offices.

teile.einleitung: The Secret Speech was given by the Soviet party leader Nikita Khrushchev in February 1956. In it he openly criticised the crimes of his predecessor Joseph Stalin for the first time. The speech changed the communist world.
wichtigste: Khrushchev gave the speech on 25 February 1956 at the 20th Congress of the CPSU.
It was titled “On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences”.
The speech lasted about four hours and took place in a closed session.
Khrushchev quoted Lenin's Testament to incriminate Stalin.
The text reached the West through a copy from Poland.
In the Soviet Union the speech was not officially published until 1989.

abschnitte.titel: The speech at the party congress
abschnitte.text: Stalin had died in 1953. **Nikita Khrushchev** then became First Secretary of the Communist Party. At the **20th Congress of the CPSU**, on 25 February 1956, he spoke in a **closed session** after the official end of the congress. Only Soviet delegates were admitted, not even foreign communist parties. He spoke for about four hours.

abschnitte.titel: Criticism of the cult of personality
abschnitte.text: The speech was called “**On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences**”. A **cult of personality** means that a leader is worshipped almost like a god. Khrushchev accused Stalin of letting himself be worshipped in this way. He spoke about **mass arrests**, torture and the execution of loyal party members. He kept quiet about his own part in these purges. Many delegates were shocked.

To incriminate Stalin, Khrushchev read from **Lenin's Testament**. In this letter from 1922 and 1923 Lenin had called Stalin too rude. He had suggested removing him as general secretary. This text had been kept secret for a long time. Now the delegates heard it for the first time.

The speech was supposed to stay secret. But in **Poland** a copy got into the hands of a journalist and from there to the Israeli secret service. In June 1956 the “New York Times” published the text. In the Soviet Union itself the speech was not officially printed until 1989, under **Gorbachev**.

The criticism of Stalin began **de-Stalinisation**. Many political prisoners were released, and Stalin's picture gradually disappeared from public life. In the Eastern Bloc the speech raised hopes of more freedom. In **Hungary** a popular uprising broke out in the autumn of 1956, which Soviet tanks crushed in November.

gewusst: Although the speech was called “secret”, it was soon read out at party meetings in the Soviet Union.
In 1961 Stalin's body was removed from the mausoleum on Red Square, where it had lain beside Lenin.

teile.einleitung: Before an election, candidates say what they want to do after the election. These are called **election promises**. It is worth looking at these promises carefully.
wichtigste: An election promise says what someone wants to do after the election.
You hear election promises before the election.
Many promises come from the party programme.
A single person needs a majority to put something into practice.
An election promise is not a contract.
At the next election, you can decide afresh.

abschnitte.text: With **election promises**, candidates want to convince voters. For example, they say that they will campaign for lower taxes, more environmental protection or better schools. Many of these promises come from the **party programme**. In it, a party writes down what it wants to work for.

A single member of the National Council cannot carry out a promise alone. In parliament, the **majority** decides. So she has to convince many others for a law to be made. In Switzerland, the people can also have a say through a **referendum**. That is why many candidates say they want to **campaign for** something.

Some things sound good but are expensive or difficult. That is why it is worth asking: is this **realistic**? Who will pay for it? A good promise is achievable. A municipal councillor, for example, can really campaign for a new **playground**. Promises that are supposed to cost nothing and solve everything, on the other hand, are questionable.

An election promise is **not a contract**. Nobody can force a politician in court to keep it. But at the end of a **term of office** you can see what has been achieved. For the National Council, that is four years. At the next election, voters can then decide afresh and elect someone else.

gewusst: After a term of office, the media often compare which promises have been kept.
Whether a promise is kept often also depends on how much money is available.

teile.einleitung: The Juche ideology is the official state ideology of North Korea. The word means roughly “self-reliance”. According to this doctrine, the country should provide for itself and follow the leader.
wichtigste: Juche means roughly self-reliance or independence.
It is laid down in North Korea's constitution.
Kim Il-sung is regarded as its founder.
The Juche Tower in Pyongyang is about 170 metres high.
The Juche calendar begins with the year Kim Il-sung was born, 1912.
From the 1990s the Songun policy put the military first.

abschnitte.text: In Korean **Juche** means roughly “**self-reliance**”. According to this idea, a country should **provide for itself** politically, economically and militarily and not depend on anyone. The Juche ideology is North Korea's official **state ideology** and is written into the constitution. It shapes politics, schools and art there.

**Kim Il-sung**, North Korea's first ruler, is regarded as its founder. He put the Juche idea in the foreground from the 1950s. According to the doctrine, the people need a great **leader** to guide them. In this way the ideology justifies the power of the **Kim family**, which has ruled the country since it was founded. His successors developed the doctrine further.

In the capital, **Pyongyang**, stands the **Juche Tower**. It was inaugurated in 1982 for Kim Il-sung's 70th birthday and, with the flame at the top, is about 170 metres high. Since 1997 there has also been the **Juche calendar**. It begins with the year 1912, when Kim Il-sung was born.

North Korea trades very little with other countries and has hardly any contact with the outside world. The country has stayed poor and isolated. In the 1990s it suffered a severe **famine**. During this time the **Songun** policy also emerged, which means “military first”. The army was given priority for money and resources.

gewusst: In the Juche calendar 1912 is year 1, so 2012 is year 101.
The Juche Tower is slightly taller than the Washington Monument in the USA.

teile.einleitung: The federal popular initiative is a special right of Swiss voters. With it, citizens can themselves propose a change to the Federal Constitution. If enough people sign, the whole country votes on it.
wichtigste: With a popular initiative, you demand something new for the Federal Constitution.
This needs 100,000 valid signatures from voters.
You have 18 months to collect the signatures.
An initiative is only accepted with a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
At federal level, an initiative can only change the constitution, not an ordinary law.
With a referendum, on the other hand, you oppose a law that parliament has passed.
Most popular initiatives are rejected by the people.

abschnitte.text: A **popular initiative** is a proposal from the people to change the **Federal Constitution**. It can call for a new article, change an existing one or delete one. Behind every initiative there is an **initiative committee** of 7 to 27 voters. Often these are parties, associations or groups of committed citizens. That way the people themselves can put topics on the political agenda.

First, the **Federal Chancellery** checks whether the signature form is correct. Then the collection period of **18 months** begins. During this time at least **100,000 valid signatures** must be collected. The municipalities check whether the people who signed really are entitled to vote. Many committees collect in the street, at markets or nowadays with the help of the internet.

Once the initiative has succeeded, the **Federal Council** and **parliament** debate it. They recommend whether people should vote yes or no. Parliament can also draw up a **counter-proposal** that takes up only part of the aim. Sometimes the initiators then withdraw their initiative. It often takes several years before the vote.

abschnitte.titel: Majority of the people and majority of the cantons
abschnitte.text: In the vote, an initiative needs a double yes. A **majority of the people** means that more than half of all voters in the whole country say yes. A **majority of the cantons** means that yes wins in most of the cantons. Six cantons, for example Basel-Stadt or Appenzell Innerrhoden, count only as half a cantonal vote. That way small cantons also have an important say.

The popular initiative for a partial revision of the constitution has existed at federal level since **1891**. Since then, over 200 initiatives have been put to the vote, but only about one in ten has been accepted. Well-known initiatives that were accepted are the **Alpine Initiative** of 1994, to protect the Alps from lorry traffic, and the initiative of 1993 to make 1 August a public holiday. The second homes initiative of 2012 was also accepted. Rejected initiatives often have an effect too, because they start an important debate.

The initiative and the **referendum** are the two most important popular rights of direct democracy. With the initiative, the people press the accelerator: they want something new. With the referendum, the people pull the brake: they oppose a decision of parliament. An optional referendum needs 50,000 signatures in 100 days. There are also initiatives in the cantons and many municipalities, where you can often change laws too.

begriffe.erklaerung: The group of people who launch an initiative and are responsible for it.
The most important law of Switzerland; it sets out the foundations of the state.
A majority of the cantons in a vote.
A proposal by parliament that takes up the aim of an initiative in a different form.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of very few countries in the world where the people can directly force a change to the constitution.
Because initiatives can only change the constitution, the Federal Constitution also contains some very specific things, for example rules on second homes.

teile.einleitung: The Berlin Wall Memorial is on Bernauer Strasse in Berlin. It recalls the division of the city from 1961 to 1989 and the people who lost their lives at the Wall.
wichtigste: The memorial is on Bernauer Strasse.
A section of the Wall with the border strip and a watchtower has been preserved there.
In the “Window of Remembrance”, photos commemorate the people who died at the Wall.
From a viewing platform you can look down on the old border strip.
In Berlin a double row of cobblestones shows where the Wall stood.

abschnitte.text: From 1961 to 1989 the **Berlin Wall** separated the eastern part of the city from the western part. On **Bernauer Strasse** the border ran right along the houses. When the Wall was built, people jumped out of windows here to get to the West. Today a section of the border installations, with the **death strip** and a **watchtower**, has been preserved at this spot. So you can see what the border really looked like.

The memorial especially remembers the people who died at the Wall, mostly while trying to escape. In the **Window of Remembrance** there is a photo with a name for many of them. The **Chapel of Reconciliation** also stands on the site. It was built where a church in the border strip used to stand; that church was blown up in 1985.

From a **viewing platform** you look down on the preserved section of the border installations. You can see how wide the border strip was and how hard it was to get across. Throughout the city, a **double row of cobblestones** in the ground also shows the course of the Wall. This lets you follow it even where nothing of it is left standing.

gewusst: Escape helpers dug several tunnels under Bernauer Strasse, through which people fled to the West.

teile.einleitung: The right to vote is the right to have a say in elections. A distinction is made between the active right to vote, meaning being allowed to vote, and the passive right to vote, meaning being allowed to be elected yourself. For a long time only a few people were allowed to vote; today the right to vote is a fundamental right in every democracy.
wichtigste: The active right to vote means you may vote.
The passive right to vote means you may be elected yourself.
In Switzerland, Swiss citizens aged 18 and over have the right to vote at federal level.
Women only gained the right to vote at federal level in 1971.
Swiss citizens living abroad may also take part in federal elections.
In some cantons and municipalities, foreigners may also vote.
Good elections are universal, equal, free and secret.

abschnitte.text: The **active right to vote** allows you to cast your vote in an election. The **passive right to vote** allows you to stand for an office yourself and be elected. At federal level in Switzerland, both rights are linked to the same age of 18. So anyone who may vote in National Council elections can also stand for the National Council. For the Federal Council, too, you only need the right to vote.

At federal level, all **Swiss citizens** aged 18 and over may vote in elections and referendums. This also applies to about 200,000 Swiss citizens living abroad who have registered to do so (as of about 2023). In the cantons and municipalities, different rules sometimes apply. In the canton of **Glarus**, you may vote in cantonal elections and referendums from the age of 16. In the cantons of Neuchâtel and Jura, foreigners with a settlement permit may vote at municipal level.

In the past, often only rich men who paid a lot of tax were allowed to vote. This is called **census suffrage**. With the Federal Constitution of 1848, all adult Swiss men in Switzerland gained the right to vote at federal level. In 1893, New Zealand was one of the first countries to introduce **women's suffrage**. In Switzerland it came at federal level only in 1971, after a popular vote by the men.

abschnitte.titel: Women's right to vote in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Many women fought for decades for their political rights. A first vote on women's suffrage was clearly rejected by the men in 1959. On 7 February 1971, the men finally said yes. The canton of **Appenzell Innerrhoden** only introduced women's suffrage at cantonal level in 1990. It was forced to do so by the **Federal Supreme Court**.

abschnitte.titel: Principles of the right to vote
abschnitte.text: A democratic right to vote is **universal**, which means nobody may be excluded because of their sex, origin or wealth. It is equal, so every vote carries the same weight. It is free: nobody may be put under pressure. And it is **secret**: you do not have to tell anyone whom you voted for. These principles are also in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to cast your vote in an election.
The right to be elected to an office yourself.
A right to vote that only people with a lot of money or property had.
The age from which you may vote in elections and referendums.

gewusst: Switzerland was one of the last countries in Europe to introduce women's suffrage.
In the canton of Glarus, 16-year-olds may have a say at the Landsgemeinde, but can only be elected to most offices themselves at 18.

teile.einleitung: Civil law governs how private individuals deal with one another. It is about contracts, family, property and inheritance. In Switzerland, the most important rules are in the Civil Code and the Code of Obligations.
wichtigste: Civil law sets out the rights and duties of private individuals towards one another.
Important laws are the Civil Code (ZGB) and the Code of Obligations (OR).
The Code of Obligations contains the rules for contracts such as buying, renting and employment.
In a civil case, the claimant files a lawsuit against the other party.
There is no public prosecutor in a civil case.
Rules on taxes belong to public law, not to civil law.

abschnitte.text: **Civil law** is also called **private law**. It governs relationships between private parties, that is between people and companies. This includes contracts, the family, property and inheritance law. If you buy a bike, for example, you make a purchase contract. What applies then is set out in civil law.

The **Civil Code**, **ZGB** for short, was drawn up by the legal scholar **Eugen Huber** and has applied since 1912. It covers, among other things, the law of persons, family law, inheritance law and property law. The **Code of Obligations**, **OR** for short, contains the rules for contracts such as buying, renting or employment contracts. Formally, it counts as the fifth part of the Civil Code.

If two parties cannot agree, one of them can go to court. The person who files the lawsuit is called the **claimant**, and the other side is the **defendant**. A typical case is a dispute between a tenant and a landlady over a **rent deposit**. Often you first have to go to a **conciliation authority**, which tries to find an agreement. Since 2011, the same **Civil Procedure Code** has applied to this throughout Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: Distinction from other areas of law
abschnitte.text: Besides civil law there is **criminal law** and **public law**. Robberies, reckless speeding or burglaries are crimes. There the **public prosecutor's office** investigates, and the court can impose a punishment. Public law governs the relationship between the **state** and individuals, for example on taxes or planning permission. In civil law, by contrast, private parties with equal rights face each other.

gewusst: In 1926, Turkey adopted the Swiss Civil Code almost completely.
The ZGB is known for its simple, easy-to-understand language.

teile.einleitung: Living together means that lots of different people get on with one another: in the family, in the school class, in the neighbourhood and in the whole country. For this to work, you need consideration, respect and a few shared rules. When everyone helps, everyone feels more comfortable.
wichtigste: Being considerate means thinking about other people.
Respect means valuing other people, even if they are different.
In an argument, it is usually best to talk to each other.
If you have hurt someone, you say sorry.
You welcome a new child in the class kindly.
Bullying is when someone is picked on again and again, and it must be stopped.
Rubbish belongs in the bin, so that things stay clean for everyone.

abschnitte.text: Being **considerate** means thinking about others. For example, you are quieter on the bus or give your seat to older people. **Respect** means valuing other people, no matter what language they speak, what they look like or what they believe in. That includes letting others finish speaking and not laughing at them. If you are respectful yourself, you are usually treated with respect too.

So that living together works, there are **rules**. Some are laws, for example on the roads. Others are agreements in the family or at school, such as the class rules. Many schools have a **class council**, in which the children talk together about rules and problems. Keeping things tidy is also part of it: rubbish belongs in the bin, and in Switzerland people separate glass, PET plastic bottles, paper and cardboard.

There are arguments everywhere; that is completely normal. What matters is how you sort them out. The best way is to talk to each other calmly and use **“I” messages** to say what is bothering you, for example “I get annoyed when you take my pencil case.” If you have hurt someone, you say sorry and try to make up for it. In some schools, trained **mediators**, known as peacemakers, help with conflicts.

When a new child joins the class, they are often unsure and do not know anyone. You can greet them kindly, show them round the school and invite them to play at break. Some children come from another country and are just learning German. In Switzerland, about a quarter of the population does not have a Swiss passport (as of about 2024). Lots of different languages and cultures make living together colourful and exciting.

**Bullying** means that someone is picked on, laughed at or left out again and again over a long time. It can also happen on the internet; then it is called **cyberbullying**. Bullying is not a joke; it hurts the people affected very much. If you see something like this, you should not look away but tell an adult. In Switzerland you can also contact Pro Juventute's advice service free of charge on 147.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thinking about others and paying attention to their needs.
Valuing other people and treating them fairly.
When someone is picked on or left out again and again.
A sentence in which you say how you feel yourself, instead of accusing the other person.

gewusst: In Switzerland, over 80 per cent of PET drinks bottles are collected and recycled, when everyone helps.
Pro Juventute's phone number 147 can be reached by children and young people around the clock.

teile.einleitung: Collectivisation means that many small farms are merged into large collective or state-run enterprises. In communist countries such as the Soviet Union, China or the GDR, this was often carried out by force. The consequences were terrible for millions of people.
wichtigste: In collectivisation, farms were merged into large state or collective farms.
In the process the farmers usually lost their own land and livestock.
In the Soviet Union, Joseph Stalin forced through collectivisation from 1929.
There the large farms were called kolkhozes and sovkhozes.
In Ukraine and other areas millions of people died in a famine in 1932 and 1933.
In China huge people's communes were set up from 1958.
In the GDR there were the Agricultural Production Cooperatives, LPG for short.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “collectivus”, meaning “gathered together”. Instead of many separate family farms, there were to be a few **large enterprises**. The land, the machines and often the animals then belonged to the community or the state. The communists believed that large farms would produce more food and that there would no longer be any rich big farmers.

From 1929 Stalin forced the farmers in the Soviet Union to bring their farms into **kolkhozes**. A kolkhoz was a collective farm, whereas a **sovkhoz** was a purely state-owned farm. Anyone who resisted was often persecuted as a “kulak”, that is, a rich farmer. Hundreds of thousands of families had their property taken away and were deported to distant regions such as Siberia.

The forced change threw agriculture into chaos. Many farmers preferred to slaughter their livestock rather than hand it over. At the same time the state demanded large amounts of grain. As a result there was a severe famine in 1932 and 1933, especially in Ukraine, where it is called the **Holodomor**.

In China, from 1958, Mao Zedong introduced the **people's communes** as part of the so-called “Great Leap Forward”. In them, often thousands of families lived and worked together. The plans were unrealistic, and the harvests were wrongly reported. In the famine that followed, from 1959 to 1961, many millions of people died.

In the GDR the farmers were grouped together in **LPGs** in the 1950s, almost completely by 1960. After the end of communism, around 1989 to 1991, many of these enterprises were dissolved or converted. Some former LPGs still exist today as large agricultural businesses. In Switzerland farmers also work together in cooperatives, but they do so voluntarily and their land remains their own property.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large farm in the Soviet Union that belonged jointly to its members but was controlled by the state.
A farm in the Soviet Union that belonged directly to the state.
An insulting term for farmers who were thought to be rich and were persecuted for that reason.
A huge community in China in which thousands of families worked and lived together.
When someone's property is taken away from them.

gewusst: In some people's communes in China, people ate in large communal canteens instead of at home.
Even in the Soviet Union, kolkhoz farmers were allowed to farm a small garden plot of their own, which often produced especially high yields.

teile.einleitung: The Brandenburg Gate stands in the middle of Berlin and is one of Germany's best-known landmarks. At the time of the wall it stood for the division of the city. Today it is a symbol of German unity.
wichtigste: The gate was built from 1788 to 1791.
On top stands the Quadriga, a goddess on a chariot with four horses.
Napoleon took the Quadriga to Paris in 1806.
The gate has five passageways.
At the time of the wall it lay in the closed border area.
On 22 December 1989 it was reopened to pedestrians.

abschnitte.text: The Brandenburg Gate was built from **1788 to 1791**, in the 18th century. The architect was **Carl Gotthard Langhans**. The gateways of the Acropolis in Athens served as a model. Between the columns there are **five passageways**. The middle one used to be reserved for the king.

On top of the gate stands the **Quadriga**. It is a goddess on a chariot pulled by **four horses**. When the French emperor **Napoleon** captured Berlin in 1806, he had the figures taken to Paris. In 1814, after Napoleon's defeat, they came back to Berlin. Since then the Quadriga has been regarded as a symbol of victory.

After the **Berlin Wall** was built in 1961, the gate stood right on the border in the **restricted zone**. Nobody could simply walk through it. So it became a symbol of Germany's **division**. In 1987 US President Ronald Reagan gave a famous speech in front of the gate. He called on Mikhail Gorbachev to tear down the wall.

After the **fall of the wall** in November 1989, a passage was opened at the Brandenburg Gate on **22 December 1989**. Thousands celebrated. Today the gate is a symbol of **united Germany**. On New Year's Eve and at big celebrations, many people often gather here.

gewusst: The Brandenburg Gate is over 200 years old and therefore much older than the wall.
The Quadriga spent eight years in Paris before it came back to Berlin.

teile.einleitung: Common property means things that do not belong to a single person but to a whole group together. The idea is very old. In Switzerland it is known, for example, from the Allmend and from cooperatives.
wichtigste: Common property belongs to everyone in a group together; private property belongs to a single person.
The word “communism” comes from the Latin “communis”, which means “shared” or “common”.
An Allmend is land that the people of a village use together.
A cooperative is a business that belongs jointly to its members.
Marx and Engels wanted to abolish the private ownership of factories.
In the Soviet Union the state controlled factories and land.

abschnitte.text: **Private property** belongs to a single person or family, and they alone may decide about it. **Common property**, on the other hand, belongs to everyone in a group together. Everyone may use it, but everyone is also responsible for it. The word **communism** comes from the Latin “communis”, meaning “shared”. In communism, many things are meant to belong to everyone together.

Switzerland has had the **Allmend** since the Middle Ages. These are meadows, pastures or forests that the people of a village use together. In the past, farmers drove their cattle together onto the common pasture. In many municipalities such land is still managed today by **corporations**. Alpine pastures are also often used jointly.

A **cooperative** is a business that belongs jointly to its members. Usually each member has one vote, no matter how much money they have put in. In Switzerland many housing cooperatives and farming businesses are organised in this way. The big retailers **Migros** and **Coop** are also cooperatives.

**Karl Marx** and **Friedrich Engels** wanted no one to own a factory on their own any more. Private ownership of factories and machines was to be abolished. In the **Soviet Union** factories and farms were handed over to the **state**, which then made the decisions about them. Many farming families had to give up their fields and work in large collective farms, the **kolkhozes**.

The first **kibbutzim** were founded in Israel at the beginning of the 20th century. In a **kibbutz** people lived and worked together and shared their possessions. In the past almost everything there belonged to everyone together, even clothes. Today many kibbutzim are organised less strictly, and members have more property of their own.

gewusst: The Allmend in Bern and the Allmend in Zurich still recall the old common land in their names.
A member of a cooperative is called a cooperative member, in German “Genossenschafter” or “Genossenschafterin”.

teile.einleitung: In a popular vote, the voters decide directly on an issue. In Switzerland, the people can go to the polls about four times a year and vote on laws, constitutional amendments and popular initiatives. This is the core of direct democracy.
wichtigste: In a popular vote, the people decide directly on a question.
The question being voted on is called a proposal.
As a rule, four voting dates are planned each year.
If more people say yes than no, the proposal is accepted.
A proposal that is turned down is rejected.
Popular initiatives need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
For a popular initiative, you collect 100,000 signatures in 18 months.
Every change to the Federal Constitution goes to the people through the mandatory referendum.

abschnitte.text: In a **popular vote**, the voters say yes or no to a question. This question is called a **proposal**. If you tick or write yes for a proposal, you agree to it. If more people say yes than no, the proposal is accepted; otherwise it is turned down, that is rejected.

For federal votes, four dates a year are usually planned, mostly in February or March, May or June, September and November. On one date, several proposals are often decided at the same time. There are also votes in the cantons and municipalities. Voting takes place on a Sunday, but most people vote by post beforehand.

With the **mandatory referendum**, the people must vote, for example on every change to the Federal Constitution. With the optional referendum, there is a vote on a law if 50,000 signatures have been collected. With a **popular initiative**, the people can propose a constitutional amendment themselves. This needs 100,000 signatures, which must be collected within 18 months.

abschnitte.titel: Majority of the people and of the cantons
abschnitte.text: A **majority of the people** means that the majority of all voters in Switzerland say yes. For constitutional amendments and popular initiatives, a majority of the cantons is also needed. In total there are 23 cantonal votes. A popular initiative is only accepted if it wins both a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.

Sometimes parliament puts a **direct counter-proposal** against a popular initiative. This is an alternative to the initiative, which is voted on at the same time. You may say yes to both and use a deciding question to state which version you would prefer. That way the people can choose between two solutions.

Before every vote, all voters receive a **voting booklet** with the Federal Council's explanations. It contains the arguments of supporters and opponents. Newspapers, radio, television and posters also report on the proposals. Since 1848, Switzerland has voted on more than 600 federal proposals.

begriffe.erklaerung: The question that is being voted on.
A majority of all voters in the whole of Switzerland.
A majority of the cantons.
To turn down a proposal.
Parliament's alternative to a popular initiative.

gewusst: Switzerland holds more national popular votes than almost any other country in the world.
Only a small share of all popular initiatives are accepted by the people; most fail.
The first federal popular initiative to be accepted, in 1893, was the ban on kosher slaughter without stunning.

teile.einleitung: When lots of people want the same thing, some order is needed. In a **queue**, everyone takes their turn. It is a simple rule that is fair for everyone.
wichtigste: In a queue, everyone waits one behind the other.
Whoever comes last joins the back.
Whoever was there first goes first.
Pushing in is unfair.
When playing, you wait until it is your turn.
On the bus, you let other people get off first.

abschnitte.text: At the kiosk, at the till or at the ski lift there are often lots of people. Then a **queue** forms. Whoever comes last joins **the back**. Whoever was there first goes first. Almost everyone knows this rule, and it applies equally to everyone.

The order in which people arrive is **fair**. Nobody is favoured, no matter how big, strong or important they are. Anyone who sneaks in at the front is **pushing in**. That is unfair, because the others have been waiting longer. It annoys the people in the queue. Shared rules make sure that living together stays peaceful.

There is an order in **board games** too. Only one person has their go at a time. The others wait patiently until it is their turn. On the playground, the rule for the **slide** is: one after the other. That way nobody bumps into each other and nobody gets hurt.

Waiting can take a long time. With **patience**, you stay calm until it is your turn. On the **bus** or train there is a special rule: first the people who want to get off get off. Then the new passengers get on. That way it is quicker for everyone. Sometimes, out of consideration, you also let someone go ahead of you, for example a person with a walking stick.

gewusst: At some counters you take a number, so the order stays clear even without a queue.
Computers also often work through tasks one after another; this is called a queue too.

teile.einleitung: The Gulag was a huge system of prison and labour camps in the Soviet Union. Millions of people had to do forced labour there in terrible conditions, often in freezing cold in Siberia. Many of them had committed no crime but were simply seen as opponents of the government.
wichtigste: The Gulag was a system of prison and labour camps in the Soviet Union.
The word is a Russian abbreviation for Main Administration of Camps.
The Gulag was at its worst under Joseph Stalin, from the 1930s to the early 1950s.
Millions of prisoners had to build canals, railway lines and mines.
Many camps were in very cold, remote areas such as Siberia or Kolyma.
Hunger, cold and hard work led to the deaths of a great many prisoners.
The writer Alexander Solzhenitsyn made the Gulag known around the world.

abschnitte.text: The word **Gulag** is an abbreviation from Russian and means **Main Administration of Camps**. From 1930 this authority ran hundreds of camps throughout the Soviet Union. There were already camps soon after the revolution, for example from 1923 on the **Solovetsky Islands** in the White Sea. Today the word Gulag is used generally for the whole camp system.

abschnitte.titel: Who was sent to the Gulag?
abschnitte.text: It was not only criminals who were sent to the camps, but also a great many **political prisoners**. Even a joke about Stalin, a visit abroad or a false accusation by neighbours could be enough. Peasants who resisted collectivisation and whole ethnic groups were also deported. Experts estimate that altogether around 18 million people passed through the camps.

abschnitte.titel: Life and work in the camps
abschnitte.text: The prisoners had to do **forced labour**, for example felling trees, mining gold or building railway lines. One well-known project was the **White Sea-Baltic Canal**, which was dug almost entirely with shovels and wheelbarrows. The camps were often in freezing regions such as **Kolyma** or Vorkuta, where it could reach minus 40 degrees in winter. There was too little food and warm clothing, so more than a million people died there.

After Stalin's death in March **1953**, many prisoners were released in an amnesty. In 1956 the new party leader Nikita Khrushchev criticised Stalin's crimes. After that the large camp system was reduced, and the Gulag authority was dissolved in 1960. But there were still political prisoners in the Soviet Union until the 1980s.

The writer **Alexander Solzhenitsyn** spent eight years in the camps himself and described everyday life there in his books. His work **The Gulag Archipelago** was published in the West in 1973 and made the camps known all over the world. For decades the Russian organisation **Memorial** collected the names and stories of the victims. It was banned in Russia in 2021 and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.

begriffe.erklaerung: Work that people have to do against their will and without fair pay.
A person who is locked up because they think differently from the government.
When the state cancels the sentences of many prisoners at once.
A group of islands; Solzhenitsyn compared the many camps to islands.

gewusst: Alexander Solzhenitsyn received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970.
The road through the Kolyma region is often called the Road of Bones, because many prisoners died building it.
After he was expelled from the Soviet Union in 1974, Solzhenitsyn first lived in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: FRELIMO is a party in Mozambique in south-east Africa. It began as a liberation movement against Portuguese colonial rule and has governed the country since independence in 1975.
wichtigste: FRELIMO was founded in 1962 in Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.
Its first president was Eduardo Mondlane, who was killed by a parcel bomb in 1969.
On 25 June 1975 Mozambique became independent, and Samora Machel became its first president.
From 1977 to 1992 there was a civil war between the FRELIMO government and RENAMO.
The peace treaty was signed in Rome in 1992.
In 1989 FRELIMO gave up Marxism-Leninism.

abschnitte.text: For a long time Mozambique was a **colony** of Portugal, which means the country was ruled by Portugal. In 1962 several groups in neighbouring Tanzania joined together to form **FRELIMO**. The name is an abbreviation of “Mozambique Liberation Front” in Portuguese. It was founded in **Dar es Salaam**. From 1964 FRELIMO waged an armed struggle against the colonial power.

The first president of FRELIMO was **Eduardo Mondlane**. He had been taught at schools of the **Swiss Mission** in Mozambique and later studied in the USA. Mondlane led the movement until 1969. In February 1969 he died in Dar es Salaam when a parcel bomb hidden in a book exploded. Those responsible were never clearly identified.

In 1974 the **Carnation Revolution** in Portugal overthrew the dictatorship. The new government wanted to release the colonies. On **25 June 1975** Mozambique became independent, and **Samora Machel** became its first president. FRELIMO became the state party and organised the country according to **Marxism-Leninism**, that is, the doctrine of the Soviet Union. At first other parties were not allowed.

From 1977 the government fought against the rebel movement **RENAMO**. It was supported first by Rhodesia and later by South Africa. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and destroyed many villages. In 1986 Samora Machel died in a plane crash in South Africa; the cause is still disputed today. In October 1992 the peace treaty was signed in **Rome**, brokered mainly by the Catholic Community of Sant'Egidio.

In 1989 FRELIMO gave up Marxism-Leninism as its guiding principle. In 1990 Mozambique got a new constitution with a **multi-party system**. In 1994 the first free elections took place, and FRELIMO won them. Since then it has formed the government, and RENAMO is the largest opposition party.

gewusst: The Swiss Mission, at whose schools Mondlane studied, was a missionary society from French-speaking Switzerland.
Independence Day on 25 June is a national holiday in Mozambique.

teile.einleitung: Who clears the snow, mends the roads and mows the grass in the park? In many municipalities it is the **works depot** (Werkhof). It makes sure that roads, squares and facilities are in good order.
wichtigste: The works depot is a municipal service for roads and facilities.
Vehicles, tools and materials are kept there.
Before winter, the works depot stores a lot of road salt.
In summer it looks after parks and green spaces.
It mends roads and repairs park benches.
Orange clothing makes sure the workers are easy to see.

abschnitte.text: The **works depot** is a municipal service. Vehicles, machines, tools and materials are kept there. From there, the staff look after **municipal roads**, squares, parks and facilities. The municipality is responsible for municipal roads. That is why small damage such as potholes is often repaired by the works depot staff. They also put up new **road signs**.
