To fight black ice, the municipality needs a lot of **road salt**. The works depot stores it in silos or sheds before winter. When it snows, the staff go out with snowploughs and gritters. After a storm, they clear away branches and stones. That way everyone can drive and walk safely again.

In summer the works depot looks after **parks** and green spaces. The staff mow the grass and cut hedges. They repair **park benches**, fountains and play equipment when something is broken. For village festivals, they often provide tables, benches and barriers and clear them away again afterwards.

Many works depot employees have done the apprenticeship as a **facilities maintenance specialist**, in the public works branch. On the road they often wear **orange** clothing. Orange is a warning colour and is very noticeable. That way drivers see the workers in good time. Their work is important, even if people often hardly notice it.

gewusst: In larger towns and cities, the works depot often has a different name, such as the civil engineering office or road inspectorate.
Many works depots also work at night in winter so that the roads are clear by morning.

teile.einleitung: The August Coup was an attempt by communist hardliners to seize power in Moscow in August 1991. They wanted to remove Mikhail Gorbachev from power and stop his reforms. After only three days the coup failed.
wichtigste: The coup lasted from 19 to 21 August 1991.
The plotters called themselves the “State Committee on the State of Emergency”.
Gorbachev was held at his holiday residence in Foros in Crimea.
The plotters wanted to prevent the new Union Treaty.
Boris Yeltsin led the resistance from the White House in Moscow.
The ballet “Swan Lake” was shown again and again on television.
After the coup failed, the break-up of the Soviet Union speeded up.

abschnitte.text: Mikhail Gorbachev wanted to renew the Soviet Union through reforms. A **new Union Treaty** was to give the republics much more independence. It was to be signed on **20 August 1991**. Communist **hardliners** saw this as the end of the Soviet Union. That is why they wanted to prevent the signing by any means.

On **19 August 1991**, eight senior officials declared a state of emergency. They included the vice-president and the head of the **KGB** secret service. They called themselves the **State Committee on the State of Emergency**. Gorbachev was on holiday in **Foros** in Crimea and was cut off from the outside world there. Instead of the news, television showed Tchaikovsky's ballet **“Swan Lake”** for hours.

The Russian president **Boris Yeltsin** opposed the plotters. In front of the **White House**, the seat of the Russian parliament, he climbed onto a tank and called for resistance. Tens of thousands of people built barricades to protect the building. Many soldiers refused to act against the people. During the night of 20 to 21 August, **three young men** were killed in a confrontation with armoured vehicles.

On **21 August 1991**, the coup collapsed. Gorbachev returned to Moscow, but his power was weakened. Yeltsin was now the strong man. The **Communist Party** lost its power, and many Soviet republics declared their independence. By the end of 1991, the **Soviet Union** no longer existed.

gewusst: After the coup, the three people who died were honoured as **Heroes of the Soviet Union**.
Many people in Russia still associate the ballet “Swan Lake” with the coup today.

teile.einleitung: Many Swiss blocks of flats have a shared **laundry room**. All the tenants share the machines. For this to work, rules and consideration are needed.
wichtigste: You wash your laundry in the laundry room.
The laundry room is often in the basement.
The laundry rota shows who may do their washing when.
You only do your washing on your own laundry day.
A “Tumbler” is a tumble dryer.
After washing, you leave the laundry room clean.

abschnitte.text: A **laundry room** is a room for washing laundry. It is often in the **basement** or on the ground floor, where there is room for the big machines. There is a washing machine, often a **tumble dryer** and sometimes a drying room. All the tenants in the building may use it. In Switzerland this is normal in many blocks of flats.

Because many families share the laundry room, there is a **laundry rota**. It shows who may do their washing on which day or at what time. On their own **laundry day**, the laundry room belongs to one particular household. Anyone who does their washing on someone else's laundry day takes away that person's time. The rules are often in the **house rules**.

A **Tumbler** is a tumble dryer. In Switzerland people usually call it a Tumbler. After each use, you clean the **lint filter**. Small bits of fluff from the laundry collect there. Without electricity, laundry dries in the air on the **washing line**. That saves energy.

Anyone who leaves the laundry room **clean and tidy** shows consideration for the next person. That includes taking your own laundry away on time. You also give the machines a quick wipe. That way there are fewer arguments in the building. The laundry room is a place where you practise **living together** on a small scale.

gewusst: Arguments about the laundry room are so well known in Switzerland that newspapers and books often write about them.
Newer flats often have their own washing machine inside the flat.

teile.einleitung: The Hitler-Stalin Pact was a treaty between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. It was signed on 23 August 1939, a few days before the start of the Second World War. In a secret addition the two dictatorships divided Eastern Europe between them.
wichtigste: The pact was signed in Moscow on 23 August 1939.
It was signed by the foreign ministers Ribbentrop and Molotov.
Officially it was a non-aggression pact.
In the secret additional protocol, Eastern Europe was divided into spheres of interest.
In September 1939 first Germany and then the Soviet Union attacked Poland.
With Operation Barbarossa, Hitler broke the pact on 22 June 1941.

abschnitte.text: Nazis and communists were bitter enemies. So the world was all the more surprised when a treaty between the two states was signed in Moscow on **23 August 1939**. Foreign Minister **Joachim von Ribbentrop** signed for Germany and **Vyacheslav Molotov** for the Soviet Union. That is why the treaty is also called the **Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact**. Officially it was a **non-aggression pact**: both promised not to attack each other.

The treaty included a **secret additional protocol**. In it Germany and the Soviet Union divided Eastern Europe into **spheres of interest**. In the Boundary and Friendship Treaty of September 1939, **Lithuania** was assigned to the Soviet side, and in return Germany received Polish territory. The Soviet Union denied that the protocol existed until 1989.

On **1 September 1939** Germany attacked **Poland**, and this started the Second World War. On 17 September the Red Army marched in from the east. Poland was divided between the two states. In 1940 the Soviet secret police, the NKVD, killed thousands of Polish prisoners, many of them in the forest of **Katyn**. The Soviet Union only admitted this crime in 1990.

The Baltic states of **Estonia**, **Latvia** and **Lithuania** had been assigned to the Soviet Union. In 1940 they were occupied and incorporated as Soviet republics. The pact also included an **economic agreement**. The Soviet Union supplied raw materials such as oil and grain and in return received machines and industrial goods.

On **22 June 1941** the German armed forces attacked the Soviet Union without a declaration of war. This attack was called **Operation Barbarossa**. Stalin had not taken warnings about it seriously. With that the pact was broken, and from then on the Soviet Union fought on the side of the Allies against Germany.

gewusst: On 23 August 1989, exactly 50 years after the pact, around two million people formed a human chain right across Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. It is called the “Baltic Way”.
In the EU, 23 August is a day of remembrance for the victims of dictatorships.

tw17pbf.t: Amendments to the United States Constitution

teile.einleitung: The Constitution of the United States has been in force since 1789. Since then it has been added to with amendments. Today there are 27 such amendments.
wichtigste: The US Constitution has 27 amendments (as of 2025); the last was added in 1992.
The first ten amendments are called the Bill of Rights and protect fundamental rights.
The 14th Amendment of 1868 guarantees citizenship to everyone born in the USA.
The 19th Amendment has given women the right to vote since 1920.
The 21st Amendment ended Prohibition in 1933.
A new amendment needs the approval of three quarters of the states, that is 38.

abschnitte.text: The US Constitution is not rewritten but added to with **amendments**. The procedure is set out in **Article V**. First, **two thirds** of both chambers of Congress must accept a proposal. Then **three quarters of the states** must agree, which with 50 states means 38. Because this hurdle is so high, most proposals have failed. In Switzerland, by contrast, the people and the cantons decide on a constitutional amendment at the ballot box.

The first ten amendments are called the **Bill of Rights**. They came into force in 1791 and protect important **fundamental rights**. The 1st Amendment, for example, guarantees freedom of speech, of the press and of religion. Other articles protect people accused in court. These rights are still the basis of many important judgements today.

After the **Civil War**, three important amendments were added. The 13th abolished **slavery** in 1865. The **14th Amendment** of 1868 guarantees **citizenship** to everyone born in the USA and equal protection under the law. This so-called **Equal Protection Clause** is still the basis of many judgements on civil rights today. In 1913 the **17th Amendment** introduced the direct election of senators by the people. Before that, the state parliaments elected them.

abschnitte.titel: The right to vote for more people
abschnitte.text: Since **1920**, the **19th Amendment** has guaranteed women the right to vote. For comparison: in Switzerland, women only received the right to vote at federal level in **1971**. In 1971 the **26th Amendment** lowered the voting age to **18**. One argument was that 18-year-olds had to fight in the Vietnam War but were not allowed to vote.

The **18th Amendment** introduced **Prohibition**, a ban on alcohol that came into force in 1920. The **21st Amendment** lifted it again in 1933. So far it is the only one that repeals an earlier amendment. The **27th Amendment** was proposed as early as 1789 but only ratified in 1992. It states that increases in pay for members of Congress only apply after the next election.

gewusst: More than 200 years passed between the proposal and the adoption of the 27th Amendment.
The late adoption was set off by a student who started a campaign in the 1980s.

teile.einleitung: Before an election, parties and candidates try to win votes. This period is called the **election campaign**. In German it is called “Wahlkampf”, literally “election fight”, but the fight here means a peaceful contest of ideas.
wichtigste: In an election campaign, parties try to convince as many people as possible.
Posters, leaflets, adverts and street stalls are typical.
At panel discussions, you can compare the candidates' views.
Smartvote shows which candidates match your own views.
Many candidates now also campaign on social media.
A fair election campaign is respectful and honest.

abschnitte.text: During an election campaign you see **posters** everywhere. Parties hand out **leaflets**, small pieces of paper with information. At a **street stall**, party members stand at a table at the market or in a square. They hand out material and talk to passers-by. There you can also meet candidates in person and ask questions.

At a **panel discussion**, several candidates sit at the front. They answer questions from the audience and debate with each other. A well-known aid in Switzerland is **Smartvote**. There you answer questions on political topics. Afterwards you can see which candidates think in a similar way.

Many candidates now present themselves with videos and pictures on **social media**. That way they also reach young people. Before the election, the media often publish **opinion polls**. A few thousand people are asked their opinion. A poll shows the general mood, but the real result can turn out differently.

Posters, leaflets and adverts have to be paid for. That is why an election campaign costs **a lot of money**. The money comes from the parties, from the candidates themselves and from supporters. Money that is given voluntarily is called a **donation**. Since 2022, rules have applied at federal level requiring large donations and campaign budgets to be disclosed.

During an election campaign you may criticise other opinions. But you should stay **respectful** and tell the truth. Personal insults damage trust in politics. After the election, those elected often have to work with their former opponents. That is another reason why a **fair** campaign is worthwhile.

gewusst: Smartvote has existed since the National Council elections of 2003.
On posters and leaflets, parties usually use their own colours, so that people recognise them quickly.

tx48crw.t: Purpose article of the Swiss Confederation

teile.einleitung: The purpose article is Article 2 of the Federal Constitution. It describes what the Swiss Confederation exists for. It sets out the state's major aims, from freedom to the environment.
wichtigste: The purpose of the Confederation is set out in Article 2 of the Federal Constitution.
First of all, it protects the freedom and rights of the people.
It safeguards the independence and security of the country.
It promotes the common welfare, sustainable development, inner cohesion and cultural diversity.
It ensures the greatest possible equality of opportunity.
It works for the natural foundations of life and for a peaceful and just international order.

abschnitte.text: Today's **Federal Constitution** has applied since 2000. Its **Article 2** is titled “Aims”. In four paragraphs it describes what the state exists for. The first paragraph reads: the Swiss Confederation protects the **freedom and rights of the people** and safeguards the **independence** and **security** of the country. Neutrality is mentioned elsewhere in the constitution.

The second paragraph names the **common welfare**. Welfare means wellbeing, in other words a good life for everyone in the country. Then there is **sustainable development**: today's needs should be met without destroying the chances of future generations. Because Switzerland has several languages and cultures, the Confederation should also promote **inner cohesion** and **cultural diversity**.

The third paragraph says that the Confederation ensures the **greatest possible equality of opportunity** among its citizens. Everyone should have similar opportunities to shape their lives. An important example is **education**: every child is entitled to sufficient and free basic schooling. The words “greatest possible” show that complete equality cannot always be achieved.

The fourth paragraph turns to nature and the world. The Confederation is committed to the **long-term preservation of the natural foundations of life**, that is water, soil, air and biodiversity. It is also committed to a **peaceful and just international order**. With that, the purpose article ends. It does not give individual rights but sets aims that the Confederation and the authorities follow.

gewusst: The Federal Constitution begins with the words “In the name of Almighty God!”.
The old Federal Constitution of 1874 also set out the purpose of the Confederation in Article 2, including independence and the common welfare.

teile.einleitung: Che Guevara was a revolutionary from Argentina who led the Cuban Revolution together with Fidel Castro. His picture in a beret is one of the best-known photos in the world. To this day, some people revere him and others criticise him for his violence.
wichtigste: Che Guevara supported Fidel Castro in the revolution in Cuba.
His real name was Ernesto Guevara, and he was born in Argentina in 1928.
He had studied medicine and was a trained doctor.
In 1959 the revolutionaries won in Cuba, and Guevara then became a minister.
In 1967 he was captured and killed in Bolivia.
A photo by Alberto Korda made him world-famous.
His role is controversial, because he was also responsible for executions.

abschnitte.text: **Ernesto Guevara** was born on 14 June 1928 in Rosario in **Argentina**. As a child he suffered from severe asthma but still did a lot of sport. He studied medicine in Buenos Aires and became a doctor. He got the nickname **Che** because Argentinians often use this word to address people, rather like “hey, you”. He was a convinced Marxist and wanted to change Latin America through a revolution.

As a young man, Guevara travelled through South America on a motorbike with his friend Alberto Granado. On the way he saw a lot of poverty, illness and exploitation. These experiences strongly shaped his political views. He published a **travel diary**, which was later made into a film. In Guatemala in 1954 he witnessed the overthrow of a government in which the USA was involved.

In Mexico in 1955, Guevara met the Cuban **Fidel Castro**. At the end of 1956 they landed in Cuba with about 80 fighters on the boat **Granma**. From the mountains of the Sierra Maestra they waged a **guerrilla war** against the dictator Fulgencio Batista. Guevara became one of the most important commanders, especially in the battle for the city of Santa Clara. On 1 January 1959 Batista fled, and the revolutionaries took power.

After the revolution, Guevara ran a prison in which many supporters of the old regime were **executed**. Later he was president of the national bank and minister of industry. He travelled around the world as Cuba's representative and spoke at the UN in New York in 1964. His attempts to rebuild the economy quickly had little success. In 1965 he left Cuba to support revolutions elsewhere.

Guevara fought first in the Congo and then in **Bolivia**, where he found hardly any support. On 8 October 1967 he was captured by Bolivian soldiers and shot on 9 October. His remains were brought to Cuba in 1997 and buried in Santa Clara. The photo **Guerrillero Heroico**, taken by Alberto Korda in 1960, can be seen on countless T-shirts and posters. For many he is a symbol of rebellion, while others see him as a violent fighter who had opponents killed.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who wants to change a government by overthrowing it.
A way of fighting in small, mobile groups, often from mountains or forests.
A ruler who governs alone and without free elections.
A follower of the ideas of Karl Marx.

gewusst: Che Guevara was a keen chess player and rugby player.
Alberto Korda's photo is regarded as one of the most reproduced images in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Fall of Saigon was the capture of the South Vietnamese capital, Saigon, by North Vietnamese troops on 30 April 1975. It ended the long Vietnam War with a victory for the communists. Shortly before, thousands of people fled the city in a dramatic helicopter rescue operation.
wichtigste: The Fall of Saigon happened on 30 April 1975.
It ended the Vietnam War with victory for the North Vietnamese communists.
American combat troops had already left Vietnam in 1973.
In Operation Frequent Wind, thousands of people were flown out by helicopter at the last minute.
A North Vietnamese tank broke through the gate of the Presidential Palace.
In 1976 Vietnam was united as a single communist state.
Saigon was then renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

abschnitte.text: After the end of French colonial rule, Vietnam was divided into two parts in **1954**. In the north the communists ruled under **Ho Chi Minh**; in the south there was a government supported by the USA. Soon communist troops and rebels, the **Viet Cong**, were fighting against the south. From the mid-1960s the USA sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers to Vietnam.

The war cost a great many lives and was becoming more and more controversial in the USA too. In January **1973** a peace agreement was signed in Paris. The American combat troops then withdrew, but the fighting between north and south went on. Without help from the USA, the South Vietnamese army grew weaker and weaker.

At the beginning of 1975 North Vietnam launched a large offensive and captured one city after another within a few weeks. In April the troops stood outside **Saigon**. On the morning of **30 April 1975** tanks rolled into the city, and one of them broke through the gate of the **Presidential Palace**. The South Vietnamese president Duong Van Minh announced the surrender.

In the last two days before the fall, American helicopters flew thousands of people out of Saigon in **Operation Frequent Wind**. Among other places, they took off from the roof of the American embassy and carried people to ships at sea. It was one of the largest helicopter rescue operations in history. However, many South Vietnamese who wanted to flee had to stay behind.

On 2 July **1976** Vietnam was reunited as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, and Saigon was renamed **Ho Chi Minh City**. Many supporters of the old government were sent to re-education camps. In the following years hundreds of thousands fled across the sea in small boats as **boat people**, and some found a new home in Switzerland. In Vietnam 30 April is a public holiday today, Reunification Day.

teile.einleitung: Bourgeoisie is a French word and roughly means the middle class or citizenry. For Karl Marx it refers to the class that owns factories, machines and raw materials. Opposite it stands the proletariat, the working class.
wichtigste: The word “bourgeoisie” comes from French.
In German it is roughly called the Bürgertum, the citizenry or middle class.
Before the rise of the middle class, power lay mainly with the nobility.
The French Revolution from 1789 strengthened the middle class.
For Marx, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production.
Marx called the conflict between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat class struggle.

abschnitte.text: Originally the word **bourgeoisie** referred to the inhabitants of a town, that is the **citizens**. In the Middle Ages and the early modern period, kings and the **nobility** controlled land and politics. With trade, crafts and later industry, rich citizens became more and more important. In the 19th century the word spread throughout Europe as a technical term.

In the **French Revolution** from 1789, the old privileges of the nobility were abolished. **Human rights** were declared. The middle class became the leading force in the state and the economy. In Switzerland, too, liberal citizens shaped the founding of the **federal state** of 1848.

**Means of production** are everything you need to make goods: factories, machines and raw materials. According to **Karl Marx**, they belong to the bourgeoisie. The workers own no means of production. They have to sell their labour for wages. That is why, for Marx, the bourgeoisie was the **ruling class** under capitalism.

Under **capitalism**, companies belong to private owners, and prices are set on the market. According to Marx, a business owner has to make as much **profit** as possible in order to survive in competition. Marx saw history as a series of **class struggles**. Under capitalism, he said, the bourgeoisie and the **proletariat** face each other. Supporters of capitalism, on the other hand, stress that competition creates prosperity and new ideas.

gewusst: In the “Communist Manifesto” of 1848, Marx and Engels describe the bourgeoisie as a class that has greatly changed the world.
In Swiss politics, people still speak of **“bürgerliche” parties** (centre-right parties) today.

teile.einleitung: From 1922 to 1991, the Soviet Union was the largest state in the world and was ruled by the Communist Party. In 1991 it broke up within a few months into 15 independent states. This also ended the Cold War between East and West.
wichtigste: The Soviet Union was officially dissolved in 1991.
15 independent states emerged from it, including Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan.
From 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev tried to modernise the country with reforms.
A failed coup in August 1991 sped up the break-up.
On 25 December 1991, Gorbachev resigned as president.
Russia took over the Soviet Union's seat on the UN Security Council.
With the end of the Soviet Union, the Cold War also ended.

abschnitte.text: The **Soviet Union**, abbreviated USSR, was founded in 1922 and consisted of 15 republics. It stretched from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific and was the largest state on Earth by area. It was ruled by the **Communist Party**; other parties were banned. Its capital was Moscow. In the **Cold War**, the Soviet Union was the rival of the USA.

From 1985, **Mikhail Gorbachev** led the Soviet Union. The economy was working badly, and many shops lacked goods. Gorbachev wanted to renew the country with **glasnost**, meaning openness, and **perestroika**, meaning restructuring. People were now allowed to say what they thought more freely. As a result, however, many problems and the wish for independence also came out into the open.

The Baltic republics of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were the first to want independence. In **August 1991**, hardliners from the party, the army and the secret service tried to overthrow Gorbachev. The coup failed after three days, mainly because **Boris Yeltsin**, the president of Russia, organised resistance in Moscow. After that, one republic after another declared its independence. In December 1991, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus agreed to dissolve the Soviet Union.

On **25 December 1991**, Gorbachev resigned as president of the Soviet Union. That same evening, the red Soviet flag was lowered over the Moscow **Kremlin** and the Russian flag was raised. The next day, the Soviet Union officially declared itself dissolved. Most of the former republics joined together loosely in the **CIS**, the Commonwealth of Independent States. Russia took over the nuclear weapons and the seat on the UN Security Council.

For many people in the successor states, the 1990s were a difficult time of poverty and high inflation. The three Baltic states joined the **EU** and NATO in 2004. Later there were conflicts and wars between Russia and some former republics, such as Ukraine and Georgia. The dissolution of the Soviet Union is regarded as one of the most important events of the 20th century. Switzerland, too, established diplomatic relations with the new states.
